HENRY ,CHRISTIAN CLAUSEN
GRAND MASTER

HENRY CHRISTIAN CLAUSEN
Grand Master
1954~1955

Henry Christian Clausen, eight-ninth Grand Master of the Grap.d
Lodge of California, ended an active and constructive year in that office when he installed his successor October 28, 1955. The record of
his travels serving the Craft, as recorded in these Proceedings, 'offers
ample evidence that the Office of Grand Master is an exacting one and
places great demands upon the time and talents of. one elected to that
position.
Brother Clausen is. a native San Franciscan, having been born in the
City by the Golden Gate June 30, 1905. He attended the public schools
in the elementary, secondary and high school divisions. Death of his
father intercepted his -high school attendance and threw upon Brother
Clausen's shoulders the role of breadwinner for himself, his mother and
sisters. He completed his high school, college and law education at night,
while employed during the .day. He was admitted to the bar and embarked upon a private law practice in 1927. His practice has been a distinguished one, including a term as Assistant United States Attorney
for the Northern District of California. When the Golden Gate Bridge
was under construction, he served as General Counsel for its Chief Engineer, Joseph B. Strauss.
On July 17, i 926, he married Virginia Palmer, and they have a
splendid family consisting of Henry, Jr., Florian, Donald and Karen.
Raised in Ingleside Lodge No. 630 on May 31, 1935, he rapidly took
an active part in all its affairs. Elected Master, in 1940, Grand Master
Wilson appointed him Grand Orator of the Grand Lodge in which capacity he served until October, 1941. In preparation for the positions
of distinction, which were forseen for him, he was assigned service on
many of ·the important committees of the Grand Lodge, and in 1951 he
was elected Junior Grand Warden. He progressed successively through
the various offices until his election as Grand Master on October 15,
1955.
Brother Clausen has paralleled his Grand Lodge interest with activity in the Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite in which he was coroneted
a Thirty-Third Degree Mason on October 23, 1953. Brother Clausen
was appointed the Deputy for the Scottish Rite in California, succeeding
Past Grand Master Francis V. Keesling, and, at the meeting of the
Supreme Council held in Washington, D. C., in October 1955, he was

elected an active member of the Supreme Council and designated Sovereign Grand Inspector General for California.
During World War II Brother Clausen volunteered his services to
the United States Army and was assigned to the Department of the
Judge Advocate General in Washingt on, D. C. He was appointed a
member of the Special Presidential Appeal Board for spy trials and
afterward s served as a member of the Army Pearl Harbor Board of
Inquiry. Secretary of War Henry L Stimson later appointed him in
charge of the Secretary's personal investigation of the Pearl Harbor
disaster.
Perhaps Brother Clausen's greatest service in civic affairs has been
in behalf of the free publi<: school system of which he is an outspoken
advocate. He has long been identified with free public school education
in San Francisco, and in more recent years he has championed it statewide. He has devoted his time and talents without fee to the protection
of the free public school system and to the preservation of the great principle of separation between church and state, which guarantees the rights
of all but permits no favors to special interests regardless of who or what
they maybe.
All Grand Masters of the Grand Lodge of California are distinquished for some particular trait or contribution, and Henry Christian
Clausen will always be remembered for his sound convictions and his
forthright courage in declaring and defending them.

Most Worshipful Sir:
Pellow Members of the Grand Lodge:
Brethren all:
My text comes from the Book of Psalms i~ whic~ the aspirations of
a great people is recorded in prayer and praise. Chief of these p~alms
· the 23rd which may be summarized as was done by a small child to
is "The Lord is my shepherd, what else could I want!" But a better
saJttmg of it is to be found in the prophecy of Isaiah. the 55th chapter
~d the 6th and 7th verses: "Seek ye the ~rd while he ma! be found,
call ye upon him while he is near: let the wic.ked forsake his way, and
the unrighteous man his thoughts and let him return unto t~e Lord.
and he will have mercy upon him: and to our God, for he Will abundantly pardon."
The function of the chaplain in a regularly constituted Lodge of
Free and Accepted Masons is to conduct the devotions of his Lodge
and bear before the throne of the Heavenly Grace the spiritual..nee~s
of his brethren; "to allure to brighter worlds and lead the way. This
privilege is no small responsibility. Never d_oe~ a. man set. forth ui:ion
this undertaking without being aware of the hm1tations of his humanity,
and of the imperfect tools of language which he must use, not to say.
of the exhaustible resources of his own spirit.
The cruciaJ feature of our troubled world is to be found in its tragic
divisions. We have often dreamed of a world united, but our lab~rs
seem all too inadequate until we remember that all men have a native
capacity to pray. As Carlyle stated in a letter to a friend: "Pr~yer is
and remains the native and deepest impulse of the soul of man. The
fact is that somewhere in every man there is the ca:pacity for worship
and prayer, for the purposeful apprehension o~ <?od. and th~ response
of gratitude and love for Him. Is this not the distinctive quality of man
and the noblest faculty which ·h e possesses?
. In the instructions given in the second degree we are retninded of
the five senses: hearing, seeing, feeling, smelling and tasting. As man
reaches up through the physical to the spiritual, ~e could lean>: n_othing
of ethics without contact with the physical. So 1f there are limits beyond which human investigations and explorations into the unknown
may not go, it is because of the limitations of the five physical se~s.es.
Not even the extension of those senses by the marvelously . sensitive
instruments of science may overcome, in the last analysis, their fundamental limits. Except for one factor----prayerl-th e incredible gathering
of these physical capacities into their noblest use. Prayer becomes.
·
indeed, a sixth and indispensable sixth sense.

Brute beasts hear, see, feel, smell, and taste, as do we. But they
gamer no facts of science, win no truths, formulate no laws through
these senses. More than flve physical senses are necessary to perceive
the relationship between thing and thing and life and life. That factor
is perception, the soul or spirit which differentiates man from all other
living beings. So in Masonry we are elevated from the Boor of the
temple by flve steps of five senses to the more sublime reaches of knowledge. We teach a sensitivity to the Great Architect of the Universe
which is useless until we remember our sixth sense, namely, the capacity to commune with the Father of our spirits. I do not state the case
too strongly when I say that the most important part of any ritual is
the prayer. And for candidates for further light, I am sure that their
moments alone in the presense of Deity, where their audible or silent
prayer is heavy with spiritual yearning, are the most crucial of all.
Brethren, we must clothe that ceremony with devout respect. No rustling of papers at the Secretary's desk. No whispered conversation on
the sidelines. No muffled laughter from the anteroom. Nothing disturbing to the solemnity of this occasion is excusable when a man stands
alone before God and reaches out with his highest and holiest hope
toward the best that we know and has a right to believe that all his
new-found brothers are there to meet with him in the presence of the
·
Most High God.
Prayer is one of our richest privileges. It excels the privileges of
all the other senses, however delightful and rewarding they may be.
Sir Wilfred Grenfell, who robustly served his fellowmen in Labrador
through many hardships and many joys once wrote: "The privilege of
prayer to me is one of the most cherished possessions, because faith
and experience alike convince me that God himself sees and answers,
and his answers I never venture to criticize. It is only my part to ask.
It is entirely his to give or withhold, as he knows best. 1£ it were otherwise, I would not dare to pray at all. In the quiet of the home, in the
heat of life and strife, in the face of death, the privilege of speech with
God is inestimable. I value it more because it calls for nothing the
wayfaring man, though a fool, cannot give--that is, the simplest expression of his simplest desires. When I can neither see, nor hear, nor
speak, still I can pray so that God can hear. When I finally pass through
the valley of the shadow of death, I expect to pass through it in conversation with him."
No man need suspect that he lacks the basis for the exercise of this
privilege. Whatever soul inhabits the body which is yours has access
to God through prayer. Let us not now pause to dwell upon the art of
prayer, although its further cultivation would be of inestimable value
to all of us. Let us just now think only for this moment of what prayer
may mean to us: that desire for a better life which animates us all at
our best moments, that search for the means to improve the social organization of men, that desire to be a full member of an infinite family

which is never ultimately broken. All this is prayer. We must know
that wherever we may be, we are not far from the All-seeing Eye and
th ever loving Heart. "I know not where his islands lift their fronded
pa~ms in air. I only know I cannot drift beyond his love and care."

10

So let us relax our posing and be natural with One who understands
the secret longings of our hearts. No man can deny this privilege to
us since it is God's gift to each one. Perhaps we should accept it
oftener. Perhaps we should remember that He listens more to our
spirits than to our words. Perhaps we have no greater lack than to
neglect this privilege. Here the words of the prophet Isaiah: "Seek
ye the Lord while he may be found: call ye upon him while he is near;
let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts:
and let him return unto the Lord, and he will have mercy upon him: and
to our God. for he will abundantly pardon."
In the early days at the dawn of history, the conquest of a people
was never complete until something was done with the gods and sacred
implements of worship belonging to the conquered people. If these
materials were destroyed or carried away to be derided, spat upon, and
blasphemed, the subjected people would, it was thought, submit the
more readily to their conquerors. They would be powerless, since no
aid could be had from their gods. In early Jewish history there was
some tendency for their several conquerors to believe that the secret
of the Hebrews was to be found in their sacred vessels, their temples,
their scrolls. However, tragic as the result of premeditated destruction
of these sacred possessions might be, this people thoroughly rebuked
their aggressors by an undying faith and the indestructible religion.
Through the voice of the prophets we see them still in communion with
Jehovah. After the long exiles they sought to build a new temple which
they had carried all the time in their hearts in spite of captivity. Here
is the classic picture of a people greatly distressed but not defeated
since their trust was reinforced by their continuous conversation with
the God of their fathers who could not be reduced to images or temples
or books.
When Solomon was ready to dedicate his temple ·h e offered a
priceless prayer. It is recorded that he stood before the altar of the
Lord in the presence of all the congregation of Israel, and spread forth
his hands toward heaven and said, "Lord God of Israel, there is no
God like thee, in heaven above, or on earth beneath, who keepest covenant and mercy with thy servants that walk before thee with all their
heart." Solomon knew full well that even the wondrous temple which he
had built was not to be identified with God for he said, "Behold, the
heaven of ·heavens cannot contain thee; how much less this house that
I have builded. Yet have thou respect unto the prayer of thy servant,
and to his su,pplication, 0 Lord, my God, to hearken unto the cry and
to the prayer, which thy servant prayeth before thee today: that thine

eyes may be open toward this house night and day." The history of
the religions of the world is richer because of this unconque rable insight: that God cannot be vanquishe d nor destroyed .
In our day the ravages of war and the inevitable tensions of postwar
years 'have alike possessed a fiendish threat to man's persistent belief
that the Great Architect of the Universe is also the governor of history.
Men whose insights were limited became fearful that they had lost all
in the swift incursion of social and political upheavals. But shining
ever brighter in the moral firmament has been the fellowship of faith
in temple, in church, in home and in the hearts of men. A renewed interest in the things of the spirit has developed not so much out of our
distress as out of our clearer vision. Now we see with refreshed clarity
that Paul was right when he declared that all things work together
for good to them that love God. We do not minimize the continued
threat to the sources of our power, but we see evidences of renewed
allegiance to human freedom and dignity, and a spiritual earnestnes s
about the deeper meanings of all life.
Along with the other great movements affecting the lives of our
contemporaries, Masonry is having such a resurgenc e of strength as
to give us all cause for rejoicing. Lodges are being multiplied and men
are seeking entrance in numbers heretofore unknown. Churches, too,
are recapturin g the attention of people so that membership and attendance is apparentl y everywhe re increasing. Religious establishments
of every kind along with their multitudinous progeny, social and character building agencies are enjoying expansion and extension. Books
and pamphlets and articles upon spiritual topics were never more
numerous or in demand. But in all of this there needs to be a reorientation beyond these evidential expressions of social solidarity and cooperation, namely, a better understan ding and practice of prayer. I am
serious about this while speaking to you, my brothers in the Masonic
fraternity. A restored prayer life within our lodges would revive the
genius of our craft.
Billy Graham and others who have been speaking to the spiritual
needs of our generation have emphasized this need for prayer. Norman
Vincent Peale has told me that all he has written in his famous book,
The Power of Positive Thinking, is summed up in a question: "Why
.
not try prayer power?" Indeed, why not?
. Critics may d_eride and ask, "Now really, do we need prayer? Or is
it merely an elective in the course of life. an e1ective that appeals to some
and lea:es others cold? Or is it perhaps a delicacy like Sunday dessert,
something for a special occasion? Or is it a kind of first aid to be used
~hen the bleeding is great and you can't get a doctor? Or is it a port
m a storm, a last resort, or final spasm of the human spirit which is
answered only when man is in his extremity and God ·h as at long last
his opportuni ty?

The answer which you and I propound through our fraternal loyalties is unequivocal. We do need prayer and we need it constantly .
It is the essential ingredient which makes life both endurable and happy.
It is like vitamins. It ought to be a part of our daily fare, building us
up in strength and fortifying us against the assault of our enemiesespecially the deadly microbes of fear, doubt, greed and pride. Along
with daily bread, the soul of man needs daily prayer, for only thus will
we have strength to stand up against the forces of destruction.
There is another reason why we stand in constant need of prayer.
It is not only its strengthen ing power we need; but we need its fellowship both with God and with one another. There is no place where we
are so conjoined in natural and satisfying fraternal fellowship than where
we pray together. Many a brother has sought the sanctuary of his
lodge with heavy heart and dispiriting loneliness, almost afraid to enter
the lodge for fear he would be hurt by indifference and coldness again.
Through the prayer, through its mysterious capacity to lift him up into
the presence of the best that we know, he has been able to forget himself. and flnd both God and his brother. Many a brother has suffered
confusion and frustration s. His way was dark and frightful until he
sat in lodge with men who prayed as he prayed. Then he has seen in
greater perspectiv e what he must do. Prayer may not reveal the uncertain future but it will always show us the next step to take toward
the light. Many a brother has feared himself most and has sought the
shelter of the lodge where great moral principles are extolled, and brothers who believe in him have given him the reassuranc e of the fraternity as they have prayed together. His temptations to despair have
often been exchanged for temptations to hope, as he has heard his
chaplain pray that God would so influence our hearts and minds that
we may each one of us practice out of the lodge those great moral duties
which are inculcated in it.
This is not all that prayer does. The same prayer that dispels our
separatene ss, that lights our path toward tomorrow in gladness, that
releases the captives to despair will also enrich us beyond our capacity to
imagine. Prayer shifts attention from worldly and transient occupations to the permanen t constructions of the houses not built with hands,
eternal in the heavens. Prayer releases us from bondage to our possessions which moth and rust corrupt and thieves break in and steal, and
gives us security in heavenly treasure.
All that I have been saying is not new information. It is said by
way of renewed emphasis. And it will take a little time to gain the
superlative benefits of which I have been speaking. Our problem may
be that a postponed development of a prayer life awaits greater freedom and leisure than we have just now. I can sympathiz e with this
problem. Remember the story of the man who could never catch up
with himself and his dream of everything .at last being completed. His

From Washington I flew to London for the Communication of the
United Grand Lodge of England, the mother Grand Lodge of the world
and the site of the inception of speculative Masonry in 1717. I found
this fountain source of all Freemasonry vigorous and carrying out the
fundamental traditions of our Craft. I felt more at home perhaps because the Grand Master, Most Worshipful. The Earl of Scarbrough.
had honored me by appointment as Representative of the United Grand
Lodge of England nearest California, a position formerly filled by our
late beloved Past Grand Master, William Rhodes Hervey. During
the Grand Lodge session I was seated alongside the Grand Master in
the East and received a most cordial and brotherly reception. The business of the Grand Lodge was transacted with dispatch, having undergone screening by efficient officers and committees, including the Board

Masonry in the Islands has its roots deep in an historic past. For
example, Lodge le Progres de l'Oceanie No. 371 was instituted by the
Scottish Rite Supreme Council of France in 1843 by the Deputy Grand
Master, Le Tellier. This was the first Masonic Lodge established in the
Pacific or on the mainland west of the Missouri River! As incorporated
into the California structure today, it retains traces of the original ritual.
In the 1905 organizational transfer, the Grand Lodge of California
granted the Lodge permission to continue conferring the 3° in a manner
similar to the original Scottish Rite French ritual.
Today the Islands comprise four natural districts formed by the
Islands of Oahu, Kauai, Maui and Hawaii. On Oahu there are the
Lodges: Hawaiian No. 21, le Progres de l'Oceanie No. 371. Honolulu
No. 409, Schofield No. 443, and .Pearl Harbor No. 598. On Kauai, the
Lodge Kauai No. 589. On Maui, the Lodge No. 472. And on Hawaii,
the Lodge Kilauea No. 330. There is a combined membership today of
3032.
I was privileged to •b e received officially by the brethren on Oahu in
a joint meeting and by each of the Lodges on the outer Islands in indi~
vidual meetings. Many of the brethren I met have given generously of
their time and performed extraordinary and outstanding service to
Masonry. Your Grand Master expressed to those assembled his deep
and grateful appreciation for their efforts and achievements.
Actually, I think the finest thing about Hawaiian Masonry is the
way it has flowered in a ground fertile with an ever increasing oppor~
tunity to demonstrathe Masonry's universality. Masonry knows no
North, no South, no East, nor West; nor do we draw any arbitrary
lines of exclusion for applicants. Instead, we open wide the portals of
our lodges to all those good men who qualify according to Masonic
standards of acceptance.
Having in mind the potentials for a great confluence of California
and Hawaiian Masonry, whereby each adds to the other its strength
in attainment of the Masonic credo, and based upon my own observa~
tions and a study of reports by my predecessors and other Grand Lodge
officers, I put into operation some means of bringing about additional
growth and strength. I recommend to this Grand Lodge also that the
name and title of our Grand Lodge be changed to "The Most Worshipful
Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the State of California
and Territory of Hawaii," and to this end that Section l, Article I, of
our Constitution be amended accordingly, with permissive abbreviations
in ritualistic and administrative work.
All visitations at home and abroad added much to my information
and to my gallery of Masonic memories. But more important, I found

In my service on the Home Board I was struck by the refusal to
admit to Decoto those old folks who were considered ineligible for
physical reasons. I do not refer to those who may have required hospitalization. I have in mind those who were considered not eligible for
admittance because of physical handicaps. Instead, they may have been
granted outside relief. or cared for in private nursing homes. It always
seemed to me, and I have voiced this belief at our meetings, that if a
private nursing home can care for one of our indigent and handicapped
brethren that we ourselves should be able to do this at Decoto. We
should not pass the buck. I realize that this may require additional facilities and staff, but I feel the Craft of California would supply the
funds for this purpose if they were aware of the need. The Board knows
the problem ( 1953: 103, 1954: 91 ) . Since no concrete proposal has
been made, however, I recommend that a special committee of Grand
Lodge be appointed to study the situation and report at the next Annual
Communication to the end that we make adequate provision at Decoto
for our needy and physically distressed brethren, their wives and widows.
While on the subject of Masonic Charity, I should mention our
concern for the brethren damaged by the recent hurricanes. I extended
to the Grand Masters of the stricken states our sympathy, fraternal interest and offers of aid. It will be recalled that similar messages cheered
those of us who were active in relieving Masonic distress during our
1906 San Francisco fire. Our Past Grand Master Oscar Lawler well
knows the deep sense of gratitude we experienced then, and in point of
truth he ~s alw~ys foremost in reminding us of his availability to help
M~sons ID afflicted areas. The hurricanes caused great disaster but,
while expressing great appreciation, none of the Grand Lodges involved
wanted outside help. They preferred themselves to handle the relief.
Indeed, the Grand Master of New York typically reported: "Our
!rouble will be to induce those who need help to accept it. Our people
ID upstate New York are rugged individualis ts!"

In a true sense the discipline imposed in Masonry means•"to teach."
We could accomplish a great deal if a system of preventive discipline
were devised. A !brother "straying from the straight and narrow path"
could be summoned by a Master or a lodge committee, and an attempt
made to remove the cause of complaint before charges become necessary. I think such a plan of prevention is worthy of trial.
There have been brought to my attention instances in a very few
lodges of that lack of fraternal feeling which has led to sharp discussions. These always catise a Grand Master unnetessary mental anxiety
and concern. I would request. if at all proper, that these brethren "bury
the hatchet." Take as an example that of Joseph when he was ruler of
Egypt and the account of his extreme forbearance and affection towards
his offending brothers. I realize this is a "consummation devoutly to be
wished," but offending brethren would earn my gratitude if they could
bring themselves to a true Masonic embrace.
Other instances. of unnecessary time and worry to a Grand Master,
rare !hut nonetheless acute, occur when lodges fail to maintain our
Masonic standards. A case in point happened within a month after my
installation. Reluctantly and regretfully I arrested the charter of one
lodge until the widespread derelictions were cleared up to my satisfaction. A detailed account is set forth as Exhibit F.

COMMISSION ON REVISION OF Ross DIGEST

The subject of gambling and speciflcally raffles, door prizes, lotteries and bingo games, like Banquo's Ghost, arises from time to time to
plague Grand Masters. They and the Craft generally have disapproved
of these practices.
·
·

The codiflcation and clariflcation of our Masonic laws has become
increasingly a must. I was most pleased, therefore, when the men on
the Committee I appointed for this purpose began to work with vigor.
They have performed a stupendous task. In a short time you should
have in your hands the flrst edition of the California Masonic Code.

Sometimes there may be, in the twilight or fringe zone, activities
which fall short of Penal Code violations. They are thought to be excused as charitable or entertaining. But, in the flnal analysis, they are
vain hopes of getting something by luck or chance, and foreign to the
fundamental purpose of Masonry.

DECISIONS

There are also appended as Exhibit E some 73 decisions. These I
gently refer to the tender mercies of the Committee on Jurisprudence.

To ask any Grand Master to police these borderline cases is unfair
and an imposition on an already crowded schedule. It is bad for everyone. The necessity for technical comparison with recurrent decisions
shows the prevalent misunderstanding, criticism and dissension.
Suffice that Masonry teaches obedience to Civil law, and to avoid
that which in the public mind is associated with gambling. This means
in practice that Masons must set the standard and should obey the spirit
no less than the letter of the law. It is no excuse to point out that other
organizations may indulge in raffles, bingo and door prizes. Our organization does not encourage evasion. We do not say the end justifles the
means. Accordingly, on June 1, 1955, I circulated a general ruling, calling attention to the necessity that we maintain our Masonic standards.

CONDITION OP THE CRAFT

We conferred the degree of Master Mason upon 8,679 members
during the year. This means there has been a healthy membership
growth. The Lodges generally are successful and prospering. There is
prevalent throughout the Craft a spirit of harmony and cooperation. The
enthusiasm that pervades seems to be expanding and growing.
But we are reminded as some wit once said that the only place to
find real peace is in the dictionary. I suppose that is true. To seek absolute peace and harmony in every Lodge would be unrealistic. Sometimes
I wonder whether we have instilled into our Initiates a firm enough
grasp of that vision and purpose which is so peculiar to Masonry.
The foundations of Masonry must be sound if we are to build toward moral. social and intellectual improvement. As we demonstrate
Masonry in our lives, so will we be judged by the world. A candidate
must learn that the designs upon the trestleboard, the rituals and the
ceremonies, the identifications upon lapels, rings, and watch chains, the
numbers of brethren, the moneys in treasuries, yes, even the magnificence of temples and manifestations of historic glories-all are important
only as they contribute to good thoughts and deeds. The newcomer to

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

25

our ranks must first and foremost reflect credit upon our fraternity. Let
us !be sure we make Masons in the true sense of that term.
The subject of stimulating attendance at lodges is recurrent. In my
opinion much success in this commendable campaign can be achieved
simply by closing lodge early. Many members must leave for work
early in the morning. Plan the meetings well in advance, conduct them
with dispatch, keep open discussion within appropriate bounds, make
timely decisions and close before ten o'clock. This leaves a period for
a short fellowship session. You will find these simple steps work like
magic in building interested attendance and a real inducement to come
again. The Master who does this will earn his popularity.
On the over-all scene, I report gladly that numbered among our
653 lodges and 224,424 members, there are many, many Masonsgood and true-who do exemplify in their daily work and lives the
teachings of Masonry in the highest sense. They are an abiding influence for good. They further the great cause of our public schools, the
expanding heart of fraternal benevolence, the laudable uplift of humanity and the diffusion of that light which dispels darkness. They have
made up their minds that the winds of freedom will continue to sweep
over this land. They confirm that the summit of our Masonic credo is
the Fatherhood of God and the Brotherhood of Man.

GooD CITIZENSHIP

You live in a land of great promise. California bids fair to exceed
in population even the most enthusiastic Chamber of Commerce prediction. Our fertile valleys, renowned climate and varied industries have
induced the greatest mass migration in modern history. We now number some thirteen million people. Newcomers are pouring across our
borders lby more than one thousand a day. A decade hence we shall
total at that rate seventeen million souls and thus become the nation's
greatest state. In keeping with our fantastic growth, last fall we had
more children in our public schools than any other state, although New
York's ·population is almost a third greater.
This influx is by those of varying backgrounds and from every part
of the earth. As a result, we are a frontier of experimentation and innovation. We are a dynamo of creative invention. And so in California
we are ever moving toward better ways of living and working.
This age of transition has brought a change also in the Masonic
mind. The Craft inquires into the mystery of its own being. We intuitively sense that we have been designed for other and more important
and higher work than yet has been revealed or accomplished. This is
certain: Our brethren are not content with mere formalities. They are
eager to join a forward march to a more glorious Masonic destiny.

27

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

In all this great change there is an even greater challenge. We do
not shirk the challenge. Indeed, it is an exciting time to be alive. We
agree with Emerson:
"If there is any period when one would desire to be born, is
it not in the age of transition: when the old and the new stand
side by side and admit of being compared; when the energies of
all men are searched by fear and hope, and when the historic
glories of the past can be compensated by the rich possibilities of
the future."
And so as we stand at the threshold of this new era there is point in
reminding ourselves of the burning question of our day as brethren did
in the time of our illustrious Masonic forebear, George Washington.
Then, in view of attempts to shackle a free people with the chains of
slavery, the question was whether they should fl.ght for American freedom.
Today the burning question is: Shall we stay American? That is so
because of alien inroads into our American life. Some forces are bent
on injecting the poison of Communism into our body politic. Others are
bent on .breaking the •back,bone of our Constitution. They would tear
down the wall of separation between church and state. To them the
symbolic stars of freedom in our flag mean nothing. They would
necessarily 1blot out all Masonry.

public criticism of Masons being asked to conduct the ceremony. The

The following quotations from the Scottish Rite magazine, "The
New Age," of October, 1955, are most pertinent on the subject of laying
cornerstones of public buildings with Masonic ceremonies. This article
was by ·Brother R. Baker Harris, 33°, Librarian of the House of the
Scottish Rite Temple in Washington, D. C.
"Is it proper and appropriate for the Masonic Fraternity to lay
cornerstones of public buildings? The answer is that it 'has been
considued both proper and appropriate in the United States ever
since the formation of our government in 1789, and for two primary reasons among others:
"1. The Masonic ceremony for laying a cornerstone is not
sectarian, though in its symbolism it appropriately proclaims the
preeminent importance of God in the affairs of mankind.
"2. It is a public ceremony surviving from the practices of the
ancient operative building craft, and its symbolic meaning is
drawn from still more ancient sources.
"In the United States, which, from its foundation, has zealously guarded the principle of religious freedom and the complete
separation of Church and State, the Masonic cornerstone ceremony has been often used in laying the foundation stones of public buildings.
"The cornerstone of the Capital of the United States was laid
with Masonic ceremony under the auspices of the Grand Lodge
of Maryland in 1793, President George Washington participating. A year earlier the cornerstone of 'The President's House,'
now known as The White House, was laid by a Maryland lodge,
Lodge No. 9 of Georgetown.
"Since that time Presidents James K. Polk, Millard Fillmore,
James Buchanan, William McKinley, William H. Taft, Warren
G. Harding, Herbert Hoover and Harry S. Truman have, as
President, participated in Masonic cornerstone or dedication ceremonies. President Franklin D. Roosevelt participated in a Mason-

26

28

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

ic cornerstone laying in 1919 when he was Assistant Secretary of
the Navy. Of the Presidents named, Polk, Fillmore and Hoover
were not themselves Masons, but they acknowledged the appropriateness of the ceremony being conducted by the Masonic
Fraternity.
"To mention only a few of the public buildings, edifices and
monuments in the nation's capital whose cornerstones were laid
with Masonic ceremonies:
"The Capitol of the United States and The White House, as
already mentioned.
"The Smithsonian Institution, May 1, 1947.
"The Extension of the U.S. Capitol, July 4, 1851.
"The House of Representatives Office Building. April 14,
1906.

"In addition, state capitols, post offices and other public buildings in many parts of the United States have cornerstones which
were laid with Masonic ceremonies.
"Recent attempts, therefore. to denominate the Masonic cornerstone as being sectarian are completely without foundation in
historical fact."
And so to all of those whatever presuasion, who prefer to bend their
knee to an alien power and who would force you to do likewise, who
teach hostility toward your most cherished traditions-hostility toward
our popular form of government-hostility toward our public schoolshostility toward your right to choice of religion, we say with all American vigor: If that's the kind of government you want, then for heaven's
sake go elsewhere! And I, for one, propose to do everything in my
power to see that we do stay American!
There is, therefore, a great mission of Masonry for America. Just
as Masons had a vital part to play in the formation of our nation, so

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

29

they have a great opportunity to make sure we stay American. Masonry
combats mtellectual enslavement. It emancipates the ·human mind. It
liberates humanity from the chains of fear, ignorance and su·perstition.
It teaches the tenets which Jesus proclaimed, "Behold! a new doctrine
I give unto you, that you love one another," and the Divine Commandment of Moses, "Thou shalt love thy neighbor as thyself." It seeks to
persuade mankind that an acceptance of these precepts will lead to the
amity and peace for which we yearn.
So, as individuals we can bend our energies to increase our American
strength, our American devotion to duty and our American consecration
to freedom-freedom of the mind, freedom of the body and freedom of
the soul.
OuR PUBLIC ScHooLs
We can remind ourselves that to meet this challenge of the times
pd to make sure we stay American we have in our hands a marvelous
tool. It was fashioned with the greatest of care largely by our Masonic
forebears. This instrument is the American public school. We Masons
of this country and of California especially should regard our heritage
in that light. Examine it carefully as did the swordsman when he looked
at his weapon, tested its blade, Hexed its steel and found it tough and
true.
The American public school, strangely enough, is far older than our
nation. In fact, this year of 1955 is the 316th anniversary of our public
school system in America. For it was in Dorchester, Massachusetts, on
May 20, 1639, that there was launched the first free public school supported by taxes on real property. Through upwards of three centuries
that plan in essence has remained the financial foundation of our free
scholastic system.
We now have nearly 30 million children in those schools. This is
projected to increase by more than a million each year. Obviously the
tax base for providing funds is not increasing at any comparable clip.i
Hence. there are proposals currently for new forms of taxation to meet
the needs. T ·hese call for careful examination lest there is exploitation
by those not friendly to public schools.
For the past thirty-six years our California Public Schools Week
has been a means of calling attention to the functions and needs of our
own public schools. It is a Masonic sponsored event. Inaugurated in
the 1920's by Past Grand Master Charles Albert Adams because of a
crisis then confronting our public schools in a shortage of teachers, funds
and facilities, today the need for the event is even more acute but for
different reasons. The Grand Lodge in 1953 recognized its great stake
in our public schools by amending our laws to provide that lodge funds
may !be spent for this event and to permit support of state-wide public
school purposes.

31

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

We should remember that years ago in a transition from church control the American public schools shook off the old world, hard dogmatism of the dark ages. They broke through layers of prejudice and superstition to emerge and grow and flower in our free soil. They now carry
out the typically American concept that pu•blic schools should •b e paid
for and run by the people, as free schools, so every boy and girl in
the land may have a chance to get ahead in life according to merit instead of money. They are a product of the free, equal-opportunity-forall spirit of American institutions. There is inherent in that idea the
further American concept that public schools should be sanctuaries of
religious freedom. They are protected iby law from sectarian intrusion.
As a vast melting ·pot in a nation of diverse creeds, religions and races,
they train our children truly into a unified, intelligent American citizenry. In the recent words of our United States Supreme Court:
"The public school is at once the symbol of our democracy
and the most pervasive means for promoting our common dignity."
Yet there are those today who seek to cripple our public schools by
unfair criticism, by calling them Godless, by draining away public funds
necessary for ·their support, by inducing competitive systems, by unsym·pathetic in8ltration into teaching, administrative and executive staffs,
or by voting down all public school 1b ond issues.
It therefore has become increasingly clear to me that our Craft
should expand its activities beyond a mere one-week event once a year.
Urging people to visit the schools during Public Schools Week, while
of great value, falls far short of meeting the need today.
The critical question today, in my opinion, is whether the children,
the teachers, the administrative staffs, the school boards and the public
know the origin, development and purpose of our public schools. Do
they teach telling comparisons with competitive systems? Are they "sold"
on public schools themselves? Do they, for example, compare the school
books of the public and competitive systems, especially those dealing
with 'history, social studies and civics? The California public schools,
strange to say, do not teach the why of our public schools. Why not?
Accordingly. by my Proclamation of April 25, 1955, I inaugurated
specific action on the subject of the origin, development and purpose of
our public schools, as follows:
1 ) Essays and compositions on that subject in the schools with
awards to winners during Public Schools Week: 2) Requests to school
authorities for inclusion of the subject in public school curricula: and
3) Plans for a Masonic Public School Scholarship Fund whereby two
annual awards of $1,000 each will be made by the Grand Master, one
in the North and one in the South, for the best thesis or dissertation on
the subject by graduate students working for doctoral degrees in the
field of education. Among other benefits this should provide fruitful
source material for use in curricula and comparative studies.

A start in pursuance of the Proclamation has been made. Essays
and compositions were held and awards were made during Public
Schools Week. Requests were made to appropriate authorities for
mdusion of the subject in the public school curricula and resulted in
promises that this would be done. The following universities and colleges responded enthusiastically to the scholarship plan and will gladly
participate in a program for Masonic Public School Scholarships if this
Grand Lodge will authorize funds for the purpose.
Claremont College, Claremont
College of the Pacific, Stockton
Stanford University, Stanford
University of California, Berkeley
University of California, Los Angeles
University of Southern California, Los Angeles.
I therefore recommend that this Grand Lodge create a standing
COMMITTEE ON PUBLIC SCHOOLS to conduct a year round
program along the lines above, including the usual Public Schools Week
activities, that funds be appropriated for the purpose, and to this end
that Section 70 R.D. be amended by adding "on Public Schools" after
"on History."

"Help thy brother's boat across,

The month of May brings into bright focus Masonic charity at its
best. It is an opportunity to "help thy brother's boat across." It reminds
us the primary duty to help, aid and assist our brethren in distress rests
·
upon the individual Mason.
He should share in the works of welfare of which we are so proudµie Homes for the old and the young at Decoto and Covina. The way
this can be done is 'by contributions to the Endowment Fund.
Such support is essential. since income is not sufficient for the pur~
pose.
I feel confident the Masons of California will respond generously
and thus express the most amiable blessing of the human breast.
I therefore proclaim the month of May, 1955 as Masonic Homes
Endowment Fund Month.
I hereby direct that:
1. All Lodges in the Jurisdiction arrange at least one meeting to
remind the brethren the purpose of this worthy program.
2. Where possible, arrange visitations under Lodge auspices to each
Home.
3. Use no drive or pressure methods, since we should observe the
principle of voluntary participation.
4. A Committee be formed in each Lodge to expedite and carry out
the above.
This Proclamation is to be read at each Stated· Meeting following its
reception, up to and including the month of May, and at such other
meetings as the Masters shall determine.

Re 36th Annual Public Schools Week
The 36th Annual Public Schools Week will be observed April 25
through April 30, 1955.
For the past thirty-six years, Public Schools Week in California has
been a means of calling attention to the functions and needs of our
public sdiools. It is a Masonic sponsored event. Inaugurated in the
1920s because of a crisis confronting our public schools in a shortage
of teachers, funds and facilities, today the need for the event is even
more critical but for different reasons.
Years ago the American public schools shook off the old world,
hard dogmatism of the dark ages. They broke through layers of prejudice and superstition to emerge and grow and flower in our free soil.
They now carry out the typically American concept that schools under
collegiate grade should be paid for and run by the people, as free schools,
so every boy and girl in the land may have a chance to get ahead in
life according to ~erit instead of money. They are a product of the
free, equal-opportunity-for-all spirit of American institutions. There
is inherent in that idea the further American concept that public schools
should be sanctuaries of religious freedom. Thus, they are protected
by law from sectarian intrusion. As a vast melting pot in a nation of
_diverse creeds, religions and races, they train our children truly into a
unified, intelligent American citizenry. In the words of our United
States Supreme Court:
"The public school is at once the symbol of our democracy
and the most pervasive means for promoting our common
destiny."

I. therefore. proclaim and direct:
That all Lodges observe the 36th Annual Public Schools WeekApril 25-30, 1955, and that no Lodge meetings be held during that
week except stated meetings and for the Public Schools Week Observances.
That all Lodges, in cooperation with the Grand Lodge, Public Schools
Week Committee, help the public, the teachers and the children attain
a ·better understanding of the origin, development and purpose of the
American Public School System: and, to this end, that Committees
arrange with local schools for contests by the children in under collegiate grades to write essays and compositions on this subject, the
winners to receive prizes donated by me of a ·beautifully embossed
Pledge of Allegiance to the Flag, containing the new words recently

PROCLAMA TION

To All Members of the Craft in California and Hawaii:

Constitution Month Observance
It has been our annual custom to observe the month of September as
a time to reflect upon the great blessings which flow from our federal
constitution. This inspired document, written largely by Masonic hands
directed by Masonic minds, came to life on September 17, 1787. John
Marshall, who fought hard for ratification and who later as the master
jurist gave vitality to its principles, was an ardent Mason and Grand
Master of Virgmia.
For some 168 years our constitution has been the backbone of our
Government. There are those who would rip out this 1backbone from the
structure of our American society. Some, for example, ask that we follow communistic lines-others that we throw away our American doctrine of church-state separation. But we firmly resolve that during our
time and our children's time we shall not see any part of our great
charter of freedoms slide like a wilted leaf down the drain of unconstitutional deviations.
It is well that we reaffirm and restate and reiterate this basic symmetry of American life. Bear in mind there are times when this calls
for courage-for "souls ablaze in bodies of bronze."
I therefore proclaim the month of September, 1955, "Constitution
Observance Month." The Masons of this jurisdiction shall join in programs of rededication to those constitutional freedoms which have made
our Nation great. Each Lodge of this jurisdiction shall hold a special
meeting for this purpose during the month of September and, if desired,
may hold such meeting with other Lodges.
This proclamation shall be read at all Lodge meetings during
September.
August 17, 1955
HENRY C. CLAUSEN

Grand Master

Attest:
LLOYD E. WILSON

Grand Secretary

PROCLAMA TION
Ground Breaking Ceremony
California Masonic Memorial Temple
One of the most important of the matters which have engaged my·
attention 'has •been the plans for building the new California Masonic
Memorial Temple. The need is obvious. When I was Grand Orator
in 1941-with a membership of about 126,000 and some 582 Lodgeseven then the facilities on Van Ness Avenue were far too cramped.
Now that we have grown with our great State to 225,000 members and
655 Lodges, the need is just that much more acute.
The Temple thus will ·b e adequate ·housing for year round administrative activities and for our annual events. It will be a memorial also
to those Brethren of our armed forces who gave their lives that we might
live, a beacon to light the way to Masonry for us and our children, and
a sym:bol high in the western sky to inspire all true lovers of American
freedom.
It will also he a place where you, your friends and families may
visit and linger while enjoying a "billion dollar view."

Reference is made to report of Jurisprudence Committee on Decision

I referred the matter to Worshipful Brother Alex Duncan, Inspector

to investigate all the facts and report to me. His report follows:
"Reference is made to letter of May 13, 1955, requesting a report on
Decision No. 11 of Grand Master Harwell and the report of the Jurisprudence Committee thereon. Investigation has disdosed the following
facts:
"A petition dated November 8. 1952, was received in Eel River
Lodge at the stated meeting for Nove!dber, 1952. Unaccountable delays
deferred actual rejection until May 9, 1953.
"Applicant presented a petition to Semper Virens Lodge dated No.vemher 20, 1953, wherein his answers to Questions 8 and 9 both read,
'Yes. Eel River Lodge, November, 1952.' This petition was not received in Semper Virens Lodge until the stated meeting for January,
1954, and the committee reporting favorably, the applicant was elected
at the stated meeting in February, 1954.
"No malice was intended hy the petitioner, inasmuch as in his ignor..
ance of our procedure he had no way of knowing the actual date of his
rejection.
"The recommenders did verify that the original petition had been
received in November, 1952, and noting that fifteen months had elapsed,
checked no further.
"A study of Ded~ion No. 11 of Grand Master Harwell and the Rep..
port of the Committee on Jurisprudence thereon, together with the facts
herein stated, causes me to recommend that no further action be taken
and that Decision No. 11 of Grand Master Harwell be upheld."
It appears to me from the above that the Investigating Committee
should have checked the date of rejection. But under the peculiar facts
set forth in Brother Duncan's letter, in my judgment there was not any
purposeful deception on the part of the applicant or any rank dereliction
of duty on the part of the Committee. I do stress, however, the impor..
tance of Investigating Committees making a thorough inquiry into the
factual data set forth in a petitioner's application.
Accordingly, I have decided that Grand Master Harwell's Decision
No. 11 should be affirmed, and I so rule.

May a lodge or temple association invest its funds in state or federal

The answer is "No:·

DECISION

47

The California Superintendent of Banks bas ruled recently as
follows:
"For your information, Chapter 1034 of the Statutes of 1939 provided that all shares issued by a Federal Savings and Loan Association
were legal for investments by savings banks, provided the association
was an insured institution, as defined in Title IV, National Housing
Act. However, as the Banking Law (Sections 1354 to 1366, Financial
Code of California) is the later enactment, we feel that the provisions
of Chapter 1034 of the Statutes of 1939 have been superseded by the
Banking Law and that the shares issued by the Federal Savings and
Loan Association are not at this time legal for investment by California
savings !banks and that no certificates, shares or other evidences of
ownership of federal or state savings and loan associations are legal at
the ·present time for investment by California savings hanks."
Since Masonic law does not permit lodge or temple association investments which are illegal for savings banks ( R.D. 151 ) and since
building and loan associations are not within any exceptions ( R.D. 152,
152.1) it follows the answer must be "no."
DECISION No. 6
May a Lodge solicit donations from its members for redecorating the
Lodge room and use its monthly bulletin to explain and solicit such
funds?
The answer is "yes".
In my opinion, R. D. 126 does not apply to solicitation by a Lodge of
its own members. It merely prohibits solicitation of others. It long has
been the practice of Lodges to obtain funds from its own memrbers, such
as for construction of lodge halls and relief.
DECISION No. 7
Where a Lodge, pursuant to resolution, has set up a trust fund and
received contributions for the purpose of building a new Temple and
preserving an old one, may the funds be diverted to building an addition
to the old Temple?
The resolution of the lodge is not too clear in its stated purpose. The
preamble clauses indicate that it is the desire of the lodge that a trust
fund be set up in its treasury to be used only "for the purpose of building
the new temple and of preserving the old one". The resolution itself,
however, is that the fund shall not be expended "for any purpose other
than that of building or acquiring a Lodge hall or temple". The next
paragraph states that all money donated "for the purpose of the acquisition of a new Masonic Temple 1b y said lodge or the preservation of the
present lodge hall". shall be placed in the building fund. The sulbscription itself states that it is "to ·be used only for the purpose of acquiring
a new Masonic lodge ·hall for the lodge so that the present hall may be
preserved" •

If the alternative purpose can be read into the resolution, then the
fund could be used to ·build an addition to the old building, as it would
be for the purpose of preserving the old building. In view of the preamble clause and the other language, it seems to me that the resolution
can reasonably be construed to include the building of a new addition
to the present hall, which would be to preserve the old one.
There is, however, a further consideration which enters into the
problem. This plan of financing was adopted by the lodge in violation of
the ordinances of Grand Lodge. R.D. 78, as it then read. provided that
no financing for the purchase or alteration of a ·building requiring expenditure of more than $2,500.00 shall be entered into without first
obtaining consent of the Committee on Lodge Financing. The term
"financing" embraced any plan or scheme whereby money was to be
obtained for the purposes.
Since the fund is only a fraction of what will be necessary. it is my
opinion that the matter should be referred at this time to the Committee
on Lodge Financing for consideration, and if not approved. that the fund
be returned to the donors.

DECISION No. 9
May a Lodge purchase with lodge ftl'1ds and present to a newly
instituted lodge a set of Deacons' rods and bases?
The answer is "yes...
The lodge desires to present to Claude H. Morrison Lodge U.D. a
set of Deacons' rods and bases, to be purchased from lodge funds.
R.D. 616(a) is a decision by Grand Master Moore in 1947 to the
effect that lodge funds cannot be used to assist another lodge.
I think, hqwever, that the basis of that decision is hardly applicable
to the question involved here.
R.D. 159 permits a lodge to expend not to exceed 30% of its total
revenue for purposes of refreshment "and the promotion of fraternal
intercourse". In R.D. 634, it was decided that the expression "promotion
of fraternal intercourse" is very comprehensive, and as long as a subordinate lodge, in good faith, uses the social funds so that the general
interest and increased activity in the work of the order is promoted, it
should be permitted so to do.
The practice of making small presents of equipment to new lodges
has become traditional and to my mind tends to promote fraternal intercourse between lodges in the community. I think this properly can be
held to be within the broad interpretation of the phrase used in R.D. 159.
DECISION No. 10

activity in the work of the Order will be promoted.

DEc1s10N No. 12
May a lodge in its operations under the Prudent Man Rule for
lodge investments employ its own investment advisor and not confer
and counsel with the investment advisor of Grand Lodge?
The answer is "no." It is required that the lodge "confer and counsel
as to any such proposed or contemplated investments with the professional investment advisor used lby Grand Lodge." ( R.D. 152.1 ) •
It is observed, 'however, that while the lodge shall "confer and
counsel" with the professional investment advisor used by Grand Lodge,
whose fees will •be paid by Grand Lodge, this does not make mandatory
that the lodge follow such advice. It may well obtain independent
advice elsewhere, such as from another investment ad.visor, if it so
desires, provided it also confers and counsels with the investment advisor of Grand Lodge.

DECISION No. 15
May lodge funds 'be used to support a bowling league or team?
The anwser is "no".
The matter is a combined policy and legal question. The line has to
be drawn some place and it ·has been held that a lodge may not pay the
ex·penses of a <brother in attending a meeting of a Masonic Veterans
Association, ~n organization not recognized by Grand Lodge or the
constituent lodges. ( 623 R.D.). It is common knowledge that a howling
league or team is supported in the form of equipment and clothing. Also
that there is a certain amount of promotion of good will thereby engendered. But I am inclined to the view that this cannot be held to be a
matter of fraternal intercourse, since there are involved a limited amount
of members. If a lodge should pay this, then it might not refuse the
support of a golf team in a golf tournament and similar athletic ventures.
And a Masonic lodge is not an athletic club.

DEasroN No. 18
What interpretation should ibe given R.D. 255, dealing with 40-year
and 75-year Masons, in respect of remission of dues under the conditions
stated?
On the matter of remission of dues for 40-year Masons and 75-year
old Masons, it is my opinion that our laws never were intended to relieve
men of the duty of paying dues, nor of the privilege of permitting them
to pay dues. To do so merely because the number of years has been
satisfied is almost the same as granting a life membership. This, of
course, is in violation of our laws. It seems to me that the Sections were
intended for distinguished service and to be applied only in those marginal cases where there may be ability to pay but where a hardship still
would be worked.
It is a privilege to pay dues in a Masonic Lodge. We frequently lose
sight of that privilege in this country where Masonic Lodges may function and where members may be known freely as Masons without fear
of reprisal by church or government. This is not true everywhere in the
world. A man should consider it a high privilege to help bear the cost
of his own Lodge and of the Grand Lodge and thus make his contribution toward the onward marc:h of Masonry.

DEasioN No. 20
What procedure should .be followed where a candidate for the degrees has refused to ,be divested of all minerals and metals, insisting on
retaining a wedding ring on his finger because of his marriage vows?
The candidate should lbe rejected.
The ritual requires the devestiture. The candidate in his application
has promised to conform to all the ancient usages and regulations.
The ritual itself is binding law ( R.D. 650, 801c) and must be adhered
to by all lodges and Masons ( R.D. 247). After a refusal to conform to
the ritual. the Master at the next regular meeting of the Lodge should
declare the candidate rejected.
There have been cases where minerals and metals cannot be removed,
such as a ring where the finger has become too large to permit its removal.
In such cases substantial compliance has been permitted and the ring has
been taped and disregarded. The question posed here, ·however, is different because the candidate actually can comply but refuses so to do.

DECISION No. 22
Does an applicant for the degrees of Masonry meet our residence
requirements when he has lived or resided within the jurisdiction of the
Lodge for six months 1before his application, hut during that time has
resided at two different addresses?
The answer is "yes".
There is no requirement that the candidate reside at the same ad ...
dress for the six months ·period. The dispensation power of Ross Digest,
Sec. 216 may be invoked if the candidate changed his address so as not
to have the qualiflcation of residence.
DEc1s10N No. 23
Is an applicant for the degrees of Masonry qualified in respect of
residence if he has been away from the State of California for three years
as a civilian employee engaged in work for our Armed Forces, although
during his absence he has maintained residence and mailing address in
the jurisdiction of the Lodge?
The answer is "yes".
I think the applicant has the required residence. R.D. 684 seems to
require residence "in fact", yet in several later rulings of Grand Lodge
the express or manifest intent of the party, as shown hy the facts of the
case, has determined residence. ( R.D. 687, 689 and 694). This seems a
more reasonable interpretation. Otherwise some of our most distin. .
guished citizens would be forever barred from Masonic membership. The
applicant in the instant case apparently never has adopted a residence
elsewhere, ·b ut had maintained his California residence and mailing ad ...
dress with the clear intent to return and have this as •his permanent
residence.

DECISION No. 25
Where a Lodge has waived jurisdiction in favor of another Lodge,
may the Lodge which had original jurisdiction also, in all cases, receive
the application?
The answer is "no".
The lodge granting the waiver surrenders its jurisdictional rights
over the applicant, including its right to receive his petition for the de...
grees. ( R.D. 575). No other lodge than the one specified in the waiver
is authorized to receive his petition ( R.D. 711 ) , unless he is rejected and
12 months have elapsed (R.D. 709).
In the present case, Coalinga Lodge granted a waiver in favor of
Welcome Lodge. The man, however, did not present his application to
Welcome Lodge. There is no time limit on the waiver and the authority
continues until an application is presented by the man to Welcome
Lodge. In my opinion, the man can present his application only to W el...
come Lodge, so long as the jurisdiction remains the same.
If, of course, the man had moved out of the Coalinga Lodge jurisdic. .
tion into the jurisdiction of another Lodge, I believe the force and effect
of the unused waiver would cease, and after he had resided 6 months in
the new residence, the other Lodge could receive his application or grant
a waiver. If he had moved into the jurisdiction of the Welcome Lodge
after residence of 6 months, Welcome Lodge would have original juris. .
diction ( R.D. 702).
The Maste"r's letter does not state whether the man moved before or
after granting the waiver, or if he has moved again. He may now be
ineligible for applying to any lo~ge for lack of sufficient residence.
DECISION No. 26
May a California Lodge confer a courtesy degree or degrees on an
amputee member of another jurisdiction?
The answer is "yes."
It appears that the applicant •became such after he received the second
degree in a recognized jurisdiction. Hence, Grand Master Paulsen's
Dec. (1951) (R.D. 515) clearly covers the point. If the applicant was
an amputee before he took any degrees, and was, nevertheless, advanced
to the degree of fellow craft in a recognized jurisdiction which did not
hold his disability disqualifying. he is none the less a fellow craft mason,
though now a resident of California. The rationale of Grand Master
Patton's Dec. ( 1900) ( R.D. 886) together with RD. 515 requires that
he be allowed to make application for his third degree in the California
Lodge.

Is a person physically qualified to receive the degrees of Masonry
who has suffered the loss of his left leg?
The answer is "no". ( R.D. 208, 888 (a), 883).
While the law in some jurisdictions differs from ours with respect to
physical qualifications it is clear that in California the man in question
would lack the requisite physical qualifications and no authority is given
to grant a dispensation to waive lack of physical qualifications.
DECISION No. 28

Where military personnel must respond to an "alert" summons in
the midst of conferral of a degree, so that necessarily the degree cannot
be completed on the day of commencement, what procedure should be
followed?
The Master must, of course, comply with R.D. 192, Third, and
complete the degree at the time it is conferred, in the absence of such
emergent situations as fire, sickness, or requirements of national defense
over which the lodge officers have no control. ( 1952, 78, 264)
Accordingly, under the facts stated, the following procedure should
govern:
First, if the Master is forewarned of a possible "alert," he should
defer commencement of the degree.
Second, if there is no forewarning, as is most apt, the Master should
proceed as outlined and approved by Grand Lodge. ( 1954, 78, 264)
DECISION No. 29
Where an applicant for the degrees of Masonry is unable without
danger to fulfill the physical requirements by reason of a back injury
from which he has not yet recovered, may the degrees be conferred in
a symbolic manner?
The answer is "no."
Under R.D. 208, an applicant must be physically alble to conform
substantially to what the several degrees require. The question as to
the physical sufficiency of the applicant is left to the sound discretion
of the lodge. The lodge in this case itself has determined the question.
I assume that the man has not actually been rejected, but that his
application has been withdrawn, as permitted by R.D. 227. That would
be the proper procedure. The secretary's letter, however, refers to both
rejection and to return of the petition. Consequently, I am of the opinion
that no one can now question the propriety of the action of the lodge
in determining that at the present time this applicant is not physically
capable of conforming.
There is no indication as to how incapacitated the applicant is at
the present time, only that he may recover sufficiently to conform.

Where successive objections are lodged against advancement of an

Under the procedure set forth in R.D. 238 to 240, if the objection
charged seems sufficient to the Master, he shall appoint a committee
to inquire into the cause of the objection, fix the time and place of meet..
ing and have the objector and applicant notified thereof. The committee
is to meet at the time and place fixed and the Secretary or some brother
appointed in his place must record the proceedings. Any statement
made is to be taken down in narrative or other form by the Secretary or
by qualified stenographer. The committee has entire charge of the
investigation and must report at the next stated meeting, stating the
cause of the dbjection and its conclusions thereon. The lodge then votes
by secret ballot and the decision of two..thirds is final.
The proceeding is in effect a trial. The committee is to hear the
evidence and report the facts. The members of the lodge are exclusive
judges whether the cause assigned was proved and if proved whether
it constitutes a valid cause. (Sec. 815).
It does not appear what evidence was taken at the hearing, but
minutes of a stated meeting show the Master reported on the objection.
It also appears that some brother reported a hearsay claim that the
candidate had served a jail sentence for deserting his family. Another
brother made a similar report and told how the candidate's family had
been deserted. The lodge proceeded to vote 39 to 1 against advance..
~ent. The master announced the result and directed the remaining fees
be returned.

What is the effect of non..compliance with R.D. 2397

DECISION No. 36
Is an applicant eligible for the degrees of Masonry when his history
shows that at the age of 18 he pleaded guilty to a felony charge, namely,
setting a fire next to a public domain, he being fatherless and without
counsel and not realizing the seriousness of the charge?
In 1875 (R.D. 875) Grand Lodge held that those who had served
prison terms were ineligible for the degrees of Masonry. In 1951 a
move was made by Grand Master Paulsen to set aside this effect of
R.D. 875, but after lengthy reports by the Committee on Policy and
General Purposes, concurred in ·b y the Committee on Jurisprudence, the
Grand Lodge adhered to the prior ruling.
It seems to me these Committees feel that imprisonment in the state
or federal prison is what debars an applicant. For example, the report
on page 267 ( 1951) said, "The man sentenced to a state prison is one

60

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

whom the trial judge considers unworthy of probation, usually because
he is before the court with a record of other criminal convictions. It is
this class whom it is now proposed to make eligi'ble to petition our
Lodges.''
In 1952 Grand Master Drapeau held that a person convicted of a
felony is ineligible even though he has served no time, and has made
complete restitution. (Proceedings. 1952, rp. 35, Ruling 30). This was
an extension of the 1875 ruling, as affirmed in the 1951 report. Grand
Master Warren,, relying on the decision of Grand Master Drapeau,
held in 1953 (Proceedings, 1953, p. 82) that a person convicted of a
felony is not eligible. even though he received a commuted sentence
and a presidential pardon. These decisions were approved by the Jurisprudence Committee and by Grand Lodge. In my opinion in so doing
we were wrong.
In 1953, Grand Lodge, on the recommendation of the Jurisprudence
Committee, overruled Grand Master Warren and held that a deserter
from the Army is eligible for membership even though he served one
year in a military prison, because under federal law a felony requires
imprisonment for more than one year.
The inconsistency of these various rulings is apparent and pose
the following considerations:
1. A person convicted of Grand Theft or Forgery who receives
only one year in the county jail, which he may under California law,
is guilty of a misdemeanor only, and is eligible, but one who is convicted of the same offense in Texas or elsewhere and receives a commuted sentence or is granted probation may be convicted of a felony
and be not eligible.
2. Is a person who serves one year under a military court martial
for armed robbery eligible because it is a misdemeanor under federal
law, while one who steals a calf (which may be a felony in Texas), and
is given a suspended sentence and a Presidential pardon not eligi'hle7
3. What about the numerous offenses in California such as Grand
Theft which provide for both jail sentences and prison terms? In view
of the Drapeau and Warren decisions, is the person receiving a misdemeanor jail sentence eligible while one receiving a suspended sentence
or probation ineligible?
4. How about the California Attorney General's opinion that one
receiving probation is not guilty of a felony in California? This, of
course, would not apply to federal violations. Because of a difference
in possible penalties or designations of crimes as to felonies and misdemeanors in the state and federal law, are we to distinguish as to
eligibility, when identical crimes are in fact committed? Many more
questions could be asked.
I think the most sensible thing to do is to go by the 1875 Grand
Lodge ruling as affirmed in 1951. Thus in my opinion the test is whether

GRAND LODGE OP CALIPORNIA

61

an applicant has served a term of imprisonment in the state or federal
prison: for, if so, he does not come under the tongue of good report as
a matter of Masonic Law.
.Jn the present case under the Drapeau and Warren rulings, the
applicant Winslow would not he eligible because he was convicted of
a felony, but in my opinion he is eligible. I therefore so rule.

DECISION No. 38
Is an applicant, who has been court-martialed for rdbbery and who
served an unstated time in a military penal institution, eligible for the
degrees?
The answer is "no.'' (Decision 36 of Grand Master Clausen).
The applicant in this case has been court martialed, and after serving an unstated time in a military penal institution, was given a dishonorable discharge. An inquiry to the Army apparently disclosed that
the applicant had not been convicted of a felony under Federal law.
I assume, therefore, that his sentence was for not more than one year.
The applicant would have ibeen convicted of a felony had he been
charged and tried under state law. Even an unloaded pistol comes
within the definition of a "dangerous" weapon. The crime committed
actually was First Degree Robbery under California law. This carries

Penal Code Sections 21 la, 212, 213, 20 McK. Dig. 4 ).
The fact that the applicant was not holding the gun would not alter
the situation. He ·should be rejected.

No. 44
In a proposed consolidation of Gravel Range Lodge No. 59 and
Forest Lodge No. 66, what steps are required in compliance with our
law on the subject?
T·his involves the construction of Sections 141 and 475. R.D. Sec..
tion 475, adopted by Grand Lodge, is a construction of Section 141.
Under this procedure, a resolution is first adopted declaring the
consolidation expedient and proposing appointment of a committee to
arrange and report terms. This is to be adopted at a stated meeting.
Ninety days' notice is not required of this meeting.
The lodge has held this stated meeting, has adopted the resolution,
DEc1s10N

63

a committee has been appointed ·b y each lodge and at a meeting of the
respective committees they have agreed upon the terms of consolidation.
This, in my opinion, covers the requirements of paragraph 1 of our
Section 475 and part of paragraph 2.
Paragraph 2 next requires, however, that the respective lodges receive and concur in the reports of their committees. It is necessary that
the lodges at a stated meeting receive and concur in the reports, because
the business can only 1be transacted at a stated meeting. This step has
not been complied with; and under the procedure provided in Section
475, this meeting cannot be avoided, although 90 days' notice thereof
is not required.
Under paragraph 3, when the lodges thus have concurred in the reports of their committees, and the terms of the consolidation have been
agreed upon, notice then must be given by the Secretary of each lodge
to all its members that at a stated meeting to ·be holden on the day named
in the notice, which must be more than 3 months after the time of service,
a resolution for consolidation will come up for final action. In the meantime, pursuant to paragraph 4, the consents of at least three-fourth s of
the members of each lodge must lbe obtained and signed, before the
time for final action.
It will be noted that the stated meeting must be after a notice
which must be more than 3 months after the time of service. Also, that
under Section 298, a notice, when practicable, must be personally served
upon the brother to 1be notified, or if this cannot be conveniently done,
it must be left at his residence or usual place of business, or sent by
ftrst-dass or .registered mail. These requirements may well extend the
3 months period; since the 3 months dates from time of service.
Thus, the steps of consolidation taken to date are in keeping with
our law, and the next steps are as outlined above.

DECISION

No. 47
Should the minutes of the Lodge show the exact time when the
stated meeting convenes?
The answer is "yes."
The minutes of a Lodge are supposed to speak the truth. They
should not record an untruth.
The l,.odge cannot, of course, be convened at any hour earlier than
that prescribed by the by-laws. ( 778-8A R.D.).
It would appear that the practice of convening a lodge in stated
meeting later than the time fixed by the by-laws is subject to censure.
A brother should have a right to rely on the by-laws and to attend at
the time set forth in the by-laws with the expectation that he can take
part in the business of the meeting. That meeting should start at the
prescribed time, as otherwise this brother may be deprived of his right
to sit in at the meeting, by reason of later commitments.

DECISION No. 48
This responds to your letter of December 28 in whic'h you ask
whether it would be permissible to present to candidates an "Interpretation of the Blue Degrees" prepared by a member of your Lodge.
The material contains esoteric matter not proper to be written and

Consequently, I do not deem it proper for any Lodge to use this
material. Esoteric matter should not be circulated regardless of whether
it might be found in book stores. The only printed authorized explanations are those in the books of the Candidate, the Entered Apprentice, the Fellow Craft and the Master Mason, issued by Grand
Lodge. Moreover, Masonry is universal and includes all sects, creeds
and colors.
