DEc1s10N No. 55
May a Lodge use a musical score and orchestra in th~ second section?
The answer is "yes" but there are matters of policy involved which
may be paramount.
Each degree conferred must conform to the ritual taught by the
Grand Lecturer and recognized by the Grand Lodge (R.D. 247). The
degrees are not operas or plays. In times past, the Ritual Committee
and the Grand Lecturer have requested that any music be purely incidental and limited to a fe:w places in the work.
The policy in regard to music is similar to that adopted and enforced
in respect of costuming, charts, slides and ftlms. The work is taught
and should be conferred without the use of such props. The emphasis
in this jurisdiction has always been on uniformity. The use of special
props by one lodge would be an incentive to another lodge for something
more elaborate and different. A degree conferred in one place should
be similar to that conferred elsewhere in the State. The use of music
and an orchestra in the conferring of a degree by one Lodge could not
be duplicated everywhere, and such an innovation would not be in
conformity with the adopted work. It is a violation of the rule of
uniformity.
DECISION No. 56
May Grand Lodge officiate in cornerstone ceremonies by inserting
the so-called cornerstone into the side of a wall or in cases where the
cornerstone is not a true supporting stone?

67

The answer is "yes."
The ceremonial and purpose of laying cornerstones is symbolic
primarily. Modern types of construction do not require a true cornerstone, such as one upon which a wall or building may rest. Consequently,
the practice has been to insert a so-called cornerstone into the side of
an outer wall of a building. This, when accom•plished by our time-honored ceremonies, should suffice for our symbolic purposes.

No. 57
May a Master ·be required by lodge resolution to appoint the Marshal in the line of advancing officers following the Junior Deacon?
The answer is "no."
A lodge would deviate from its by-laws in ordering the Master to
appoint the Marshal as Junior Deacon. This is also the sort of action
which could lead to discord.
Article II, Section 1 of the uniform code of By-Laws states that
all appointive officers shall be appointed by the Master. There is no
provision made for the Lodge to order him to appoint any individual
to any certain o~ce. It rests solely in the hands of the Master.

No. 58
May a brother, who shot and killed his mother and then committed
suicide, be buried with Masonic honors?
The answer is "no."
The Mastu, with concurrence of the Wardens, may determine the
propriety of burying a suicide (R.D. 265).
But since the suicide in this case had shot and killed his mother,
it seems to me there is some overriding principle of propriety involved.
For. exa~ple, R.D'. 265 prohibits a ·~rother, fallen in a duel, from being
buried with Masonic honors. Masonic policy would seem to indicate that
a brother who ·h ad shot and killed his mother should not be 1buried with
Masonic 'honors.
It was claimed that the brother must have been insane at the time
to have done such a deed. But it should be borne in mind that the law
presumes against insanity. Certainly there was no court adjudication
to that effect. There was no claim of other acts which would indicate
Insanity in law sufficient to excuse a murder.

No. 59
. May a Mason sojourning in California possess and use a sypher
ntual he has lawfully received in another jurisdiction and which contains the work of such other jurisdiction?
DECISION

PROCEEDINGS OF THB

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

The answer is "no."
The Grand Lodge of California has made it a Masonic offense to
possess or use cypher rituals in California ( R.D. 502-4: 752).
Hence, a sojourning Mason in California who would use or possess
a cypher ritual in California containing the work of another jurisdiction,
would by such acts violate the Masonic law of California. ( R.D. 590..A).
For such violation, California could enforce its California law on
the subject by disciplinary action against such sojourning Mason ( R.D.
211, 289, 599-A, Landmark 17, page 577 R.D.).
California adheres to the trust of preserving the Ancient Craft
Ritual, with constant vigilance, to the end that, from generation to
generation as the faithful die, the ritual shall be transmitted unimpaired
by the attentive ear, the instructive tongue, and the faithful breast.
W 'hile we realize some other independent and sovereign Grand Lodges
may dispense with secrecy in the preservation of the ritual, nevertheless
California, within the sovereign limits of its jurisdiction, will follow the
admonition of Dr. Albert Mackey, the great American Masonic scholar,
who said: "Freemasonry, as a secret association, has lived unchanged
for centuries-as an open society it would not last for as many years."
Consequently, the California Grand Lodge must, albeit perhaps
reluctantly, in this respect impose its Masonic law upon any sojourning
Mason within the jurisdiction of California.

DECISION No. 61
Does Section 223 R.D. require the waiting period before membership
may be obtained in a so-called Benefit Club which is not a Square Club
or a Social Club, does not visit other Lodges nor participate in "Boor
work," and whose membership is made up only of members of one
Lodge: the purpose of which organization is to aid and assist in charity
work and provide for mutual benefl.ts?
The answer is "yes."
The language of Section 223 R.D. is sweeping and all inclusive, so
that "initiation" in any "organization," as the section presently is
worded. would include the Benefl.t Club. This is so regardless of
whether degree work is or is not performed.
Your attention is invited to the provisions of Masonic law prohibiting lodges from engaging in collateral financial undertakings, including sponsoring widows and orphans' funds ( R.D. 912). Please
study this section. the annotations thereto, and the pertinent provisions
of civil law to see if the activities of your Club are within the bounds
of legality.
A club, controlled or operated by or through a lodge, in reality is
the lodge itself. Hence, what the lodge may not do directly, it may
not do indirectly through a club.
It should also be borne in mind as a matter of policy, if not law,
that a Masonic club within a lodge is not recommended. Experience
has shown they lead to departures from propriety, to loss of direct
lodge supervision, and to cliques and quarrels.

acting under lodge auspices: ( 1) doing through "Clubs" indirectly what
cannot be done directly: ( 2) playing bingo: and ( 3 ) making trips to
Nevada without dispensation of the Grand Master and for purposes
prohibited in California.
One lodge bulletin, for example, set forth the following as proposed
lodge functions:
"RENO BY PLANE!! !! HERE IT IS!! The complete cost is only
$35.00 rper person and you receive a $10.00 refund on arrival in Reno
as a gift from Harold's Club. Included ... Four Cocktail Parties."
"GIFT NITE. Well, that's what we have to call it, even though
it's true. You know, it's that game where you put beans on numbered
squares in straight rows."
It is mandatory upon me as Grand Master to "see that the Constitution and Regulations of the Grand Lodge are strictly maintained, supported, and obeyed" (R.D. 38, 4th).
Accordingly, I call to your attention the following:
The scheme of a dub within a lodge is against Masonic policy
( G. M. Siems, 1949:27). When used as a device to circumvent Masonic
law applicable to lodges, it is an obvious subterfuge.
The playing of bingo, with its public connotation of gambling, is
against Masonic law and policy, regardless whether any consideration
is.paid directly for chances. (Compare, G. M. Harwell, 1954:77: G. M.
Meyer, 1950:27: G. M. Warren, 1936:14).
Trips without dispensation to another State, and in any case when
practices prohibited in California are there pursued, violate Masonic
law ( R.D. 156, 288, 735 and 739). Moreover, a lodge may not engage
in collateral financial undertaking, outside the orbit of authorized lodge
activities ( R.D. 127).
I hope a "word to the wise" shall be sufficient. I ask the help of the
brethren to see that our Masonic standards are maintained. If we ever
lower those standards we may destroy the nature of our institution and
Bnd birds roosting in our rafters and cobwebs on our doors.

under whose auspices or for what purpose it is conducted. ( R.D. 288,
739, 740).
The public brands and associates Bingo with gambling, regardless
of whether there is a monetary or other consideration paid directly to
play the game. As such, it has been banned in many States, including
California, when it violates our Penal Code. For example, there are
presently ·stron~ protestations being made against attempts in some
States to legalize Bingo. Moreover, the players of Bingo, when gambling,
undermine the solid virtues of industry, thrift and morality which a
Mason must uphold.

May a Lodge or members of a Lodge conduct and play Bingo games
under Lodge auspices?
The answer is "no."
Gambling long has been frowned upon in Masonry since it is im~
moral, especially when for the purpose of monetary gain, and no matter

If the playing of Bingo be soug'ht to be justiBed on the ground that
no monetary consideration is paid directly, then it at least verges upon
the illegal to such an extent that it falls within the purview of activities
which should not he pursued as a matter of policy. Grand Master Harwell held that a turkey shoot violated Masonic law. ( 1954:77) ). Meyer
1950:27: Gaylord 1932:71: Warren 1953:80.
Consequently, as a matter of policy and of Masonic law, and in
order that our craft may not trail in the dust its claim to moral leadership.
I have decided that Bingo should not lbe played by a Lodge or mem•bers
of a Lodge under Lodge auspices. We must maintain our standards.
No. 65
Where a !lo~called col1ateral Masonic organiiation selects a public
picnic ground to hold a picnic, the affair being held under the auspices
of the organization, although not limited to members of the Masonic
fraternity and their families, and an admission fee is charged by the
owner of the property, a drawing is held, no speciBc charge being made
for the tickets, and presents are awarded, some of which are donated
and some purchased from the funds of the organization, does this violate
Masonic law?
DECISION

The answer is "yes."
A consideration being paid, directly or indirectly, I am of the opinion
the procedure would constitute a lottery, and no Mason may participate
in it.
Such practices are illegal under Masonic law if they constitute a
lottery. Under our California Penal Code, when a consideration is
paid, direct or indirect, for the right of participating in a drawing, it is
a lottery. In cases where a price is paid directly for a chance to win a
prize, or where an admittance charge is made, and as an incident thereto,

72

PROCEEDINGS OP THB

the purchaser accepts the right to participate in a drawing, the transaction is illegal.
Where such an organization mentioned above holds a card party,
not necessarily in a Masonic Temple, at which those in attendance play
bridge, whist, or canasta, and a charge is made for attendance with
prizes being awarded to holders of the highest scores, such prizes having
been purchased from moneys collected as admission fees, does this
violate Masonic law?
The answer is "yes."
See the detailed answer above.
Where such an organization holds a dinner or luncheon, not neces•
sarily in the Masonic Temple, for which a dinner or luncheon charge is
made, or men hold a business meeting, or Masons in a Masonic Temple
confer a degree, following which those present engage in a social game
of !bridge, whist or canasta, with prizes donated or purcliased from the
receipts of the dinner or luncheon and awarded to those holding the
highest scores, does this violate Masonic law?
The answer is "yes~" in the event consideration is paid, direct or
indirect, such as through purchase of prizes from receipts. In the event
there is no such consideration, and no prohiobition of Masonic law,
then a question of Masonic policy and ethics are involved. For example, "Bingo Games" have been held improper for play in Masonic
Temples. (Ruling No. 64 of Grand Master Clausen). On the other
hand, but subject to the above, card games as such are not un-Masonic
although objections of the members should be considered. ( R.D. 794).
DEc1s10N No. 66
After charges have been filed and a trial has been had and a verdict
of acquittal rendered, may a transcript of the record of the trial for
transmittal to the Grand Secretary be dispensed with?
The answer is "no."
312 R.D. requires that a full record of the proceedings be kept. Sec.
324 provides that the record of the trial shall be signed by the Master
or Past Master presiding thereat. Sec. 327 states that in all cases,
whether appealed or not, the Master or Past Master presiding shall
cause the Secretary to prepare a transcript of the record of the trial,
to be transmitted to the Grand Secretary.
The correctness of the trial master's rulings is a matter for the submission to the Grievance Committee, and to which the record will be
referred for that purpose.

No. 67
May a Temple Association add the word "Memorial" to its name?
There appears to be no restriction in Masonic Law which would prohibit the addition of the word "Memorial" to the name of a Temple
Association, although it is not dear that the mere addition of that word
would thereby create tax deductibility for contributions. This latter
appears to present the real purpose of the request for the name, but it is
felt. however, that study of the legal requirements will disclose that the
mere name will not confer tax exemption.

No. 69
Where the Visalia Masonic Building Association desires to pur..
chase a new carpet for the Temple, said Association being a separate
corporation, and Visalia Lodge being one of three stockholders, must
the Association submit this proposed expenditure to the Lodge or to
the Grand Lodge Committee on Lodge Fnancing. even though it exceeds $2,500.007
The answer is "no."
R.D. 78, 78.1 and 151 as amended in 1954, do not so require. The replacement of carpet could not be reasonably interpreted as an alteration
of the buildin9. Consequently, the Association does not have to submit
the expenditure to the Grand Lodge Committee on Lodge Finandng.
nor to the lodge as such, even though the cost exceeds $2,500.00.
The Visalia Lodge has ratified the Association's proposed action.
I assume therefore that the question posed concerns "Grand Lodge"
instead of "Lodge."
In my opinion, the replacement of carpet reasonably falls within
the term "maintenance" as used in Swanson's Will, the source of funds
for that purpose.

Dear Mr. Widup:

All of Decision No. 71.
All of Decision No. 72.

This will summarize the situation affecting Far West Lodge No. 673
and my decision in light of plans •proposed for restoring its charter.
On or about November 10, 1954, you officially reported to me an
irregular condition existing for some time within the lodge. A Club
had been organized within the lodge, directed hy the Junior Warden,
which bought and sold liquor for lodge social functions. Guests at these
functions bought tickets which were exchanged for drinks dispensed
by lodge members over a ~ar from the stock of liquor acquired by the
Club. The Junior Warden made periodic accounts to the Master, as
Junior Warden, along with separate reports of other activities as Junior
Warden. The account attached is an example, and reports, among other
things, on a lodge Fall Dinner Dance publicized in the lodge October
Bulletin. Apparently, though recently discovered by you, the practice
had persisted for some years. The matter came to light when requests
were made to use some of the liquor for an Officers and Coaches party.
These were obvious and long standing violations of elementary
Masonic Law dealing with liquor ( R.D. 156, 210, 467).
The Club was flagrant subterfuge, as was the separate report of the
Junior Warden, to circumvent the law. The scheme of a Club was subject to criticism in any event (G. M. Siems, 1949:27).
Moreover, the practice violated penal provisions of civil law ( Bus.
& Prof. Code, 23025-6, 23300-1, 2405).
Accordingly, since the violations were flagrant, long standing and
Widespread among the officers and some members, I reluctantly reached
the difficult decision that I should suspend the Master and arrest the
charter. I did so on November 18, 1954. (R.D. 34, 147).
Investigation then disclosed charges of misconduct and excessive
drinking during a fraternal out-of-town visitation by the lodge. Bills
for damage done at a motel were paid hy the Club and is referred to in
the attached report of the Junior Warden.
The facts indicate that the officers, present and past, who originated
and carried on the violations of Masonic and civil law are subject to the
most severe censure. Those implicated should be truly contrite. They
haThve brought down upon the lodge and the Craft a condition of shame.
e lodge and its members who were innocent must, unfortunately.

suffer and share acutely in the sorrow that its leaders went so far astray
from realities of Masonic standards. If those standards are not maintained then birds will roost in the rafters of our temples and cobwebs
will collect on the doors.
The Past Masters of the lodge met in March, 1955 and represented
to me that, if the charter were restored, an honest endeavor would be
made to avoid in the future "the several violations of the Masonic Code
which apparently had been permitted to flourish in Far West Lodge,
and which ultimately resulted in the arrest of its Charter." It was further
represented and the elective officers at the time of arrest concurred that
they would resign and not again seek or hold Masonic office without
consent of Grand Lodge.
The elective officers later stated their "regret that certain violations
of the Masonic Code were permitted during their respective term of
office" and pleaded for restoration of the Charter and resigned conditioned on that event. A slate of elective and appointive new officers,
designed to effect the necessary corrective action, was proposed by your
letter of April 3, 1955.
On the assumption that the suggested corrective action will be carried into effect, I restore the charter (R.D. 8, 20, 467). You and the
lodge are authorized and directed to convene the lodge to request of
me dispensation for an election to fill the vacancies in office created by
the resignations. Whereupon, after receiving such dispensation, to
convene the lodge again for the contemplated elections (R.D. 834, 181 ).
The contemplated appointments would be made then by the newly
elected master (R.D. 835).
Fraternally yours,
(Signed) HENRY C. CLAUSEN

To the Most Worshipf ul Grand Lodge of California:
Whereas, The eight Masonic Lodges of the Hawaiian Islands are
Chartered by the Grand ·Lodge F. & A. M. of California, and
Whereas, the aforementioned Lodges are geopraphically located
on four separate Islands of the Hawaiian Group and are divided into
three lnspectorial Districts, and
Whereas, it is felt that this arrangement is unsatisfactory from an
administrative viewpoint and is detrimental to the progress and growth
of Masonry in the Hawaiian Islands.
Now, therefore, be it resolved: That the Grand Lodge F. & A. M.
of California create the Office of District Deputy Grand Master to
administer the affairs of the Grand Lodge to the aforementioned constituent Lodges. That the incumbent in this newly created office be
appointed by, and serve at the will and pleasure of the Most Worshipf ul
Grand Master.

TEMPLE ASSESSMENT

81

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
WHEREA S, at each Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge for
the past 8 years, beginning with 1947. the proposal to build a new
Masonic Memorial Temple has been before the Grand Lodge for its
tonsideration, and
WHEREA S. there have been in attendance at these 8 Communications
a total of 15,504 Masters. Wardens and Past Masters, representing
an average of 575 Lodges at each Session, and
WHEREA S, after full and free discussion of each and every proposal
these representatives of the Lodges have voted to construct such a
Memorial Temple, and
WHEREA S. these representatives of Lodges approved the ultimate
plan as now proposed, and

82

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

WHEREAS. to finance the construction, in part, these representatives
of Lodges approved a campaign for voluntary contributions with
the objective of securing at least $10.00 per member, and
WHEREAS. such a campaign has been in progress since March 14,
1954, and has :produced in cash contributions and pledges $1,142,000.00, and
WHEREAS. many Lodges and their members have made a magnificent
contribution to this program, averaging more than $10.00 per member, and others have done very well. and
WHEREAS, some Lodges and their members have not effectively promoted the campaign for contributions, and
WHEREAS, the failure of these Lodges to reach $10.00 per member
creates an inequity among the Lodges and the members which results in an unequal bearing of the burden, and
WHEREAS, it is the essence of Freemasonry that the will of the majority shall always govern the entire Craft and the burdens and
responsibilities shall fall equally upon all, and
WHEREAS, it is now desirable that this fundamental of Freemasonry
be carried out in the Masonic Memorial Temple project,
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that the representatives
of the Lodges at this 106th Annual Communication levy an assessment on the Lodges of $10.00 for each Master Mason carried on
its rolls as of July 31, 1956, and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that each Lodge have credited against
its total assessment the full amount of all its contributions in the
hands of the Grand Secretary prior to July 1, 1956, and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that the difference between the amount
of the total assessment and the amount of contributions received shall
be due and payable with the Annual Returns in five installments,
commencing with the Annual Returns of 1956, and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that such portion of each annual installment as is not contributed voluntarily by the members shall be
paid from the Lodge treasury.
JoHN C. BovEY, P.M. No. 166
OTTO H. FISCHER, P.M. No. 215
PAUL A. PFLUEGER, P.M. No. 370
EDWARD H. SIEMS, P.M. No. 560

FUNERAL RITUAL AMENDMENT
Following changes jn Funeral Ritual are proposed:
1. The one officiating at the service should wear the Jewel and
Apron of that office; not the hat. Dignity is needed badly in our
service and this will add materially.
2. Have the Senior and Junior Deacons with crossed staffs over
the casket at all times during the service, except during the
prayers. He was made a Mason under these staffs and it is my
belief t,bat he should pass on that way.
3. Delete the words "by chilling blasts of death'' in the very last
paragraph of our ritual. To me this not only is depressing and
also chilling to the bereaved but also superfluous. I have eliminated it in the last few funerals I have put on.
Respectfully submitted
Fraternally yours,
CLARENCE G. HUSTLER, P.M.

the cost ·and the capacity.
FIRST: Regarding the site, it is claimed that it would take 500
taxicabs hauling the legal limit of 5 Brethren each to transport 2500
Brethren to the Nob Hill location, and 500 taxicabs to repeat the performance at our usual unpredictable adjournmen t hour, each day. Then,

attending Grand Lodge from outside ·San Francisco usually stay at
hotels not within easy walking distance of Nob Hill, and many like to
walk to and from the meeting place because of having to sit so constantly
all day for five days, but would have to forego doing this if our meeting
place is on Nob Hill. Many Brethren attending Grand Lodge are elderly
or have had heart trouble. and surely no good physician would approve
their having to contend with climbing the steep streets around Nob Hill.
Now let us consider the objections to the proposed capacity and
cost: It is written that where there is no vision, the people perish. By
the year 1975. the population of California is expected to be 20 millions:
and if Free Masonry continues to grow proportiona tely. the capacity of
3100 proposed, would accommodate only three fourths of those desiring
and entitled to attend Grand Lodge. Consequent ly a 6 million dollar
investment, and meeting only a total of 100 days in 20 years, would
represent a cost of $60.000 per DAY, or $300,000 per YEAR for using
the Auditorium only 5 days each year. For more than a Century, we
have been a "Speculativ e" Society of Free and Accepted Masons: we
should not be asked to pay for so costly an edifice which we can use
only 5 days each year, while the public could use it 360 days per year
at a rental nowhere nearly commensura te with the cost of the building.

never to suffer our passions and prejudices to become the master of
our judgment. Is it using good judgment for us to hastily build a
glamorous, luxurious auditorium by going into great debt, involving
tremendous interest-cost, when we need it FOR ONLY 5 DAYS EACH
YEAR? Many other organization s with larger attendance at their
Annual Communications do NOT own their auditorium. Let's stick to
the Committee's "ONE" motto-"Ma ke Haste Slowly"-an d let's
build without Interest.
The Brethren on the Grand Lodge Committee, headed by our very
able and popular Past Grand Master, Brother Ed. Siems, are of such
high calibre and such high standing in the Fraternity that they surely
do not want to be placed in the position of disregarding the objections
of two-thirds of our Brethren, by persisting in forcing their proposed

respectfully offered as an alternative:
Now therefore be it resolved:
That the land presently owned on Nob Hill be resold for not less
than total gross cost of same, and proceeds placed in fund with
other moneys for a new Temple.
That $9.00 be collected from each new applicant for the Degrees:
and that the $1.00 per capita assessment be continued for the
next ten ( 10) years to accumulate a fund to build an adequate
meeting place, seating five thousand ( 5,000): said meeting place
to be built of reinforced concrete, but of unpretentious architecture and design, air-conditioned, to have comfortable seats,
be conveniently locate~ to ample public transportation, and
within easy walking distance of major downtown hotels, be on
more level ground, and if possible be located in the vicinity of
Market street.
That the new Temple be planned so as to hav~ a public garage
underneath the entire building, and enough Lodge Halls and/or
offices built above .the Auditorium to provide sufficient rental
revenue to cover, as near as can be determined, the cost of maintenance and taxes.
That the total cost of new Temple be approved by Grand Lodge
before any construction be started.
That the Grand Lodge Annual Communications continue to meet
in the Civic Auditorium in San Francisco or such other place
designated by Grand Lodge until new Auditorium is completed.

such declared intent the Grand Lodge hereby formally transfers

EDWARD H. SIEMS, P.M. No. 560

JoHN C. BoVEY, P.M. No. 166
Referred to Committee on Finance.

RESOLVED: That Ross Digest be amended by inserting the
language quoted below as subparagraph E. under subsection 1. of Sec.
86. and as subparagraph ( e) under subsection 1. of Sec. 152.1 :
"Investment certificates issued by a building and loan association
or a savings and loan association organized and existing under
the laws of the State of California which is an insured institution
as defined by Title IV of the National Housing Ad, and shares
issued by any such association which issues no investment certifl..
cates and which is an insured institution as defined by said Title
IV, and shares issued by any federal savings and loan association."
Reason~ for suggested amendment:
Under our existing law as recently construed by our Grand Master,
neither shares nor certificates issued by state or federal building or
savings and loan associations are eligible for investment of Lodge funds,
or Grand Lodge funds.
This amendment would therefore eliminate the discrimination which
now exists against the securities of such state and federal associations.
All .federal savings and loan associations are insured institutions.
Since the amendment is limited to securities issued by insured insti•
tutions and to the types of securities which are insured, the suggested
amendment is conservative in its character.
Respectfully submitted,
JOHN R. MOORE
Past Master,
Meridian Lodge No. 667
Referred to Committees on Jurisprudence, Investment and on Policy
and General Purposes.

RESTORATION BY GRAND LODGE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
WHEREAS, under sections 344 and 345 of Ross Digest it is possible for a Mason who has been suspended or expelled for unmasonic
conduct to be restored to all the rights and .privileges of Masonry upon
a showing of good cause therefor: and
WHEREAS, a Mason who has been suspended for nonpayment of
dues for more than two years should be equally entitled to apply to
this Grand Lodge for restoration: and
WHEREAS, it appears doubtful if a Mason who has been suspended for nonpayment of dues is entitled to proceed under the cited
sections 344 and 345;
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that sections 344
and 345 of Ross Digest be amended to read as follows:
Sec. 344. T.he Grand Lodge may, at any Annual Communication, if good cause therefor be shown and proof be given of the
notice hereinafter prescribed, restore to the rights and privileges
of Masonry, any Mason who for cause, including nonpayment
of dues, has been suspended or expelled within its jurisdiction,
but such restoration shall not restore him to membership in the
Lodge by which he was suspended or expelled.
Sec. 345. Whenever any Mason, suspended for nonpayment of
dues or for unmasonic conduct, desires to petition the Grand
Lodge for restoration to the rights and privileges of Masonry,
he shall first make application for such restoration to the Lodge
by which he was suspended, if it still be in existence. If his application be there refused, it may then be made to the Grand
Lodge, provided that notice, in writing, be given to the Lodge
of such intended application, not less than forty days preceding
the Annual Communication.
WM. NANKERVIS, JR.
P.M., Oak Grove ·Lodge No. 215
Referred to Committees on Jurisprudence and on Policy and General
Pur.poses.

UNETHICAL PROMOTION
The following resolution included in the report of the Committee on
Publications was presented with the concurrence of the Committees on
Policy and General Purposes and on Jurisprudence.
RESOLVED: That a new section numbered 126.1 be added to the
Ordinances of Grand Lodge and inserted in Ross Digest, reading as
follows:
"Section 126.1. No Lodge or body, or organization requiring
Masonic affiliation as a condition to membership, or member
thereof shall, directly or indirectly, engage in any business, project, venture, promotion, scheme or plan which is unethical, fraudulent, misleading or illegal. Any violation of this section shall be
deemed un-Masonic conduct."

INTERPRETAT ION OF APPLICATION QUESTION 13
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
WHEREAS. so-called Masonic Clubs and Social Organizations,
the prerequisite of which requires membership in a Blue Lodge, were

96

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

ruled by Grand Master Morrison in 1944 under the prohibitions of
question 13 in the application for the Degrees of Masonry, as not being
affected by the 6 months rule-which ruling was changed in 1953 to
12 months plus the additional requirement of proficiency in the Candidates Lecture of the 3rd Degree, and
WHEREAS, said so-called Masonic Clubs do definitely tend to
create increased Blue Lodge activities, interest and attendance, and
WHEREAS, the existence of and interest in such Clubs also helps
to awaken a desire in many prospective applicants to become interested
in Masonry by reason of their fellow workers' Blue Lodge activities in
which they as co-workers are not invited to ·participate, and
WHEREAS, it is .t he opinion of the undersigned and many others
with whom this has been discussed, that it was not the intention of the
sponsors of the 1953 Resolution to include such Clubs in the prohibitions,
but merely to increase the time to 12 months and require the new member to make his proficiency in the 3rd degree before being allowed to
take any of the so-called higher degrees of Masonry, or to join any affiliate groups such as the Eastern Star, Sciots, etc.,
BE IT THEREFORE RESOLVED, question 13 of the application
not apply to so-called Masonic Clubs, etc.: that they are strictly Blue
Lodge activities wherein there are not formal initiations and have no
connections with the so-called higher orders of Masonry and/ or affiliate
groups.
Respectfully submitted,

F. T. NAGLE

REPORT OF GRAND TREASURER
For Fiscal Year Ended July 31, 1955
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Your Grand Treasurer, succeeded to this office only because of the
seriousness of the illness of our beloved P.G.M. Francis V. Keesling.
Our fond hopes for his speedy and complete recovery have not been
realized. It is my information that members of his immediate family
suggested that his best interest would be served by relieving him of the
ttsponsibility of the office.
Immediately following the election on October 15, 1954, your Grand
Treasurer consulted with the Assistant Grand Treasurer, Brother Paul
Pflueger and the Grand Secretary, Lloyd E. Wilson, in order to become
conversant with the affairs of the office. The fact that Brother Paul
Pflueger had actually functioned as Acting Grand Treasurer for the
previous two years simplified the problem considerably.

As of the first of the fiscal year Brother Walter A. Parker, who had
served ten years as auditor, found it desirable to retire from the public
accounting field and voluntarily relinquished the auditing of all of our
accounts. Afte,r careful investigation we retained the firm of Skinner &
Hammond, Certified Public Accountants, of which Brother James E.
Hammond, P.M. of Park Boulevard Lodge No. 568, is a partner. Brother
Hammond has been in active charge and supervision of the auditing of
all of our funds and accounts for the current fiscal year.
The printed reports of the auditors containing detailed financial
statements of Grand Lodge F. & A. M., the Masonic Homes of California, including the permanent Endowment Fund, and the California
Masonic Memorial Temple, are available to all our Lodges. Also,
included in these reports are complete lists of all securities owned. These
securities are all held in safekeeping by the Trust Department of the
Anglo California National Bank at its main office in San Francisco.
Heretofore the Grand Treasurer in his annual report also reported
on the activities of the Investment Committee since the Grand Treasurer
from its inception has been the Chairman of that Committee. No one
has or could question this policy since, by legislation, all funds and
securities of the Grand Lodge, the Masonic Homes, the Endowment
Fund, Temple Funds and other special funds are placed in the custody
of the Grand Treasurer of the Grand Lodge, to be held by him as such

102

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

and to be by him accounted for and disbursed pursuant to the provisions
of the constitution and ordinances of the Grand Lodge.
Even with such strong precedent, tradition and legislation your
Grand Treasurer, after consultation with the Grand Master and others,
felt that the Grand Lodge could best be served at the present time by
recommending to the Investment Committee that we break precedent
in this instance and have Brother Paul A. Pflueger, Assistant Grand
Treasurer, continue acting as Chairman of the Investment Committee,
the position he had held all during the current illness of Grand Treasurer,
Francis V. Keesling.
Brother Pflueger has been on the Investment Committee since its
inception. He did much of the necessary research and planning in establishing our present investment policy under the modified prudent man
rule. He is eminently qualified for he has celebrated over 50 active years
of success in the field of finance. Brethren, we are indeed fortunate to
have such a capable and experienced person to head this important
committee. These extenuating circumstances in the opinion of the Investment Committee justified breaking tradition in this instance and their
concurrence in your Grand Treasurer's recommendation was unanimous.
A separate report for the Investment Committee will be presented by
our Assistant Grand Treasurer, Brother Paul A. Pflueger at a later date.
Following is a summary of the income and capital receipts and the
expense disbursements of Grand Lodge F. & A. M., the Masonic Homes
of California, including the Permanent and Other Endowment Funds,
and the California Masonic Memorial Temple for the fiscal year ended
July 31, 1955:

REPORT OF THE PRESIDENT OF THE CALIFORNIA

It is hoped this brief summary will stimulate your real interest and
encourage each officer present to study the audit reports on Grand
Lodge F. & A. M. of ~alifornia, the Masonic Homes of California, including the Permanent and Other Endowment Funds, and the California
Masonic Memorial Temple. It is recommended that some time be set
aside at an early stated meeting of your lodge to review them. I am
confident that most every lodge has within its membership a certified

affiliated organizations and their own lodge.

connection with the audit service.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Under authority heretofore granted by this Grand Lodge, the California Masonic Memorial Temple Corporation was incorporated on
January 6, 1954. The by-laws of that corporation provide for eleven
trustees, eight of whom shall be appointed by the Grand Master and
the three others to consist of the Deputy Grand Master and the Senior
and Junior Grand Wardens who shall be ex-officio trustees.
The corporation has held a number of meetings since its incorporation. The Grand Master, who has acted as legal advisor to the corporation, has drawn and/or approved all technical documents and resolutions presented for action by the Board of Trustees.
Under prior authority granted by this Grand Lodge, title to the
property located on California Street between Jones and Taylor Streets,
in San Francisco, California, owned by the corporation, has now been
transferred into the name of the corporation, and on October 5, 1955
properly executed documents covering financing of the proposed California Masonic Memorial Temple were signed and recorded. Th.is offi ..
cially cleared the way for the California Masonic Memorial Temple
Committee to enter into additional contracts, clearing the property, preparatory to actual construction of the proposed California Masonic
Memorial Temple.
Respectfully submitted,
EDWARD H. SIEMS
President, Board of Trustees

REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California, F. 6 A. M.
In presenting this the eighth annual report of your Special Committee on California Masonic Memorial Temple, we do so with a feeling of culmination in anticipation of action. Through the cooperation
of our Masonic leadership throughout the jurisdiction, this Grand Lodge
will on Wednesday, October 26, 1955, break ground ofBcially starting
construction of that which was once but a dream, the California
Masonic Memorial Temple-the first official Home ever owned in its
entirety by this Grand Lodge.
At the risk of repetition, it is suggested that because so many brethren attending this Grand Lodge Session are here for the first time
(estimated to be about 40% of total attendance) that all reports of this
Special Committee and all action by Grand Lodge heretofore taken in
connection with the California Masonic Memorial Building project be
incorporated by reference and be made a part of this 1955 Committee
Report. To assist any of those brethren here who may be interested in
reviewing these prior reports, copies of the printed proceedings for the
years 1948 through 1954 are available at the California Masonic Memorial Temple exhibit located in the hall of this building, or in the office
of the Grand Lodge at 25 Van Ness Avenue, San Francisco.

PROGRESS SINCE OCTOBER

PLANNING

The general working plans have been completed. The arChitect,
Brother Albert F. Roller, a member of Excelsior Lodge No. 166, and
his staff, in cooperation with your Committee, have devoted many hours
of thought and time to every detail with particular emphasis on utility,
functional quality, appearance, dignity, sculpture, the memorial fea ..
tures, and the comfort of those attending our annual sessions, with the
hope, of course, that the combined efforts will be accepted with favor
by the general membership of California Masons and all Masons and
friends who visit and use the Temple.
Before final decisions were made we tried to answer the question,
·"Is this in keeping with the mandate of Grand Lodge?" The many sug ..
gestions and recommendations made by the brethren received full Committee consideration. In this connection, we are grateful to Past Grand
Master Leon 0. W·hitsell, Chairman of the Masonic History Committee,
and its members for their valuable suggestions on the historical matter
to be portrayed in the endomosaic window over the entrance. Many

FUND RAISING EFFORT

In October 1953, the Grand Lodge adopted the following general
policy recommendations affecting the financing and construction of the
California Masonic Memorial Temple:
(a) The program of financing should contemplate long-term bor..
rowing;
( b) The goal for each constituent lodge was set at a minimum average contribution of not less than $10.00 per member;
( c) The $1.00 annual per capita theretofore adopted be made a
constitutional provision of our regulations;
( d) Section 100 ( b) of the Constitution was amended to provide
for a $9.00 contribution to the California Masonic Memorial
Temple fund by each applicant for the degrees of masonry:
( e) Your committee was authorized to have working plans completed and bids taken by not less than five contractors when
satisfactory plans for financing were complete.
The above' recommendations, although ,briefed here, may be found
on pages 139-141 in the 1953 proceedings.
Immediately following the close of the 1953 annual communication
your Committee set in motion the execution of the policies theretofore
adopted. Actually, because of the time involved in planning, preparing
and organizing a workable program, the fund raising effort was launched
about March 15, 1954. During the first seven months, or up to Grand
Lodge (Octo'b er 9, 1954), there had :been subscribed through voluntary
contributions $866,065.27 by 49,431 members of California lodges.
At the 1954 annual commmunication your Committee recommended
and Grand Lodge adopted as policy, that the fund raising effort on a
voluntary basis ·be extended to July 31, 1955, reaffirming the minimum
average of $10.00 per member. The Committee was also authorized to
negotiate the sale of the Masonic Temple stock owned by the Grand
Lodge in the Temple at 25 Van Ness Avenue.
Following the 1954 annual communication most of the constituent
lodges continued the fund raising effort in "high gear." Many developed new and original ideas to suit the local situation. Assistance
offered ·b y your Committee was used to advantage by many lodges. The

111

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

effort has been productive of splendid results. As of noon, October 24, '
1955, an additional $356,991.64 was subscribed, making a grand total
through voluntary contributions since the start of this program, March
15, 1954, of $1,223,056.91. This amount ·b as been subscribed by 72,985
Masons representing 648 lodges for an average of $16.75 per individual
subscription. Of the grand total subscribed all but $177,391.90 has been
paid in cash. Many of the brethren have anticipated their pledges and
are paid in full. This is truly a ndble effort and all praise to those whose
contributions have made possible the program of ground-breaking on
October 26, 1955.
Every dollar contributed to this building fund will be used 100%
for construction. The expense of the fund raising effort was paid by
Grand Lodge.

This program will obviously result in a balance due at the end of
the l 0 year term unless we are able to take advantage of the privilege
which we have of anticipating payments without penalty, should our
financial position permit.
It is the considered judgment of your Committee, based on the
studies made to date and requests for use of the building by outside
groups, that revenue from the building and garage should within a
few years cover the cost of operation.

SALB OF 25 VAN NESS AVENUE TEMPLE STOCK
Pursuant to authority of the Grand Lodge granted at the 1954 annual communication, a special committee consisting of your Grand
Treasurer, Edward H. Siems, your Assistant Grand Treasurer, Paul A.
P8ueger, and Past Grand Master, Arthur M. Warren, met a number
of times with a special committee of the Board of Directors of the Temple
Association, consisting of Brothers Ira W. Cdburn, Grand Marshal and
Past Master of Doric Lodge No. 216, R. W. Blosser, Past Master of
Ingleside ·Lodge No. 630, and C. C. Trowbridge, Jr., Past Master of
California Lodge No. 1.
After a thorough exploration and a most cooperative undertaking,
an agreement was reached whereby the 33,985 shares of stock owned
by the Grand Lodge was sold to the Masonic Temple Association of
California for $7.50 per share, or a total of $254,887.50.
A resolution has been presented to Grand Lodge for official approval at this session to make the funds received therefrom available to
the California Masonic Memorial Temple Fund.
l.oNG-TERM BoRROWING
Six San Francisco Banks, namely, American Trust Company, Anglo
Califo~ia National Bank, Bank of America, N. T. and S. A., The
Bank of California, N. A., Crocker First National Bank and Wells
Fargo Bank have agreed to loan to the California Masonic Memorial
Temple, a California corporation, 50% of the cost of the construction
and cost of land, but not to exceed $3,000,000 at 4% interest per annum on declining balances. The loan is for a period of l 0 years, amortized at 4% annually of the original commitment, or on whatever lesser
sum may be borrowed. No commitment fee is being charged. Interest
will accrue only as the money is drawn, and we may repay as much
annually on the principal as we wish without penalty. We express our
appreciation to these Banks for their cooperation.

On behalf of the entire Committee and all others active in the Campaign, we desire to pay a well-deserved tribute to Brother Harold D.
Weber, Committee Coordinator, and the office staff which, under his
direction, so efficiently handled the details of the Campaign.

RESOLUTION
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California, F. 5 A.M.:
WHEREAS, at each Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge for
the past 8 years, beginning with 1947, the proposal to build a new Masonic Memorial Temple has been before the Grand Lodge for its consideration, and
WHEREAS, there have been in attendance at these 8 Communications
a total of 15,504 Masters, Wardens and Past Masters, representing an
average of 575 Lodges at each Session, and
WHEREAS, after full and free discussion of each and every proposal
these representatives of the Lodges have voted to construct such a Memorial Temple, and

113

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

WHEREAS, these representatives of Lodges approved the ultimate
plan as now proposed, and
WHEREAS, to finance the construction, in part, these representatives
of Lodges approved a campaign for voluntary contributions with the
objective of securing at least $10.00 per member, and
WHEREAS, such a campaign has been in progress since March 14,
1954, and has produced in cash contributions and pledges $1,223,056.91,
.
·
and
WHEREAS, many Lodges and their members have made a magnificent
contribution to this program, averaging more than $10.00 per member,
and others have done very well, and
WHEREAS, some Lodges and their members have not effectively promoted the campaign for contributions, and
WHEREAS, the failure of these Lodges to reach $10.00 per member
creates an inequity among the Lodges and the members which results
in an unequal bearing of the burden, and
WHEREAS, it is the essence of Freemasonry that the will of the
majority shall always govern the entire Craft and the burdens and
responsibilities shall fall equally upon all, and
WHEREAS, it is now desirable that this fundamental of Freemasonry
be carried out in the Masonic Memorial Temple project,
Now, Therefore, Be It Resolved that the representatives of the
Lodges at this 106th Annual Communication levy an assessment on the
Lodges of $10.00 for each Master Mason carried on its rolls as of July
31, 1956, and
Be It Further Resolved that each Lodge have credited against its
total assessment the full amount of all its contributions in the hands of
the Grand Secretary prior to July 1, 1956, and
Be It Further Resolved that the difference between the amount of
the total assessment and the amount of contributions received shall be
due and payable with the Annual Returns in five installments, commencing with the Annual Returns of 1956, and
Be It Further Resolved that such portion of each annual installment
as is not contributed voluntarily by the members shall be paid from the
Lodge treasury.

MEMBERSHIP

In presenting the members'hip totals for the year I have also given
the Bgures for the preceding four years in order that there may be
readily shown the progress being made in this present decade.
There have been 17 new Lodges formed during the year, and there
are many others whkh are in some stage of organization and will,
undoubtedly. request a dispensation during the coming year. The membership continues to grow and is at an all time high of 224,887 including
463 plural members.
Since I · was Grand Master in 1940-41 we have added approximately 100 Lodges and almost 100,000 members. It is clear that Masonry
is growing in this state and that we are not likely to have any worries
as far as "quantity" is concerned. The emphasis on "quality" must,
however, never be relaxed if we are to maintain our own fundamentals
and merit the general good pu:blic opinion of the Fraternity.

CONSOLIDATION

Forest Lodge No. 66, located at Alleghany, has in recent years been
a victim of the curtailing of gold mining. It is reminiscent of the early
days that ghost towns are created when mining ceases and Masons,
along with others, depart for more productive fields. This has been true
in the case of Forest Lodge No. 66 where only four members remain
in Alleghany.
The difficulties of continuing a Lodge are obvious, and after several
years of devoted effort the members have reluctantly voted to consolidate with Gravel Range Lodge No. 59 at Camptonville, with which
Lodge they have always had the most friendly relations.
All the requirements of the constitution have been met, and the
new Lodge desires to ·be known as Gravel Range Lodge No. 59.
Once more, due to circumstances beyond our control, we bid a
sorrowful farewell to a splendid old Lodge which always upheld the
finest principles of the institution in the mining area which it served.
CENTENNIAL CELEBRATION

When the Grand Lodge of California celebrated its Centennial in
October, 1950, the Grand Lodge of Canada in the Province of Ontario
was ably represented lby its Grand Secretary, Right Worshipful Ewart
G. Dixon. At that time Brother Dixon extended an invitation to California to be present in Toronto when the Centennial of the Grand Lodge
of Canada was observed.
Most Worshipful Henry C. Clausen, Grand Master, was unable
to attend due to his own heavy S<:hedule, and ·he designated the Grand
Secretary to ·be the official representative of the Grand Lodge of California and the special representative of the Grand Master. The Grand
Secretary attended the Centennial Celebration July 13th to 17th, and
tdbute must be paid to our Canadian Brethren for the magnificent manner in which the observance was conducted. Everything possible was
done for the entertainment of the guests, and all were impressed with
the 'SOiemnity and dignity with which the program was carried out.
California was honored by the selection of Most Worshipful Ellsworth Meyer, Past Grand Master, as the principal speaker. His address
was delivered at a !banquet attended by 3,300 Master Masons. Past
Grand Master Meyer, always a most effective speaker, was at his best
and everyone who had the opportunity to hear him profited greatly.

REPORT OF THE TRUSTEE S
OF THE MASONIC HOMES
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
The Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California herewith present
the Sixty-Third Annual Report for the year ending July 31, 1955, together with the reports of the Superintendents of our Homes and the
flnandal reports of the Treasurer and Secretary.
The Board of Trustees met in Covina, California, on November 27,
1954, for the transaction of regular business and for the purpose of
organization. The election of Edgar V. Stewart, Jr., Deputy Grand
Master, L. Harold Anderson, Senior Grand Warden, and Leo E. Anderson, Junior Grand Warden, was formally reported to the Board and
on motion duly made, seconded and carried, they were elected members
of the Board.
President Wollenberg reported the reappointment of Arthur M.
Warren and Ralph Head for a term of three years each and on motion
duly made, seconded and carried, they were elected members of the
Board.
·
To ftll the vacancy created by the election of Leo E. Anderson to
the office of Junior Grand Warden the Grand Master announced the
appointment of Guy B. Mize for the unexpired term and on motion
duly made, seconded and carried he was elected a member of the Board.
In addition to the Deputy Grand Master, Senior and Junior Grand
Wardens, the Board is composed of the following Trustees:
Charles Albert Aclams..................19SS............................ Myron E. Smith
Charles M. Wollenherg ................ 1956...•......•-·······-··········Guy B. Mize
Arthur M. W arren.....••.........,.......1957.........•.......,..........•. Ralph H. Head
On motion duly made, seconded and carried, Charles M. Wollenberg was elected President of the Board.
On motion duly made, seconded and carried Myron E. Smith was
elected Vice-President of the Board.
By virtue of his office as Grand Treasurer of Grand Lodge, F. & A.M.
of California, Past Grand Master Edward H. Siems is Treasurer of
Masonic Homes of California.

GENERAL

The Board urges all members of the Fraternity to read carefully the
reports of Superintendent James R. Eubanks of the Home for the Aged
at Decoto, and Superintendent Robert M. Henry of the Home for Children at Covina which are a part of this report.
. .
Two types or classes of Decoto admission problems ar.e ~1vmg your
Board of Trustees increasing concern. Our Rules of Adm1ss1on, for ~e
Decoto Home, adopted by the Grand Lodge many years ago, requ1~e
that applicants be (a) in financial need and ( b) am~ulatory, ~at. is,
able to take care of themselves and their rooms at th~ time of ad~1ss10~.
More and more cases are coming before us in which the applicant 1s
not entirely ambulatory. but is either a partial inval~d, requiring nursi~g
home care, or is an aged senile, requiring custodial or semi-custod1~l
care. Technically, under our Rules, neither of these classes of cases is
eligible for admission to Decoto.
NuRSING HoME CASES

Through the extension of Outside Relief we are endeavoring to provide for the partial invalids, whom we classify as the nursing home type
of cases. At the present time we have on Outside Relief seven who are
in nursing homes and seven who are residing with relatives or friends.
In cooperation with the Lodges, we are contributing ~o or meeting p~rt
or all of the cqst of such nursing home care-the aid extended being
limited to a maximum equivalent to the per capita cost of care at Decoto.
The suggestion has come to your Board tha~ ~ way be ~ound to
admit to Decoto such nursing home cases. Realizing that this would
require a revision of the Rules of Admission and an expansion of the
facilities at the Decoto Home, your Trustees are giving the p1'0blem and
its potential costs. careful study, investigation and analysis.
AGED SENILE CASES

Applications from the aged senile, who are neither dangerous to
themselves nor others, but who require custodial or semi-custodial care.
present our most difficult problem. In former years, such cases were
cared for largely by the State of California but, in recent years, the
State has adopted a policy ·placing upon the Counties total responsibility for these people. The Counties themselves are not equipped to meet
the problem, with the result that more applications of this type have
been coming to your Board.
We have met this ·problem partially but have been unable to under·
take a total solution. In the North Wing of the Decoto Home we have
added twenty-eight beds and arranged facilities and assigned personnel

140

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

for the care of a limited number of such applicants. To meet the total
problem, however, would require a considerable enlargement of our
present hospital unit and a substantially higher overhead in the costs
of operation of the Home at Decoto.
As with the nursing home care problem, we are making an extensive
study of how best to care for the increasing number of the aged senile
who are turning to the Masonic Fraternity for help. At this time we
have no recommendations to submit, but desire only to acquaint the
Brethren with the problems before us.

CONSTRUCTION AT DECOTO

LETTER OF APPRECIATION

While your Board gives every attention to criticisms of any kind,
we sometimes think we do not pay sufficient attention to letters of appreciation of which a great many are received. The following letter
from Mrs. Peairs, admitted to the Home on February 11, 1935, is so
pleasing to us that we would like to share it with you.
Sky View Porch
August 26, 1955
Mr. Charles M. Wollenberg,
President, Board of Trustees
Dear Sir and Esteemed Friend:
Ever since I told you I would try to express in writing what I had
just said about our new North Wing and our wonderful porch (I like
porch bette~. tha~ sol~~ium) I ha~e tried to find a new word expressing
more than gratitude but my eighty-seven year old brain refuses to
coin a new word-so it must remain deep gratitude.
To have the consideration given us in this our life's afterglow when
our usefulness has faded with the sunset prompts feelings words cannot
express. After twenty years of happy service-now to sit and watch the
beauty of the clouds so near they tangle with the tree tops, 'and at night
the myriads of lights below dodging in and out, and all around up here
the silent, quiet stars.
In this beautiful place and the care which you provide so bountifully,
I feel we may have and know "The Peace of God that passeth understanding." So to you and all who have made this possible, my heartfelt
thanks.
And thank you, too, for our Mr. Eubanks; as I have known him so
well over the years, he has become to me the epitome of patience and
kindliness and a desire to increase the comfort and happiness of every
member of our Home.
So I thank you and bless you all.
Sincerely,
Lillian W. Peairs
441 North
Masonic Home

141

Much has been done this past year to improve the physical condition of our Home at Decoto.
Three old elevators have 1been replaced by three automatic Otis
elevators and these are now operating very satisfactorily.
The operating equipment for the north elevator has been raised in
order to enable that elevator to serve the fifth floor; this has added
to the convenience of the residents.
A large window at the intersection of the east and north wings on
the fourth Boor has been installed and a concrete deck at the north end
of the fourth floor has been covered and glassed in.
A dining room and a kitchen have been arranged in the north wing
of the fourth floor. This cares for 30 to 35 of the semi-invalid members
of the Home.
During the year a new well was bored and is now producing water
in excess of the Home's needs. It supplies water for our 95 head of
cattle and irrigates our orchard and five acres of alfalfa.
THE HOME AT COVINA

In the Home for Children at Covina a wonderful spirit prevails
among the children and the splendid staff responsible for their care.
Under the administration of Superintendent Robert M. Henry, the children are making excellent progress and every California Mason may
be justly proud of them.
Throughout the community, our children receive recognition for
good citizenshi,p, for scholarship, for leadership and for their participation in character building youth activities. Upon graduation they are,
with your help and inspiration, finding their way on into gainful and
useful occupations and becoming upstanding American citizens.
For increased efficiency of the staff at the Home, we have added to
the personnel an Assistant to the Superintendent, whose function it is
to aid and assist the Superintendent in the administration of the Home.
His presence is extending greatly the effectiveness of the Superintendent, the houseparents and the entire staff, particularly in supplying the
counsel and guidance so important to children today. That adequate
housing might be available, a new residence is in process of construction for the Superintendent, following the completion of which the old
residence will be occupied by the Assistant.
We are especially happy and pleased that our new Assistant's wife
is a graduate of the Covina Home. We should like also to report that
our Southern Social Welfare Worker is a graduate of the Home at
Covina.
The problem of establishing a per capita tax for the operation of
the Homes is difficult due to certain variables which are not easy to
forecast.

142

143

GRAND LODGE OP CALIPORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

Among them are the number of candidates who pay the $25.00
Homes' Fee: the uncertainty of investment markets two years hence in
connection with security income and the unknown factor of profits or
losses from sales of securities and real estate which depend upon mar~
ket conditions.
It is appropriate to point out that the per capita tax is levied at one
communication, payable at the close of the fiscal year nine months later
and the moneys collected therefrom provide for the fiscal year ending
one year thereafter.
A study of reports for the last twelve years indicates a falling off of
initiates who 'have provided as high as $389,000 in 1947 to a low of
$246,000 in the year just closed. On the other hand, investment income
has risen from $57,000 in 1944 to $264,000 in the current year. Further,
sales of securities and real estate. etc. provided $89,000 in 1955 which
was the highest in the years under review. Three of those years provided
no income from this source and others very moderately. This brings
forcibly the conclusion that in making forecasts this source of revenue
should be disregarded.
In the expense category our experience has been the same as all
institutions and businesses who have to compete in the open market for
services and supplies. Total expenses have risen from $242,800 in 1945
to $651,300 in 1955-an increase of 270%.

To the Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California:
Brethren: Once again I am privileged to present for your consideration this, the 56th Superintendent's report of the operation of the
Masonic Home here at Decoto, and the 15th during my stewardship,
for the year ending July 31, 1955.
It is always a pleasure to report that conditions at the Home are
satisfactory, and no drastic change has taken place in the Home during
the past 12 months.
At the beginning of the year there were 122 men and 197 women, a
total c>f 319. Thirty-seven women, average age 79 years, and thirty-two
men, average age 80 years, were admitted during the year. During the
same period 21 women, average age 83 years, and 22 men, average age
80 years, passed away, 3 men and 1 woman were withdrawn. The population on August 1, 1955, was 128 men and 212 women, a total of 340.
Included in this number are thirteen married couples.

The above jnformation indicates that a large majority o£ the residents
of the Home have lived far beyond that proverbial four-score and ten.
The fact that only 74 members are hospitalized further indicates that a
very large majority of the members are enjoying fairly good health.
Those who must be 1hospitalized are receiving excellent care, in a
most kindly and efficient manner, under the watchful eye of Miss Bess
Payne, our Head Nurse.
Doctors from the Palo Alto Clinic visit the sick in our hospital 6ve
days a week. On these visits arrangements are made for any mem·ber of
the Home who feels the need of a doctor's advice, to see the doctor.
The doctors' orders for these cases are referred to Miss Payne, whose
ttsponsibility it is to see that these orders, in all cases, a.re carried out.
Dr. William O'Connor, of Hayward, spends every Wednesday
forenoon in our Dental Clinic, which was added to our hospital facilities
last year. This dental arrangement enables Dr. O'Connor to render a
much !better service to a greater number of our members, especially those
who find it impossible, due to infirmities, to get to his office in Hayward.
We have 1been faced, in the past, with the problem of serving meals
to members in the main building when their physical condition ·became
such that they could no longer make the trip to the dining room. The

H7

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CAJ.IPORNIA

problem was solved, not very satisfactorily. however, by sending such
members to the hospital. This was not a very desirable arrangement from
the mem!bers' point of view, and very often it worked a hardship on the
hospital inasmuch as quite often beds used by such members were needed
for hospital patients.
In an effort to correct this condition, and to enable such members to
live a somewhat normal existence without over exertion, quarters were
arranged on the North and East wings of the fourth floor. Here they
have a private room, and a dining room where meals are served from an
adjoining kitchenette. For diversion, they have a Television Room where
they are privil~ged to have programs of their own choice. A covered
closed-in glass sun deck, and a large wide window have been provided
where they can sit by the hour and enjoy the scenery of the valley below.
Mrs. Maud Teass assumed the responsilbilities of the very important
office of Matron of the Home abour a year ago. During her short tenure
of office, she has met every prOblem squarely, and proven herself very
capable, and through friendliness and square dealing, is becoming very
popular. In addition to her many other duties, Mrs. Teass found time
to have the furniture placed in the rooms in the North wing and assign
the members to their rooms. She also staffed the department and has it
operating quite smoothly.
Brother Gail David, who was appointed Assistant Superintendent a
year ago, is handling the details of his office in a very satisfactory manner. He is quite busy trying to put our stock farm on a paying basis, and
the development of the well will be very helpful. He will now be able
to produce more ·feed to fatten the stock.
The other important department heads remain the same as last year,
and are operating very efficiently.
I am pleased to report that the installation of the three elevators,
mentioned in my last year's report, has ibeen completed and are all
operating very satisfactorily. The lift machinery of the North Wing
elevator was raised to enable this elevator to serve the fifth floor of the
Administration Building. This change, needless to say. is appreciated
by the ladies who have rooms on that floor.
For some time past, our water supply was very limited, and at times
not sufficient. Last fall the well dried up completely, and as a result, we
had to purchase water from the Peoples Utility Co. of Niles. The first
part of the year we decided we would make an effort to develop a well
that would provide an ample supply of water for the Home. A location
was decided on, and a 12 inch well, 248 .feet deep, was drilled. At the
completion of the drilling operation we found that our efforts were well
rewarded. We had 174 feet of water in the well. A pump was placed
on the well and 168,000 gallons were pumped during an eight hour
test run.

Following this test run the water was again measured, and we found
that the water level had been lowered only 14 feet. We feel. therefore,
that the water problem of the Home has been solved for the present, and
from all indications for the far distant future as well.
Our guest register indicates that 4,089 visitors signed the register
during the year. Representatives from 411 California Lodges, 29 states
and 4 foreign jurisdictions are represented in that total.
During the year 26 degrees w~re exemplified in Siminoff Temple by
Lodges from various parts of the jurisdiction, some as far south as Los
Angeles. The 50 entertainments, whkh were presented by various
groups were enjoyed very much by the Home folks. Fifty-five movie
programs were provided gratis by the following Film Distributing Companies of San Francisco: RKO, Columbia Pictures, United Artists,
Warner Brothers and Twentieth Century Fox. All of these programs
were enjoyed immensely by the members of the Masonic Home. We,
therefore, want to assure the above mentioned Film Distributing Companies that their generosity is deeply appreciated by the Home folks.
The East Bay Past Matrons' Association, under the leadership of
their President, Mrs. Beatrice Rule, P. M., made their annual visit to
the Masonic Home on August 25, 1954. This yearly visit has ·become
known as our "Jam and Jelly Day." On this occasion, in addition to the
7,899 jars of jam, jelly, fruit juices, etc., our hospital was presented with
92 hospital gowns, which the good ladies had made; 16 bedspreads, also
an assortment of women's clothing, needles, thread, dress material,
custom-made jewelry and $37.00 in cash.
After the above business was taken care of. a delicious luncheon was
served in our Banquet Room in honor of Worthy Grand Matron Bernice
Jan Basich and her Grand Lodge Officers. Following the luncheon, the
ladies adjourned to the Auditorium, where a delightful reception was
held in honor of Worthy Grand Matron Basich and her Grand Lodge
Officers.

To the Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California:
It is a privilege and a pleasure to present to you my seventh annual
report as Superintendent of the Masonic Home for Children at Covina,
for the year ending July 31, 1955.
HOME MEMBERSHIP

The population of our Covina Home Family for the year ending July
31, 1955, numbered seventy-four children, thirty-five girls and thirtynine boys. This is an increase of eight children over the preceding year.
During the year twenty-two children were ad·mitted to the Home, thirteen hoys and nine girls. In this same period ten boys and four girls
departed from the Home. Of this number, three girls and four boys were
graduated from Covina High School and six boys and one girl returned
to the re-established homes of their parents. Five of our graduates will
enter various colleges this fall, one girl graduate is employed by the
Telephone Company. while another, having successfully completed a
course in I. B. M .• is employed in industry. Three boys and three girls
were graduated from Charter Oak Grammar School and will enter
Covina High School at the beginning of the fall term.

HOME, SCHOOL AND COMMUNITY ACTMTIES

Full participation in school and civic youth activities is encouraged,
not only for training in good citizenship, hut for the benefits of such
participation in the rounding out of our family life at the Home. The
older children have represented the Home successfully in High School
through scholastic honors, service clubs, social activities and athletic
competition: while the younger children assume their full share of the
responsibility for the success of the Charter Oak Grammar School Car-

nival and other school activities. T 1he younger boys are members of Culb

HEALTH AND WELFARE PROGRAM

We are h~ppy to report no serious health problems this past year.
Under the guidance of Dr. W. P. Magan and his associates, and the
watchful eye of our nurse, Mrs. Hetty Fairfield, our children continue
to 1~ in excellent physical condition. Health progress reports are made
possible by the complete physical examination of each child at regular
interva~s. Special nourishment, extra rest and vitamin supplement, has
been given when needed. D. P. T. booster shots were administered to
all children in May__;before the beginning of our Summer Campin9 Program. Two patients reported for surgery, one for orthopedic surgery
and one for a tonsilectomy. One hundred and one dental treatments
were given in the Home Dental Clinic iby Dr. Elmer King, an alumnus
of Covina Home, who made examinations of the children's teeth at
periodic intervals. Fourteen children received orthodontia care with a
total of one hundred and thirty-two orthodontia treatments recorded for
the year. Dr. Wayne D. Kuettel, Covina, continued opthalmic examinations and visual treatments as a part of our health plan. Two hundred
and nineteen individual hospital admissions are recorded, with a total
of four hundred and thirty-two hospital days. Four thousand five hundred and four Home Hospital Clinic treatments were administered and
tfghty-seven prophylactic treatments were given. We cannot adequately
~press the depth of our appreciation to Dr. W. P. Magan and his assoaates for their constant ·Watchfulness and never ceasing devotion in
behalf of our boys and girls.

The painting' of the exterior of all building~ and the renovation and

To the Most Worshipfu l Grand Lodge of California:
I am presenting my third annual report, covering my own activities
as Grand Lecturer and those of the Ritual Committee.
Shortly after the Annual Communication last year, Brother Guy B.
Mize retired as Assistant Grand Lecturer for Division Five, to become
one of the trustees of the Masonic Homes. While we have lost an exceptionally able ritualist and administrator, we have been fortunate in
the appointme nt of his successor, Brother Donald G. Campbell, who
comes to the Committee with excellent experience.
The usual Conferenc es of Inspectors were conducted by the Assistant Grand Lecturers as foJJow:s:
Divisions 1 and 2 at Bijou, Lake Tahoe, June 17-18, 1955, conducted Jointly by Worshipf ul Clare B. CampbeJJ and Worshipf ul Ralph
M. Foote.
Division 3, at GuerneviJJe, May 6-8, 1955, conducted by Worshipf ul
Arthur J. Kahn.
Division 4, at Yosemite VaJJey, June 3-5, 1955, conducted by Worshipful Raymond G. Taylor.
Division 5, at Ojai, April 22-24, 1955, conducted by Worshipf ul
Donald G. Campbell.
Division 6, at Riverside, MarC'h 25-27, 1955, conducted by Worshipful Clark H. Shaw.
I had the priviJege of attending aJJ of these conferences, at which
the work was fuJJy and exceJJently done by the Inspectors of the reapective divisions. The Inspectors of Divisions One, Two and Six had
perfect attendanc e at their conferences.
At each of the conferences, the Inspectors were addressed by the
Grand Master and by the Grand Secretary on matters of interest and
Fportanc e.

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

At each of the conferences, meetings of the Ritual Committee were
held, to consider various matters of ritual. In addition, a special meeting of the Committee was held on December 3rd and 4th, 1954, at San
Francisco, with all members of the Committee present, at which meeting the entire work of the three degrees was reviewed and performed.
Annual reports have been received from all Inspectors in the jurisdiction, as required by Section 53 of the Ordinances. These reports
again reveal that our lodges, for the most part, are in good working condition and actively at work. As usual, however, certain weak spots have
appeared, to which special attention is being given by the Inspectors.
The matter of codes and ciphers, to which I referred last year, has
received our attention, and the Inspectors have been requested to warn
the officers of their districts that the use or even the possession of these
ciphers is ground for Masonic discipline. The Grand Master has further ruled that foreign ciphers, even though lawfully received, are nevertheless unlawful for the recipient to have or use in this jurisdiction.
The Inspectors 'have had difficulty in the past with the performance
of degree teams. At the commencement of this year, we adopted a rule
to require conformity to the adopted ritual on the part of all degree
teams, by requiring that before their appearance in any lodge they have
the approval of the Inspector as to each member of the team who intends to work. We believe that this has had a very salutary effect and
will tend to eliminate incapable and non-conforming degree teams. It
has placed some additional burdens on the Inspectors, particularly in
metropolitan areas. but they ·have responded with their usual fine spirit.
If the present rule does not have the desired effect, your Committee
will recommend more drastic supervision, because we believe that a degree team should be at least as efficient as the officers of any lodge.
Pursuant to the resolution adopted by Grand Lodge last year, for
a revision of the Funeral Service, the Grand Master referred the revision to the Ritual Committee, and a special report of the Committee has
been in your hands for several weeks and will be presented for action
later in this session.
The Committee has no suggestions for any changes in the esoteric
work.
In closing, may I express my personal appreciation to the Grand
Master for his courtesies during the year, and to the Grand Secretary
and Assistant Grand Secretary for their many helpful acts during the
year, and also my thanks to you brethren for giving me the opportunity
of serving you for the past year.
