155

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Masonic Homes Endowment Board takes great pleasure in
presenting, herewith, its twenty-third annual report covering the period
from August 1, 1954, to July 31, 1955, inclusive.
FAITH

A communication directed to the Inspectors, Masters, Wardens, and
Brethren of the Jurisdiction in 1933, by the Most Worshipful Frank W.
Mixter, reads in part, as follows: "The Grand Lodge at its eighty-third
annual communication, recognizing the necessity for the stabilization of
some system for financing the support of our Homes, by unanimous
vote adopted the report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes, thereby establishing such policy and later, by similar vote, adopted
the report of the Committee on Jurisprudence, enacting the legislation
to carry into effect the newly established policy." Thus, your Endowment Board was created with its purpose indicated.
It was an evidence of FAITH. "To believe, is to be strong. Doubt
cramps energy. Belief is power." Grand Lodge in its eighty-third annual
communication had FAITH in a most important program, that, relating
to the financing of our Homes. "Faith marches at the head of the army
of progress. It is found beside the most refined light, the freest government, the profoundest philosophy, the noblest poetry, the purest humanity." It is for us to carry on with the FAITH that was manifested by
those who demonstrated their confidence in the future of the jurisdiction.
HOPE

"You cannot put a great HOPE into a small soul." Our pioneers
believed in the size of the soul of those in whom they trusted the progress
of the Endowment Fund. Their HOPES are gradually and surely being
realized. The Fund is increasing in a satisfactory manner. The number
of participants is likewise gratifying. The number of Honor Lodges is
most pleasing to your Board. Every reasonable effort has been made by
your Board to spread information about the Homes. We've done this
by word and pictures, by reports to Grand Lodge, by reports and information to the constituent Lodges, their officers and those interested in
our work. The activities of the Homes have been depicted in pictures,
both stills and movies. These have been well received and enjoyed by
the Craft all over the Jurisdiction, including the Hawaiian Islands. The
opportunity to make Bequests has been presented in various ways. We
acknowledge and show appreciation of the many Memorials that have
been made for the benefit of the Fund.

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

We have lived by the HOPE that each year is to be better. Our aim
is to improve the job that has been done :before and justify the confidence
that has been shown us over the years. Ours has been a great opportunity and many of our HOPES have been realized, but such realization
has only beeen possible by the stalwart help of the Most Worshipful
Grand Master, Grand Lodge officers, officers of the Constituent Lodges,
the Inspectors, and a vast horde of others, who, throughout the years,
have manifested an unusual interest in our two One Homes.

CHARITY
FAITH, HOPE AND CHARITY, but the greatest of these is
CHARITY. After all, that is the purpose of our entire program. The
results can best be judged by surveying the figures showing the increase
in the total amount of the Endowment Fund, the number of Memorials,
the Bequests, the individual contributions through Lodges. The following report is for your interest and edification. We urge you not only to
read it •but to consider yourself a stockholder in this great organization
of ours. Ask yourself: Am I satisfied with my own participation, that of
my Lodge, and that of the entire Jurisdiction? Your efforts and help will
lbe appreciated. Your Masonic Homes Endowment Board, again, gratefully thanks all who have served so well.

REPORT OF THE BOARD OF CONTROL
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
The Grand Jurisdiction of California maintains eighteen Boards of
Relief. Seven of these Boards have Employment Bureaus to further
assist our Masonic brethren and their families. In addition, seven of our
Boards operate Masonic Blood Banks.
These Boards of Relief are controlled and supervised by the Board
of Control of Grand Lodge. Under the ordinances, the Board of Control
is empowered to make such rules and regulations as it may deem necessary for their effectual operation, and to standardize their work so
that their operations may be conducted economically and efBciently. The
Boards of Relief are required to report annually to Grand Lodge showing their work, their receipts and disbursements in detail, specifying
what has been expended for relief and how much thereof has been
repaid.
Conforming to these requirements, the Board of Control has prepared a set of rules and regulations for the effectual operation of Boards
of Relief. It 'has standardized their work by setting up a uniform accounting system, subject to annual audits, which now assures us that
each oftlce is economically operated and that their work is efficiently
accomplished. The uniform compact under which our Boards of Relief
operate and which ·has been signed by all member lodges, together with
the rules and regulations of the Board of Control and the Uniform
Accounting System, are all contained in a volume known as the "Standard Practice Bulletin." It also contains four forms which each Board
of Relief is re~uired to use as an annual report to the Board of Control.
These provide all of the information required by the ordinances and
permit the preparation of comparative statistics for closer scrutiny by
the Board of Control.
During the past year the work of the Board of Control has been
unusual and in some respects critical.
The unusual aspect of our work came about through the many
changes made in the management of our various ofBces. Since the last
Communication of Grand Lodge, it became necessary to replace seven
of the former secretaries of our Boards of Relief.
Early in November, Willard Tanzer, secretary of the Fresno Masonic Board of Relief. died after many years of faithful service to the
Fraternity. In April, the secretary of the Richmond Board, Harry '.P.
Chapman, died, leaving a vacancy in the Richmond office. As of January 1, Earl Trimmer of the Sacramento Board, Sam Worswick of the
East Bay Board, and Frank Wolff of Santa Monica Bay, retired. Robert Dill of San Diego resigned because of his wife's ill health. Jerry
Ritch left Glendale to become the controller for the City of Redding.
These changes of necessity placed an additional burden upon the Board

164

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

of Control in acquainting the new men with the duties of their office,
the requirements of Grand Lodge and of the Board of Control. Special
attention should be called to Earl Trimmer, Willard Tanzer and Frank
Wolff. They had served as secretaries of their boards since the date
of their original organization. We regret that time will not permit a full
review of the faithful Masonic activities of each of these Brothers. In
brief, let us record that the Fraternity is indebted to them for their
work and is proud to point to them as outstanding members of our Craft.
These changes in management in themselves pointed to a possible
critical year in our Boards of Relief. Yet, other problems added to the
seriousness of the picture. For example, a personal misunderstanding
within one of our Boards required the patient, serious and careful thinking of the Board of Control to prevent its reaching a critical stage.
Errors on both sides were aired and we believe that today there is a
complete understanding. Other problems being watched by the Board
of Control to prevent their development into the critical column have
to do with the problem of our Employment Bureaus and the many deli..
cate situations which surround the surplus funds of our Boards of Relief.
Briefly. the Board of Control would like to review these critical items
for your benefit.
Considerable thought has been given by the Board of Control to the
increasing costs of placing our members in jobs. Figures which will
appear later in this report will show that during the past year we have
placed 2,731 eligible persons in employment at a total cost of $50,680.00.
This means that each job secured cost us $18.55. The Board of Control. as was reported last year, continues its study of Employment Bureaus to determine the advisability and feasibility of maintaining such
a service from which relatively few receive benefits.
For many years, it was the practice of our Boards of Relief to create
surplus funds sufficient to meet emergencies. In this they were encouraged by the Board of Control. Several years back, it was determined
that some of these surplus accounts had grown way beyond their required need.
The Board of Control then suggested to the various Boards that a
reduction be made to an amount equal to their operating expense for
one year. Gradually these surplus funds have approximated that amount.
It is the opinion of the Board of Control that this surplus fund may
still be too great. It represents the impounding of monies obtained by
assessment from Blue Lodges. It has always been the thought of our
Boards of Relief and the Board of Control that they should be prepared to meet any catastrophe which might arise. It can be argued on
the other side that any great catastrophe will require the assistance of
Grand Lodge and probably all California Masonry should sucli an
occasion occur and it is now the sincere thinking of the Board of Con-

GRAND LODGI'! OP CALIFORNIA

165

trol that perhaps the surplus funds held in trust by our Boards of Relief
should be further reduced.
T'hese and similar problems are receiving constant consideration by
the Board of Control and we wish to assure this Grand Lodge that
they will continue to be watched until each problem is solved to the
ultimate good of this Jurisdiction.

Case No. 5-The Masonic Board of Relief of San Francisco requests

Case No. 6-The Masonic Board of Relief of San Francisco requests

BoARD OF CONTROL

representatives of our Boards of Relief. It has been a pleasure to work
with these brethren. We wish, also, to express our sincere appreciation
to those secretaries who for one reason or another have left their positions during the past year.

To the Most Worshipf ul Grand Lodge of California:

This is the sixth year that it has been my pleasure to report to you
the activities of the Public Schools Week Committee.
Public Schools Week has been one of the outstandin g public service
features of the Grand Lodge since 1919.
It was conceived as a means of arousing public interest in our schools
at a time of crisis following World War I when many schools were
understaffed. Many teachers failed to return at the conclusion of their
war service.
As an aftermath of the war, too, there was a marked increase in
school populations and practically no new classrooms to take care of
the augmente d enrollments.
The Grand Lodge sponsored a statewide movement to bring the
proportions of this desperate situation to the attention of the people.
Condition s improved, but one year was not enough. The need that
created Public Schools Week has never been completely met.
Gradually the realization developed that whether this need is ever
met, Public Schools Week still will serve a worthy purpose in providing for an annual accounting of what the schools are doing and in
keeping alive the people's interest in an institution that has been a part
of our life since early colonial days.
So through the years Grand Lodge has underwrit ten and conducted
the Observan ce with modesty and with sincerity.
We have conducted the Observan ce on a good, sound public relations basis. There are many definitions of public relations but the one
I like best is "Public Relations is doing the deed rather than talking
about it." I believe, that the good which you do, always catches up
with you.
Public Schools Week observance in the program commemorating
its 36th anniversa ry again demonstra ted that it is a Jive and growing
activity by the increasing number of schools and organizations par·
ticipating and by the larger attendanc e recorded.

has already been made of the California Legislature, which this year
joined in a most unusual testimonial.
The press, radio and television stations, innumerable ftrms who
helped in a multitude of ways to further the ends of the observance
can only be given this blanket expression of appreciation.
Our written report which will be distributed to you carries a list of
the many leaders or organizations who have furnished us with supporting statements.
To the concordant Masonic organizations we give a special vote of
thanks for their continued cooperation with our General Committee in
the promotion program.
After more than three decades of experience, certainly Public Schools
Week has had its full opportunity to demonstrate its worth, the soundness of its cause and the effectiveness of its program.
We believe Public Schools Week has done just that as attested by
the ever increasing army of volunteers who serve in its ranks under the
s·ponsorship of Masonry.
However, all recurring events, anniversaries and other occasions
that periodically call for public attention require review from time to
time. At the holiday season we are urged to remember the true meaning
and purpose of Christmas; on the Fourth of July in many ways we are
urged to rededicate our lives to the Democracy that the Fourth symbolizes.
Thus it is that Public Schools Week keeps alive the interest of
parents and all thoughtful citizens in the welfare of our schools, the
effectiveness of their courses of study in the matter of preparing our
youth for citizenship.
We believe that Masonry can be justly proud of heading the legion
of civic-minded men and women who annually rally to the cause of
this program.
Neither piety, virtue nor liberty can long flourish in a community
where the education of youth is neglected.
It is our recommendation that the Public Schools Week Committee
be continued and that the sum of $4,000 be appropriated to carry on
the Observance.

The "Why" of Public Schools Week
Although Public Schools Week has been one of the outstanding
public service features of the Grand Lodge since 1919 it is perhaps
pertinent in a report such as this to go on the assumption that these
pages may be read by some who are unfamiliar with its background and
plli'poses.
· Public School Week was conceived as a means of arousing public
interest in our schools at a time of crisis following World War I when
many schools were understaffed. Many teachers failed to return at the
conclusion of their war service.
As an aftermath of the war, too, there was a marked increase in
school populations and practically no new classrooms to take care of
the augmented enrollments.
·
The Grand Lodge sponsored a statewide movement to bring the
proportions of this desperate situation to the attention of the people.
Minute men addressed rallies of parents. Newspapers were asked to
point up the issue with editorials and print news accounts of local needs.
Conditions improved, but one year was not enough. The need that
. created Pulblic Schools Week has never 1been completely met. A measurable lag in classroom teachers and classrooms has continued to trail
behind California's booming school population.
Gradually the realization developed that whether this need is ever
met Public Schools Week still will serve a worthy purpose in providing
for an annual accounting of what the schools are doing and in keeping
alive the people's interest in an institution that :has been a part of our
life since early colonial days.
1

The Mechanics of the Program
Public Schools Week functions through a General Committee, composed of mem'bers selected from various parts of the jurisdiction and
some six hundred local committees named !by the Masters of the Lodges.
The General Committee begins its active work in December, although
its work is never completely suspended due to the volume of correspondence required to take care of inquiries from lodges outside the jurisdiction, school officials and others. The General Chairman holds conferences to review the previous year's program and develop new ideas,
new approaches for the oncoming observance.
A preliminary letter is prepared to be mailed early in January to all
Masters. This letter calls attention to the dates of the up.-coming program, urges early appointment of the committee and outlines the material
that will be supplied by the General Committee, the highlights of the
latter's plans to stimulate the event on a statewide 1basis and a suggested
list of promotion suggestions for local committees.

173

At the same time a letter is prepared to !be mailed simultaneously to
some 1400 school administrators and principals, calling their attention
to the dates of Public Schools Week and urging early planning and
consultation with local committees.
The participation of various statewide organizations is solicited at
this time, with requests for statements that can be used for publicity
purposes. This sometimes requires numerous follow-up letters before the
task is consummated.
The succeeding weeks are filled with negotiations, development of
special features and the production of materials promised to the local
committees. These include a special press book with suggested new~
paper stories and editorials: a radio and television book: a speaker's
handbook: a copy of "Guide for Planning," when requested: a list of
materials to be ordered from a central printing arrangement, and the
cost thereof (all other materials being supplied free of charge by the
General Committee).
All of this material is distributed as early as possible. The timing
is entirely determined by the receipt of publicity statements received
from various organizations. Every effort, however, is made to expedite
this part of the program.
Once this mailing goes forward the General Committee then turns
all of its attention to the supplemental things done to help promote the
program on a statewide basis. This includes follow-up with various
Masonic and other fraternal bodies, the development of our metered
mail program with lai"ge corporations, special radio and television network tie-ins and numerous other projects.
·

•

Back to School
The General Committee recommends that the local committees endeavor to organize their programs within six to eight weeks. This refers
to the intensive part of the work. There are always preliminary steps
to be taken, reviewing past ·programs, getting the dates fixed in the local
environment in order to prevent conflicting interests and other details.
The entire drive is to get the public to go back to school, if for just
a day. What the school authorities have to offer of course depends on
the teacher but they are always responsive to ideas and suggestions of
the local committee where practical and within the authority of the
school officials.
However, local committees are finding it highly effective to also
reverse this procedure. They encourage the people to go to the schools
but in order to doubly assure the school message getting over they also
devise ways and means of bringing the schools to the people. They do
this in various ways-dubs' programs, exhibits of school work in stores,
radio and television panel discussions and other devices.

California Teacher• A.aaociation Help•
It was a happy day when the General Committee approached Dr.

stimulating the widest possible participation of the schools in the program of Public Schools Week. His quick acceptance of the invitation
was followed at once with a series of suggestions to the school authorities that immediately activated many schools in the undertaking that
had not formerly participated.
In addition to general communications on the subject to school officials the Association in the 36th annual Observance produced its own
helpful brochure telling the teachers how to plan and develop such a
program. In this mailing also went copies of a suggested proclamation
to be issued by the Mayor or other governing officials, a form of resolution for any organization to adopt and radio announcements. Every
television station was presented with three slides ·promoting Public
Schools week.
Perhaps the most impressive contribution to the 1955 program by
this resourceful organization was a pamphlet entitled "Be Proud California," dedicated to the public schools of the state and setting forth the
reasons for Public Schools Week. These were offered to the 450 ·chapters of the Association, to school districts and local teacher clubs at cost.
A total of 310,000 copies were puKhased on this basis and given
statewide distn"bution to parents and others visiting the schools during
the week. This is an impressive testimonial of the effectiveness of the
cooperation of the California Teachers Association in Public Schools
Week observance.

RADIO AND TELEVISION
The General Committee was fortunate indeed to have James Connolly, vice-president of the American Broadcasting Company, to serve
as chairman of radio and television for the 36th annual program. Much
of the success of this phase of the observance is due to his energy and
resourcefulness in shaping up plans for the industry's participation.
Over his own signature and on his own stationery he addressed a
personal letter to the top executives of all stations in the state calling
attention to the im·p ortance of the job done by Public Schools Week
and urging the fullest possible participation.
"This is a public service program that I think commends itself to
all of us in the industry and calls for an all-out effort to make it a success," he said in his appeal for support.

THE SUPPORT OF THE PRESS
In any undertaking such as Pulblic Schools Week the press continues to be the first line of defense. Public Schools Week down through
the years has enjoyed wide support, both editorially and in the generous
amount of news space devoted to the event.
Due to the growing participation of schools and the increasing activity of local committees a marked growth in volume of newspaper space
is noted. Some newspapers now have adopted a plan of devoting an
entire section to the schools and to the program of the week.
The General Committee, as has been its custom for a number of
years, prepared a press book of fifteen pages, containing suggested newspaper stories, editorials and other usable material. Each local committee
was supplied with a copy of this with instructions as to its use.
Although unsolicited, much of the newspaper accounts of the event
as well as the·editorial comment have given Masonry credit for its sponsorship of a cause so vital to American democracy.

PROCLAMATION OF THE GRAND MASTER

RECAPITULATION
After more than three decades of experience, certainly Public Schools
Week has had its full opportunity to demonstrate its worth, the soundness of its cause and the effectiveness of its program.
We believe Public Schools Week has done just that as attested by
the ever increasing army of volunteers who serve in its ranks under the
sponsorship of Masonry.
.
However, all recurring events, anniversaries and other oc~asions
that periodically call for public attention require review from time. to
time. At the holiday season we are urged to remember the true meaning
and purpose of Christmas; on the Fourth of July in many ways we are
urged to rededicate our lives to the Democracy that the Fourth symbolizes.
Thus it is that Public Schools Week keeps alive the interest of parents and all thoughtful citizens in the welfare of our schools, the effectiveness of their courses of study in the matter of preparing our youth
for citizenship.
We ·believe that Masonry can be justly proud of heading the legion
of civic-minded men and women who annually rally to the cause of this
program.

w. HENRY c. CLAUSEN

The 36th Annual Public Schools Week will be observed April 25
through April 30, 1955.
For the past thirty-six years, Public School Week in California has
been a means of calling attention to the functions and needs of our public
schools. It is a Masonic sponsored event. Inaugurated in the 1920's
because of a crisis confronting our public schools in a shortage of teachers, funds and facilities, today the need for the event is even more critical
but for different reasons.
Years ago the American public schools shook off the old world, hard
dogmatism of the dark ages. They broke through layers of prejudice
and superstition to emerge and grow and Bower in our free soil. They
now carry out the typically American concept that schools under college
grade should be paid for and run by the people, as free schools, so every
boy and girl in the land may have a chance to get ahead in life according
to merit instead of money. They are a product of the free, equal-opportunity-for-all spirit of American institutions. There is inherent in that idea
the further American concept that public schools should ·be sanctuaries
of religious freedom. Thus, they are protected by law from sectarian
intrusion. As a vast melting pot in a nation of diverse creeds, religions
and races, they train our children truly into a unified, intelligent American citizenry. In the words of our United States Supreme Court:
"The pu'blic school is at once the symbol of our democracy and
the most pervasive means for promoting our common destiny."
I, therefore;, proclaim and direct:
That all Lodges observe the 36th Annual PU'blic Schools WeekApril 25-30, 1955, and that no Lodge meeting be held during that week
except stated meetings and for the Public Schools Week Observances.
That all Lodges. in cooperation 'with the Grand Lodge PU'blic Schools

Proclam ation of

THE GOVER NOR OF CAUFO RNIA

HoN. GooDWIN J. KNIGHT
The foundations of our Republic rest firmly upon the knowledge
and intelligence of Americans of past, present and future generations
and upon the sound education of our young men and women depends
the security and destiny of our beloved country.
Our public schools today offer broad opportunities for the youth of
America to gain appreciation for the manifold blessings of our institutions. A vigorous school system is an effective economical weapon for
the defense of the nation against all its enemies, foreign and domestic.
Our national independence and personal Jioberties could not long flourish
if the education of our rising generations were to 'be neglected.
With our growing population and constant ly expanding economy,
we in California have a responsibility to maintain the highest posstble
standard s of education in our schools. The necessary expansion of
school facilities must be matched with vigorous efforts to attract greater
numbers of able, well trained and loyal men and women to accept the
profession of teaching, .a s lifetime careers.
Recognizing the importance of citizen cooperation in the development
of better public schools, I, Goodwin J. Knight, Governor of California,
proclaim April 25-30, 1955, as PUBLIC SCHOO LS WEEK througho ut
our State. I urge my fellow Californians to avail themselves of the opportunities offered to become better informed on the problems, accomplishments and aims of those who serve our public schools as teachers, administrators and trustees.

meeting place.

CALIFORNIA LEGISLATURE PASSES RESOLUTIONS
The California Legislature continued its ·practice of recognizing
Public Schools Week by adopting two resolutions, one sponsored
in ·the Assembly by four members, and another resolution was sponsored
by seventy-five mem'bers lby the same 'body, which is practically the entire
Assembly.
March 24, 1955

Assembly Concurrent Resolution No. /'4
Introduced by Mr. Ernest R. Geddes, Miss Donahoe, Messrs. Samuel
R. Geddes, and Bee.
Assembly Concurrent Resolution No. 74-Relative to the observance
of Public Schools Week.
WHEREAS, There has been a rapid growth in the population of California in recent years, and especially in the number of children of school
age: and
WHEREAS, This has resulted in a critical situation in our .Public
Schools System that demands the fullest understanding of the problems
involved: and
WHEREAS, It is customary each year to observe Public Schools Week
to bring all citizens and our future citizens into closer contact with the
public schools of California; and
WHEREAS, 'rhe sole purpose of Public Schools Week is to afford
this opportunity for the people to see education in action, meet both students and teachers and get acquainted with the needs of our school system and to know at first hand the work ·being done to prepare our boys
and girls for citizenship duties: now, therefore, be it
Resolved by the Assembly of the State of California, the Senate
thereof concurring, That the Legislature does hertby endorse the purposes of Public Schools Week, and urges our citizens to visit one or
more schools during the period of the thirty-sixth annual Pulblic Schools
Week, April 25-30, that there may be a wider and better understanding
April 5, 1955
of our schools and their work.

Assembly Concurrent Resolution No. 86--Commending the Grand
Lodge of the State of California. Free and Accepted Masons, for their
leadership in sponsoring the annual Public Schools Week.
WHEREAS, The Thirty-sixth Annual Public Schools Week will be
observed in the pulblic schools of California during the week of April
25th to April 30th: and
WHEREAS, In its inception Public Schools Week was a Masonic
undertaking, having first been observed during the week of September
27, 1920, pursuant to a proclamation issued to the Masonic Lodges by
the Honorable Charles Albert Adams, past Grand Master of Masons
in California, calling attention to the crisis then confronting the public
schools of this State: and
WHEREAS, With the passing of the then existing crisis it was recognized that such annual gatherings in observation of Public Schools Week
were of momentous value in keeping public education in the minds of
the people: thus, the annual observance became a community affair
rather than a Masonic event, with such organizations as the American
Legion, Parent-Teachers Association, Ministerial Association, various
service clubs in the community, and other fraternal and civic organizations participating in the activities: and
WHEREAS, throughout the years of the annual observance of Public
Schools Week the Masonic order has sougb,t no gain for Masonry or
credit for any service rendered the pulblic schools, but has 'been motivated
purely lby a desire to render a public service, to the end that each year
there will 'be afforded to the champions of free, public education an
opportunity to join in bringing about that close contact 'between the
people and their public schools which is so essential to a continuance
of the friendship, faith, and confidence upon which they necessarily
depend: now, therefore, be it
Resolved. by the Assembly of the State of California. the Senate
thereof concurring. That the Grand Lodge of the State of California,
Free and Accepted Masons, are hereby commended for initiating and
sponsoring Pu'blic Schools Week in the public schools of the State of
California: and be it further
Resolved. That the Ohief Clerk of the Assemhly is hereby instructed
to forward a suitably engrossed copy of this resolution to the Grand
Lodge of the State of California, Free and Accepted Masons.

ORIGINAL VERSION-"! pledge allegiance to my flag and to
the Republic for which it stands, one nation, indivisible, with Uberty
and Justice for all."
This was modified June 14, 1923, from my flag to flag of the United
States: again modified in 1924 to include after words United States the
words "of America." Changed again by an act of Congre.SS, June 14,
1954, as Public Law No. 396, •to its present form.

MORNING SESSION, TUESDAY, OCTOBER 25, 1955
Grand Lodge was called on at 10:00 A.M., the Grand Master presiding. The Grand Chaplain delivered the invocation. The minutes of
the morning and afternoon sessions of Monday, October 2ith, were
read and approved.

REPORT OF COMMIT TEE ON FINANCE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
GRAND TREASURER'S REPORT
The Grand Treasurer's report was referred to this Committee. We
have reviewed it and it •has our entire approval.
The report of the Investment Committee was referred to this Committee and we not only approve the report, but extend our commendation to the members of the Investment Committee for the excellent results which the report shows are being accomplished.
GRAND SECRETARY'S REPORT
There was referred to your Committee that portion of the report of
the Grand Secretary in which he requested that lodges under dispensation be not required to ipay the per capita tax. We have considered this
request and it has the approval of the Committee.
SALE OP STOCK IN MASONIC TEMPLE AssocIATION, SAN FRANCISCO
At the annual Communication of 195i the Committee on Policy
and General Purposes recommended "that in pursuance of the plan for
building, maintenance and operating of a Memorial Temple, that the
Grand Lodge by and through the Grand Master and the Grand Secretary, subject to the prior approval of the Grand Master, the Deputy
Grand Master, the Grand Treasurer and the Ohairman of the Committee
on Finance, may sell at the best price obtainable, when in their judgment the time is opportune, the stock which the Grand Lodge owns in
the Corporation holding title to the Grand Lodge's present location at
25 Van Ness Avenue, San Francisco, California."
This recommendation was adopted by Grand Lodge.
Accordingly, the sale of this stock has been effected with the approval of the designated parties and the proceeds ·paid into the general
funds of Grand Lodge. A careful check was made of the income and
capital accounts of the Temple Association, as well as the current and
prospective condition of the physical assets. In the light of the facts
obtained the price which Grand Lodge received was deemed to be entirely satisfactory, and the Finance Committee concurs in the sale.
There has been referred to this Committee the resolution introduced
by members of the Memorial Temple Committee under which the proceeds of $25i,877.50 from the sale of the stock owned by Grand Lodge

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

191

in the Temple Association will be transferred from the General Funds
of Grand Lodge to the Building Fund of the California Masonic Memorial Temple. It is clear from the words previously quoted from the
adopted recommendation of the Policy and General Purposes Committee that it was intended that the proceeds from the sale of this stock
be used for the Memorial Temple. We, therefore, approve and recommend the adoption of the resolution.
EXPENDITURE IN EXCESS OP THE BUDGET
The audit of Grand Lodge accounts shows that certain expenditure s
we~e made in excess of the budget, and in each case were not paid
until approved by the Grand Master. We bring this to your attention
in order that, with the adoption of this report in its entirety, you will
approve this action of the Grand Master. These additional expenditure s
will be found itemized in the proceedings of Grand Lodge.
It is the recommendation of this committee that hereafter the Grand
Master, in his Message, report any such additional authorizations for
Grand Lodge approval.
AUDIT OP ACCOUNTS

.Jn accordance with the provision of Ordinances, an audit of accounts

of Grand Lodge for the fiscal year ended July 31, 1955 has been made
by the firm of Skinner and Hammond, Certified Public Accountant s of
which firm Brother James E. Hammond is a senior member. Each m~m­
ber ~f your Finance Committee has received and carefully examined the
audit report, and we have discussed it with Brother Hammond. It is
our opinion that the report presents the true condititon of the finances
of the Grand oLpge. We commend Brother Hammond for the excellent
manner in whicli the report is prepared.
MASONIC HOMES
Your Committee has reviewed the report of the audit of the accounts
of the Masonic Homes of California as well as the report of the Trustees
and after consultation on the amount ()f funds needed to support their
operations for the next fiscal year we find that a renewal of the per
capita tax of 50c will be sufficient. We, therefore, offer the following
resolution and move its adoption:
RESOLVE D: That the sum of 50c per capita be levied for the
fiscal year ending July 31, 1956, the proceeds to be paid to the Trustees
of the Masonic Homes.
PREPARATION OP BUDGET
Your Committee continued the procedure begun last year of meeting well in advance of the Communication with the Grand Treasurer,
Grand Secretary, and the Chairmen of the various Boards and Committees for a review of proposed budgets and proposed administrative
and general expense. This has made it possible to give more time and
objective planning to the budget which we submit for your approval.

192

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

We have endeavored to be realistic in setting up the appropriations,
thereby presenting as far as possible a true picture of anticipated income and expense.
A few comments on certain items in the budget seem to be appropriate. A material reduction has been made in the appropriation for the
Memorial Temple Committee. After discussion with the Chairman it
is felt that regardless of the nature of the future program under which
additional funds may be realized, the expenses in raising such funds
will be much less than in the past.
SALARIES

Your Committee has discussed with the Grand Secretary the salary
needs for the coming year. We are including in this item his estimate
of the increases which will be needed for the office staff. In addition
we are recommending increases for the Grand Secreta ry and the Assistant Grand Secreta ry of $1,800 and $1,000 per year, respectively.
The scope of the work and responsibility of the Grand Secreta ry
and his Assistant has greatly increased in the last decade and a half.
The efficiency with which the administrative affairs are discharged in
California is, in our opinion, not second to that of any jurisdiction in
this country.
A larger increase than we are recommending would be justified, but
we 'hope that our finances will permit a further adjustment in the future.
GRAND LoDGE LITIGATION

At the annual Communication of 1954 Grand Lodge unanimously
adopted the recommendatiton of the Publications Committee that the
Grand Master be authorized to institute action in the courts of this
state on behalf of our Grand Lodge, to establish that our name and
certain Masonic words and phrases shall not be used for fraudulent
purposes nor for private gain or profit; that all costs and expenses
thereof shall be a proper charge against the general funds of this Grand
Lodge.
So far no expense in this matter has been reported to your Committee, but we are informed that suits have been instituted and that
there may be costs in the coming year in the estimated amount of $5,000.
Therefo re, we have included this amount in the budget.
RETIREM ENT PLAN

The Proceedings of Grand Lodge, 1947, show that the Trustee s of
the Homes Board were directed to set up and adopt a retirement plan
for the employees of the Homes, and it was recommended that the plan
be so arrange d that. if in the future it was considered desirable that
employees of Grand Lodge be brough t under the Homes plan, this would
be possible.
We have been advised by the Trustee s that ·such a plan was adopted
and became effective January 1, 1955.

193

Your Committee has given serious consideration to the matter of
now placing Grand Lodge office employees under this plan and it is our
conclusion that this should be done and we so recommend, to be eft'ective January 1, 1956.
Based upon the figures arrived at by our actuarial advisors, we estimate that for the seven months of the current fiscal year remaining after
January 1 the net cost of this plan to Grand Lodge will be approximately
$4,000, which amount we 'have included in the proposed budget.
Your Committee is aware of the fact that there are employees of
Grand Lodge other than those in the office, such as Masonic Clubhouses, Boards of Relief. Employment Bureaus, etc. However, we do
not have the necessary data on all these employees to make it possible
for us to estimate the cost of including them under this plan at this
time. A study will be made and we will attempt to bring to you at the
next annual Communication a recommendation on the employees falling into these categories.

REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON
OLD MASONIC HALL AT LOS ANGELES
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
.
In accordance with the direction of Grand Lodge, your Committee
was appointed by the Grand Master to keep in touch with developments
relating to the building located at 416 North Main Street in .Los Angeles, the first Masonic Hall in that city and the second meeting place
of Los Angeles Lodge No. 42.
.
.
You will recall from a previous report that this property is no;'
owned by the City of Los Angeles and is in such a bad state of repa~r
that it has faced demolition. However, because of the prospect that 1t
may be included in the Pueblo de Los Angeles State ~istori~al Monument we have assurances from city officials that demolition will not take
plac~, if at all, until the complete area of the Monument is det~~ined.
By action of the state legislature there h~.s be~n c~eated the Pu.eblo
de Los Angeles State Historical Monument which 1s under the direction and supervision of the Division of Beaches and Parks, State Dept.

REPORT· OF THE COMMITTEE ON PUBLICATIONS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
At the annual communication in 1954, the representatives of this
Grand Lodge struck from the second paragraph of Section 127 the
words "without sanction of Grand Lodge." This deletion had the immediate effect of prohibiting advertising in any publication purporting
to be Masonic in name or character or operated by or for any body or
organization which required Masonic affiliation as a condition to membership.

In that session your representatives authorized the incoming Grand
Master to institute suits to enjoin any publication or periodical from
using our name or symbols in the pursuit of advertising revenues.
The Grand Master continued the Publications Committee to assist
him in dealing with the problems arising out of these two actions. He,
in addition, has referred to this Committee a large number of cases
involving the use of the good name of our fraternity in commercial
enterprises carried on by prerequisite organizations but which commercial enterprises are not directly connected with the advertising evil.
Our report will, therefore, be made in three parts:
( 1 ) The enforcement of Section 127;
( 2) The facts concerning publications put out by non-Masons who
are using the name of Masonry to solicit advertising; and
( 3) The investigation of and recommendations for dealing with the
growing problem of the use of the good name and reputation of Masonry in commercial promotions by so-called prerequisite bodies masking
as charity but, in many instances. bordering on fraud.
We can report that the individual Lodges of the jurisdiction, without
known exception, have willingly obeyed our Masonic law and produced
Trestle Boards and bulletins free from advertising. The joint Trestle
Board issued by the Lodges of Kern and Santa Barbara Counties have
replaced the commercial magazines to whom they previously paid tribute, and every member of these Lodges is now receiving his own Lodge
bulletin, as well as those of neighboring Lodges, as a part of his dues.
It is to be hoped that other areas will, within their own borders, join
in such mutual endeavors. The Masters of our Lodges are to be congratulated on their devotion to the fundamental concept that Masonry
is for the enrichment of men's minds and spirits, and not the lining of
their pockets.
We cannot, in good conscience, say the same of many of those organizations which make membership in a Masonic Lodge a prerequisite
to mem'bership in their own 'body. It appears that a long period of education will be necessary before these prerequisite bodies learn that we
must be Masons, not only first, but also, always.

For an example of this prdblem, consider the case of Southern California Shriner, a magazine published in the Los Angeles area and devoted to the publicizing of some twenty-odd Shrine Clubs. This ~as a
periodical containing advertising which, prior to 1954, had ~~nction ~o

Club news, pictures and lists of officers, retained identity as a periodical
published for the benefit of those Shrine Clubs.
The Committee reported this matter in full to the Grand Master.
His action in the matter has resulted in the trial of this Master Mason.
Distressing, however. was the attitude of many of the heads of the
Shrine Clubs involved as they continued to ignore good counsel to cease

A second area of violation remains in the bulletins of these and other
Shrine luncheon clubs. Some of the clubs have carried business cards in
their rosters. Others have advertised a so-called "sponsor" at their
luncheons, dinners or other programmed events, spreading the name of
the "sponsor" and. in many cases, pictures of his establishment over the
entire mailing list of the club.
Lest it be inferred that this practice is limited to the Los Angeles
area, a large and prominent Shrine luncheon clUJb in the Sa~ Francisco
area included. in addition to the sponsor on the front of their program,
a box devoted to those charitable brothers who were donating the door
•prizes of the day, including liquor stores as well as other do~ors .. We
are told that the address slip of the program becomes the drawing ticket
for the ensuing raffie.
The carrying of advertising in such rosters, bulletins and programs
has, of course, been prohibited since 1951, as no sanction was t_h~n
granted for a Mason to advertise his wares in a Lodge or prerequisite
body's bulletin or programs or in other media.
We cannot but believe that this is but a phase or part of the continual struggle to use Masonry for personal gain and profit. Since it is
difficult to capitalize on symbolic Masonry. the more loosely governed

prerequisite organizations 'become the focal point for the individual who
therein seeks to spread his name and his business before his fellows.
Lest we be misunderstood. we repeat that advertising. in its proper
place, is a force for great good in this free enterprise land of ours. We
do also repeat, however. that each one of us. including the members of
prerequisite organizations, came into this great fraternity, like our fathers before us, "uninfluenced by mercenary motives." But, When this
Grand Lodge is accused of being a "1bunch of bigotted blue-nosed bums"
and this Committee of being "the ringleaders." you will understand. with
us, that "time. patience and perseverance" will be required to educate
our less informed brethren.
We recommend eternal vigilance on the part of the Inspectors of
the several districts and the Masters of the various Lodges.
What to do about those publications. put out by non-Masons. which
are using the name and symbols of Masonry to practice fraud upon the
public in the solicitation of advertising?
Several of these publishers had been members of the fraternity. They
were tried and expelled. They continued to sell advertising in magazines
with non-existent circulation.
We recommend court action and your present Grand Master was
specifically authorized to institute such actions as he might deem advis·
able.
To assist in this direction and to give protection, not only to Masonry, but to other similarly situated organizations, Assembly Bills Nos.
2797 and 2798 were introduced in the 1955 session of the California
State Legislature by Assemblyman Joe Shell of Los Angeles. These
Bills were dra'Wn by Brother Clay Robbins, a member of Garfield Lodge
No. 566. They were passed by both houses of the Legislature. signed
by the Governor, and became Article 5, Division 6. Chapter 3 of the
Business and Professions Code and Sections 21308. 21309 and 21310
of the Corporations Code. The primary purpose of this legislation is to
prevent the "use of the name of any association (such as ours) in a
commercial venture, trade or business or in the solicitation of subscriptions for advertising in any newspaper or other publication, or in the
solicitation of donations by any person representing directly or indirectly that such commercial venture, trade or business, newspaper or
other publication or donation or solicitation for donation. is sponsored,
endorsed or being offered by any association. unless the person so using
the name is entitled to the name under the constitution. by-laws, or
rules of the association or by the written consent of such association to
such use."
The legislation then provides that. where violation occurs, injunctive
relief may be granted without allegation or proof of actual damages.

Code the names and symbols used by this Grand Lodge and its con-

Whether we like it or not Masonry in the public mind is confused
not only with the seemingly endless array of fezzed "fun groups" which
require Masonic affiliation, ·b ut with the clubs within them, the ladies'
counterparts of them and the mixed groups as well. There is good reason for this confusion because these various groups have, by their actions and activities, led the public to believe that they are in truth and
in fact, Masonic.
In their actions and activities the . good name and reputation of

Other complaints have been received by your Committee from Brethren pertaining to door prizes, raffles, and even shows of questionable
character, but time does .not permit the cataloguing of them all. Ours
is not the only jurisdiction which is plagued. Most Worshipful Whitfield W. Johnson, Grand Master of Massachusetts, had this to say at
a quarterly communication in 1954:
"The question of raffles, door prizes, lotteries, etc., seems to
arise constantly for the consideration of Grand Masters.
"Much has been written 1by Grand Masters of this and other
jurisdictions about gambling. Their disapproval. and that of the
craft, has been unanimous. There is, however, a twilight zone in
which are found many activities that fall short of gambling and "
that even partake of entertainment and voluntary charity, but
which find their final excuse for existence solely in the element of
a chance to get pecuniary value for nothing. ,
"To ask the Grand Master to be constantly acting as a censor
of these 'borderline cases is unfair to him and bad for the craft,
for every such decision prompts some criticism and misunderstanding, and comparison with other decisions: and the cumulative effect is to spread dissension and weaken the solidarity of
our Fraternity."
The activities of organizations whose prerequisite to membership is
that one be a Master Mason causes this Committee to pose this question:
May Master Masons, by the formation of, and membership
in, an organization which requires Masonic affiliation to membershi:p, but which organization is not chartered by or recognized by
Grand Lodge, exempt themselves from the principles, tenets,
ideals, rules and regulations which govern them as members of
a Symbolic Blue Lodge?

Your Committee knows, as should all Master Masons, that the answer is a resounding NO.
Do not all Master Masons kneel at the same altar? Do not all Master Masons freely and willingly assume the same obligations? Are not
all Master Masons bound to conform to and bide by the laws, rules
and regulations of the Grand Lodge under which his Lodge is holden
and in whose jurisdiction he resides? Is there anything in our ritual,
laws, rules or regulations, which exempts a Master Mason simply because he belongs to such an organization?
·
The answers to these questions are so obvious that they need not
be here recorded. Yet, many of our Brethren who proudly boast of mem·bershiip in a Blue Lodge, cry out against the shackles of fundamental
Masonic restraint when applied to their membership in such organizations. Then this Grand ·Lodge becomes, and we repeat, "a bunch of
ibigotted !blue-nosed bums" and this Committee "the ringleaders."
We are charged that Masonry is:
" ••. an Institution having for its foundation the practice of
the social and moral virtues; and to so high an eminence has its
credit been advanced that, in every age and in every country,
men preeminent for their moral and intellectual attainments have
encouraged and prompted its interests."
Masonry holds a place of preeminence in every community in which
a Blue Lodge exists, and throughout the ages it has held and now holds
the hearts and minds of men.
Have we now reached an era in our Masonic history when adherence to the fundamental principles of Masonry is a cloak to be worn or
discarded, depending upon whether we sit in a Blue Lodge or in a prerequisite :body? Is the shadow of commercialism now to engulf our beloved Fraternity through the sponsorship of commercial enterprises and
by begging from the ipublic in the name of or under the guise of Masonry?
This Committee cannot stem the tide. No Grand Master can, in his
busy year, cope with the number of known violations of Masonic law
and ethics, if treated on an individual basis.
Here, as in the case of advertising, legislation must necessarily be
the answer. We have sought the advice and counsel of men preeminent
in Masonic law. It is with their help that the following proposed addi,tfon to our Ordinances has been hammered out and for that purpose we
offer the following resolution:

thereof shall, directly or indirectly, engage in any business, project, venture. promotion, scheme or plan which is unethical. fraudulent, misleading or illegal. Any violation of this section shall be
deemed un-Masonic conduct."
The work of this Committee has been arduous and oft times unpleasant. Each member of the Committee has borne his full share of
the 'burdens and responsibilities, and to ea~h the chairman extends his
heartfelt thanks.
Brethren, the members of your Committee ask you to join with us
in a toast to a Man and a Mason.
To Henry Christian Clausen, Grand Master of Masons in California. By his strength he has strengthened us. By his leadership he has
lead us into higher realms of Masonic understanding. By his character
and integrity he has fortified us in our knowledge that right shall triumph over wrong. By his devotion to Masonic principles and ideals
he has taught us that service to our beloved Fraternity is in itself just
compensation. To him we owe a debt that can never ·be repaid. To him
we offer our humble thanks and a friendship that shall cease only when
time shall .b e no more.
We recommend that the Committee, without reference to its present
personnel. be continued.

AMENDME NT OF SECTION 127

How, by whom, and by what authority could determination as to
the official character or the contents of the publication be made?
If the determination is made, who and by what means is conformity to
be ascertained or enforced 1
As to the last two conditions, how, by whom and by what means
can the existence of net profits from the soliciting or sponsoring be determined: and, if such profits exist, whether they are or will be used for
charitable purposes?
How, by whom and by what means can it be determined that O.nancial
profit will or will not accrue, or has or has not accrued to, a member of
the sponsoring body?
These and other insoluble policing problems prevented the success
of attempted palliatives and were accountable for the broad prohibitions
of existing Section 127.
While, to a minor degree, honest and well-intentioned persons may
be inconvenienced, the necessity of putting a stop to fraudulent practices
indulged in the name of Masonry whereby Masons in general and
newly initiated members of the Craft in particular were being persistently
victimized, the public misled, and Masonry brought into disrepute, made
prohibitive legislation imperative.

Brother Milton E. Ballengee, Past Master of Honolulu Lodge No.
409, presents resolution proposing to amend Section 127 of our Ordinances. The above resolution was referred to this Committee. For the
following reasons we recommend that it be not adopted:
Section 127 was amended to read as it now stands in 1954 (Proc.
1954, pp. 155 & 161 ). In substance, it forbids any Lodge or member
from soliciting, sponsoring, inserting. placing or printing advertising
of any kind in or for any medium or publication which purports to be
Masonic in name or character, or which is published by or for any organization requiring Masonic affiliation as a condition to membership.
These broad prohibitions were the result of investigation and research, extending over several years, by Grand Masters, by the Grand
Lodge Committee on Policy, and by special committees on Publications
of the Grand Lodge, and following trial of various remedial measures.
The abuses had assumed the proportions of a constantly recurring
racket, and are extensively set forth in reports of such committees and
in messages of successive Grand Masters. (Proc. 1951, 131-138: 1952
Proc. 56-57, 75-78, 320-324: 1953 Proc. 73, 88-91, 168-176: and 1954
Proc. 71-75, 148-166B.)
Not the least of the difficulties encountered in the remedial efforts
was the impossibility of 1policing persons, publications and organizations
not accountable to this Grand Lodge.
The proposed amendment is decidedly counter to the obvious policy
of amended Section 127 and would defeat its policy and purpose. It
provides in effect that, notwithstandin g the prohibition, a Master Mason
may solicit, sponsor, insert, place or print advertising in a publication
purporting to be Masonic in character or published by an organization
requiring Masonic affiliation as a condition to membership,
( 1 ) if the publication is the official publication of such an organization:
( 2) if it does not indicate the name, symbol or emblem of the organization:
( 3) if it does not indicate that the publication is in fact Masonic or
of "affiliated origin":
( 4) if all net profits from "solicitation or sponsoring" are used by
the sponsoring body for charity: and
( 5) if no financial :profit therefrom is permitted r to accrue to any
member of the sponsoring body.
Obviously, in order to be effective, the first three prescribed conditions would have to be determined in advance of the sponsoring, solicitation or printing.

WE ARE FREE
MILTON D. SAPIRO, Grand Orator

Most Worshipful Grand Master, and Past Grand Masters, Officers
and Brethren of the Grand Lodge of California, and Distinguished
Masonic Guests:
Once more we are privileged to assemble in our Annual Communication. We gather here from the many sections of this glorious state so
that we might continue to consult concerning the welfare of our institution, its members and our people, for surely no official gathering of
Masons can ever take place that shall not reflect a concern for the whole
of the people with whom we live.
Our Most Worthy Grand Master and Grand Secretary and others
have presented their reports on the state of the Craft and these records
will portray a healthy, sound, growing organization. They will demonstrate the strength of our body in numbers and in material worth and
we in our Communication will want to absorb those facts and analyze
and weigh them so that we may determine how to use the power that
such a force can generate in the lives of our community.
As one journeys from one end of this state to the other observing
the operations of our brethren in its variety of communities, one receives
a tremendous impression of the reserves of manpower and of the formidable volume of energy stored in its Lodges and of the flood of influence represented in our various units. At constitutions and institution of
Lodges, laying of cornerstones, dedications, receptions, and various types
of ceremonies which we have attended there has been manifested the
human strengths that make this Craft strong and that have made it live.
Here, of course, in our Annual Communication, we witness the most
expressive demonstration as to the type of men who constitute its leadership, drawn from the great mass of our membership, representative of
all fields of endeavor and endowed with what should be a thirst and
eagerness to declare their attachment for the ideals and truths that have
brought this institution down through the ages until now when it attains
the support of the greatest number ever known in the centuries of its
existence.
Never before have so many men been a part of this Ancient Order,
although you and I must well recognize that it is not by mere numbers
alone that we will measure its advance or that it will thrive and continue
to be. The quantity of members alone did not keep alive those Ancient
Charges which have been characteristic of Freemasonry. Even when
the adherents of Freemasonry were few, even when they clung together
in small groups, harassed by dictators, spiritual and temporal. Masonic

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

213

truths stirred them and caused them to draw other men to them and so
enabled them to pass from generation to generation those everlasting
truths. Ever has been their loyalty to God, their dedication to honorable conduct, their exemplification of moral and temperate habits. their
respect for the secrets of a brother and the constant regard for his welfare.
As we hold our Annual Communication we again remind ourselves
of the history of Masonry and think of its ancient origin and accomplishments. We remember the founding of the Grand Lodge organization as
we know it today, from its English Beginnings in 1717. We know of
the earlier ancient German stonemasons and the French guilds, which
practiced an observance of the same tenets and truths we accept today:
and we learn that even farther back in the deep past, delving into the
mysteries of ancient religions that have stirred the thinking of mankind.
there is evidence of the physical designs and the moral teachings by
which we continue to conduct our affairs. These matters can all bear
repetition for if we are to be loyal to our present day designation of
Freemasons, the truths taught in these ancient forms and that have survived must be a complete part of our makeup and they must ever be
present to guide us and those Master Masons who serve with us. They
can only be understood by a constant attention to them. In each of our
Annual Communications we must ever renew our faith in our destiny as
Freemasons, as we again dedicate ourselves to its noble purposes.
We meet here in the character of Masons, but we must always
remember that we meet not merely as Masons but as Freemasons, for
as the world has shaped its affairs in our generation that word "free"
has become our most precious symbol. If it were not for the spirit it
represents, we· would be just another fraternal organization, but with
if we establish ourselves as active faithful descendants of an ancient
and honorable family. dedicated to those tenets of brotherly love and
truth for which the term "free" itself has become the motive, and which
exist in their highest form only when men are free.
It was once believed that the term "Freemason" referred to a Mason
who worked with freestone, but that idea was soon discarded. It became
evident that the term characterized those operative Masons who comprised the guilds and companies of Masons that were bold enough to
exercise a freedom of movement, a freedom of artistic design and thought
even in the Middle and Dark Ages when such activity was vigorously
discouraged--even then there existed men who would not permit their
feet to be fettered, their souls to be made captive, their minds to be subjugated. Somehow these m~n contrived to secure unusual freedom in days
when the ability to secure an education and increase one's knowledge
was limited to a small select group: in days when independent thinking
was regarded as evil and as a crime against the ruling dominant force;
in the days when men of science were punished for searching out the
truths of our existence and were compelled under the torture of the rack

214

to recant what their scientific research had taught. In those days the
minds of men were subject to strictures so that their thinking as well
as their art ·had to follow narrow set-out trails, or be deemed blasphe mous; even in those days men gained courage togethe r to break away
from some of the restrictions and in their groupings were denomi nated
"free" to mark the development of their aspirati ons and the enlargin g
scope of their activities and considerations.
Then, as Freema sonry developed in the form in which we now know
it, a product of an organiz ed a:Q.d soundly constitu ted institution, the
term "free' persiste d to have meaning and give life to our order. Where
its Lodges existed and men met at its altars and under its signs, we
found inspiration for human .progress and advance. Under the quicken~
ing influence of its simple truths, men yearned for the opportu nity for
human freedom. In nations were Masonic lodges prospered, chains of
tyranny were stricken and people as such began to enjoy the great
opportunities that mark freedom. If we underta ke to study those other
countries where human beings most enjoy the advanta ges of democracy, such as Englan d, France, and the Scandin avian groups, we will
.find that those who matured at Masonic altars were in the foreground
of all those movements that advance d the course of and fixed the rights
of Freemen. Even today in many countries where a type of dictator ship
dominates the lives and seeks to control the minds of its citizens, we
will find that Masoni c institutions are still guardin g the treasure s of
freedom and prepari ng the minds and hearts of men for self-government
when they shall be free. These Lodges encoura ge their members, even
under bitterly adverse conditions, as men of courage to stand firm and
fast and prepare themselves for that day when the rights of freemen
shall obtain on the soil of their land.
This freedom for men in which we believe and which we in this
generat ion and nation take for granted , is threaten ed in all parts of our
globe. So we who proclaim ourselves free had better talk of freedom so
that we may underst and it and so that we may live it and have the
courage to preserv e it.
Let us consider our being free as we enjoy it here in these United
States, where men have attained heights of freedom which the early
great philosophers pictured only as a literary utopia and the average
man never contemplated in the history of the human race. I doubt
whethe r even the Foundi ng Fathers of this nation, except in their most
imaginative dreams, could have foreseen that such a vast nation of people would enjoy the type of indepen dence and civil liberty that we
enjoy, that has taken us out of economic slavery, has given all the
opportu nity for being freed from the depress ion of ignorance, and that
has freed us from so many of the ills and inconveniences that have
plagued mankind over the centuries. Those early Americans lived in the
days when human slavery was a part of their economic system. For so
many years and in all states, propert y and other voting qualifications

produces these natural disturbances; to ascertain why the earth quakes

Man has split the atom and has seemed to reverse the processes of

The world however moves forward as we keep open the door of
opportunity for clear, untrammeled thinking, as we remove all fetters
that would bind the human mind, as we permit it to look forward and
backward without restraint and without requiring it to peep through
colored glasses and permit it with boldness to discover and dis~ern the
truth. This will produce material advances but we must be continuously
aware that these material achievements can be of real service to man
only as we recognize the spiritual values they must indicate and preserve.
The spirit of the pioneer, that spirit which caused men and women
to stride forth courageously over our Western plains, facing perils
known and unknown but with a firm determination to establish a home
for themselves and their families at whatever cost, must be permitted
to continue to pervade our lives and drive us on with like courage and
eagerness to meet the problems that this advancing age presents to us,
especially as it concerns our relations with our fellowmen.
This is the field of endeavor in which we as Freemasons are particularly designed to carry on as we are free to serve, and do for and
respect our fellow men. Never has Masonry .existed . for itself ~one,
nor has an individual Mason, true to its teachings, existed for himself
alone. This cannot be, for our strongest virtue is in our dedication to

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

217

brotherhood and every move we make in our fraternal association is
intimately bound with the good it should bring about for each individual
and 'his neighbor.
Scan the history of our institution and you will find that it has oppressed no man. It has compelled no man to enter its Lodges. To it
inquisition and persecution have been abhorrent. Our concern has been
to assist and forward human welfare and build through those humanitarian efforts that give men strength, peace, ·harmony and dignity. This
we have been able to do as we served our fellowmen because we were
Freemen and Freemasons. We have accepted as the crowning glory
of God's handiwork a virtuous, law-abiding, right-thinking and acting
man.
At our altars we have welcomed men of every creed. We have respected the thinking of every man. We ask only that he believe in God,
but we do not dictate to him the road to pursue as he approaches the
worship of his God. He shares with us our philosophies, our teachings,
our fellowship and companionship, and this constitutes no interference
with the mode of worship he has chosen.
This is the tolerance of which we so proudly boast. Not tolerance
in the sense of a gracious acceptance of the other man's difference, but
tolerance in the sense of the understanding of the equal rights which
every man .possesses to follow the religious creed of his choice. This is
the kind of relationship that is clear and free from every bigotry and
prejudice and should characterize the fellowship of all men. This is the
kind of religious freedom Freemasons wrote into the Constitution of the
United States. We know that man is capable of hating and having
and maintaining prejudice and discrimination, but not so a Mason. Our
freedom to think and our association one with the other must have
taught us that we necessarily judge each man by his individual worth
and merit and weigh by exact and similar standards: and if we fail to
do so then we have missed entirely the spirit of the words we utter at
our Lodge altars and have failed entirely to absorb the lessons of our
Masonic teachings.
This is so important to remember in days like these when contact
between many peoples has become such a simple everyday fact. We
meet with persons from all over the globe. Many of them even set their
goal of life to be found in this, our own nation. Many will apply to
our Lodges for admission. Are we going to continue to judge them by
What they are or are we going to look to and check their religious background and the creed they follow to see if they conform? And are we
going to set up some other artificial test? If we do that, we make our
words as we pledge anyone to ourselves, a sham and a deceit. Hypoc- .
risy in our life we must avoid, for such false pretense has contributed
so much to the world's difficulties. So we must from time to time examine into our own souls deeply in order that we may determine and know

how Masonry has fashioned our lives. What would you have done if
a Dr. Sammy Lee, that stalwart patriotic American officer and athlete
of Korean descent, had sought to purchase a house in the tract where
you live? Would you have been true to the Masonic ideals you profess,

Doing this has made our truths living truths and has contributed to
keeping our institution alive and active throughout the ag~s. Doing.this,

strengthened for continued existence and service.
What we teach in Masonry can only be of value as we make it a
part of our personal everyday life. This has been so thoroughly emphasized in the history of this, our own nation, and is being illustrated
constantly in our daily civil existence. From the very beginning of the
national aspirations of the United States, Freemasons have played a
most important part in shaping its destiny. From the teachings in their
Lodge rooms they obtained a reverent respect for t~e rights of hu~an
beings and a yearning and regard for freedom. Fortified by that which
had been inculcated in them in Masonic meetings, they were the leaders
in the effort to advance the general welfare and lift the weight of royal
oppression from the shoulders of our people. When it became necessary
to set up a new nation to obtain and assure freedom, they had the fortitude to be the leaders in that movement. Many of the signers of the
Declaration of Independence were of our Fraternity, and for its support
pledged 'their lives, their fortunes and their s~cred honor. w.e know. well
their activities in defense of this newborn nation and how, wtth unstinted
courage from Washing ton down, they contributed so much to the successful formation of these United States. They acted as individuals, but
they were stimulated by what they had absorbed from their Masonic
affiliations. History has revealed what George Washington thought of
his Masonic institution-and how he recognized and wrote of its liberal
principles, founded on the immutable laws of truth and justice and whose
object was to promote the happiness of the human race--so that, und~r
the in,fluence of such ideals, it is understandable how he took the position he did when freedom was at stake. He reflected in his life the effect
of Masonic teachings. He, of course, did not stand alone as a member

of the Fraternity. So many of our brethren participated with him that
the history of this nation is graced in many volumes with the lives ot
those affiliated with us. It might well be said that American freedom
would never have been attained without the leadership of our fraternal
brethren.

219

Those of us who are familiar with the development of law in this
nation and particularly that law which shaped and outlined the paths
that our new nation should follow into strength after the Constitution
had been adopted, know that Jdhn Marshall, Chief Justice of the United
States Supreme Court for some 34 years, a Past Grand Master of Virginia, was responsible for giving us our present day conception of national unity. Incidentally, this year is the 200th anniversary of his birthand the American Bar Association dedicated its annual meeting to that
great American judicial leader, our brother Freemason who charted the
course of our national strength and destiny in the courts. He made his
Freemasonry a living force in his life and expressed its everlasting principles in his decisions. And again making history on that court with his
noble grasp and concept of human relationships is a Past Grand Master
of California, the present Chief Justice, Earl Warren.
All of these men who brought this nation into being and helped
carry it on truly represented the highest values in their Masonic indoctrination. They must be driving and exhilarating examples for us. Freedom is not something that, once obtained, will be ours just because we
had it. Can any words be more apt and especially today than those of
Washington when he said "eternal vigilance is the price of liberty"?
We are free to maintain our political liberty and it is important to us
as Freemasons that we do so, for it is in such an atmosphere that Masonry best flourishes and works and develops its program for the good
of all. We know well that our institution as such takes no part in the
political activities of the nation; but it certainly must serve to inspire the
individual member to an active participation in the life of the nation,
to an acceptance of responsibility for the protection of the nation and
to all necessary activity for a realization of its ideals, guided as were
its Masonic founders by the principles and philosophies of life developed
through our Masonic association.
Let us not ever forget that if we become indolent or careless or
casual or in any way weaken our will to maintain those freedoms, they
may become lost to us. Once we assume any such attitude we become
unfit for liberty and are not likely to enjoy the liberty and freedom we
possess. Certainly you cannot be unaware of the fact that there are
those in these United States who would gladly assume the role of dictators. This is not only confined to those who stupidly believe that life
might be enriched or that they themselves might enjoy power if they
allied themselves with such a cause as Communism. There are others
also who would deride the American freedoms as established by our
