The second contention of the accused, that he understood a letter
from Grand Master Drapeau to mean that he might continue with his
publication, is hardly believable upon a reading of the correspondence
between the accused and the Grand Master and the Grand Secretary.
At all events, the trial com.missioners, by their unanimous verdict, found
against this contention of the accused after having heard his testimony
and having examined such correspondence, and this Grand Lodge should
not under such circumstances reverse that finding of fact by the trial
commissioners.
As to the tird contention of the accused, we must point out that if,
in fact, the Masonic Citizen was beneficial to Masonry that fact is
entirely immaterial. Our Grand Lodge. the final Masonic authority in
California, after due debate and deliberation determined what the
policy of Grand Lodge should be as to such publications, givi~g due
thought to what would be detrimental and what would be beneficial and
for the best interests of Masonry in this jurisdiction, and no Mason may
test the wisdom of that policy by violation of the statute.
The amendment by Grand Lodge in 1951 of Section 127 was as
follows:
"RESOLVED: That Section 127 of Ordinances be amended by
adding at the end thereof the following:
No Lodge or member of a Lodge, without the express sanction
of Grand Lodge. shall solicit, sponsor, insert, place or print advertising of any kind in or for any medium or publication which
purports to be Masonic in name or character, or which is published by or for any body, order or organization requiring Masonic affilijition as a condition to membership."
On November 7th. 1951, the Grand Secretary forwarded to the
accused a letter in which the foregoing amendment was quoted verbatim,
and which letter stated: "The quoted language above is now Masonic
law of this jurisdiction and it is expected that you will not offend it."
The accused relies upon a letter received by him from the then
Grand Master. dated November 13, 1951, which was in reply to a letter
of inquiry written by the accused, and in which the foregoing language
was used:
"I again made a very careful study of the law and am convinced that I have no power to grant any permits at all. All I can
do is to say that the prohibition by Grand Lodge to Masons to
publish and/or insert advertising in so-called Masonic magazines
may be suspended until the next session of Grand Lodge. And I
can't do that until the committee reports favorably upon the applications."
He also relies upon a directive issued generally by the Grand Master
on November 20th, 1951, in which the following language was used:
"The Grand Master has no power to suspend or abrogate any

Trial Record No. 1413
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Grievances to which was referred Trial Record
No. 1413, begs leave to report as follows:
The accused, F. T., a member of America Lodge No. 475, was, by
order of the Grand Master, charged and tried in Hollywood Lodge No.
335 with unMasonic conduct based upon a specification to the effect
that, in violation of Section 127 of the Ordinances, he did solicit, insert
and print advertising during the years l 952, 1953 and 1954 in the
Masonic Citizen, a publication purporting to be Masonic in name and
character, without the express sanction of the Grand Lodge.
On this charge the accused was brought to trial, he being personally
present and represented by able counsel, and at the conclusion of such
trial com.missioners unanimously found him guilty as to the specification
and as to the charge of unMasonic conduct. The commissioners fixed
penalty at suspension.
The accused has appealed. Hls attorney has supported the appeal
by the submission of a trial brief. He urges in this brief that Grand
Lodge should reverse this conviction because: First, that although the
accused had made application for a sanction from Grand Lodge authorizing ·him to solicit advertising and to publish the Masonic Citizen and
was denied such sanction, such denial of sanction was improper; Second,
that his violation was an innocent one because he solicited and published under what he believed to be permission of the then Grand
Master, Louis C. Drapeau; and, Third, that the content of his publication, the Masonic Citizen, was, in fact, highly beneficial to Masonry.
Each member of your committee has carefully examined the entire
record of this proceeding and the appeal Bled by the accused. Without
unduly extending this report by discussing all the detail set forth in
the appeal brief. we are unanimous (except Judge Pierson, who deems
himself disqualified) in believing that the record establishes that none
of the contentions of the accused are sufficiently supported.
As to the :first contention of the accused we point out that in the
Masonic jurisdiction of California the authority of our Grand Lodge
is and must necessarily be supreme. If our Grand Lodge, by ordinance,
prohibits specific conduct by Masons, a violation of such ordinance
constitutes a Masonic offense, and to justify disciplinary action for such
violation requires no proof of actual moral turpitude, nor of fraud.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

part of Masonic Law. So when I am asked for temporary permits
I am sure I have no power to grant them. No permit to print or
circulate any publication will be issued by me. As I read the law,
my power stops when I say to any publication, until Grand Lodge
meets next October, Masons may continue to operate such publications and other Masons may continue to advertise in them. I
have no power to recognize or sanction any publication."
But the accused does not quote the further language in the said
directive by which Grand Master Drapeau made it clear that he might
authorize the continuance of such publications until the 1952 Communication of Grand Lodge but that such authorization would be absolutely
conditioned upon the publisher obtaining a favorable recommendation
from the Committee on Publications. We quote the following language
to that effect:
"So I must follow the mandate of Grand Lodge, and require
as a prerequisite to any action by me, the recommendation of the
Committee."
"Moreover, neither my time nor my strength would permit me
to consider, study and determine alone what, if any, publications
shall be permitted to publish, and what publications Masons may
advertise in."
" ... I must have the recommendation of the Committee: I cannot change or abrogate the law: I cannot say to one publication,
"You can go ahead," and to another, "You can not." Indeed, I
don't think I can say to any publication, "You can go ahead."
"If you go ahead, you will have to do that on your own responsibility."
This directive ends with the following statement:
"But this I can say to all of you: Get your petition before the
Committee as soon as possible. And I can say to you that I know
the Committee understands this problem, and will give your application immediate attention and disposition."
Thereafter, on December 19, 1951, the accused submitted his application for a permit to publish the Masonic Citizen, and on January
11, 1952, the Grand Secretary wrote to him, in part as follows:
"After due consideration the Committee has recommended
that the application be denied, and Most Worshipful Louis C.
Draipeau, Grand Master, has directed me to inform you that the
requested permission is denied."
Following the receipt of this notice from the Grand Secretary the
accused nevertheless continued the publication of the Masonic Citizen
in direct violation of t'he order of the Grand Master. How could he,
at his trial, and now, successfully urge that he had permission to do so
from the Grand Master?
We shall not undertake to recite the substantial evidence heard by

the trial commissioners which supports their findings, but it was strong
and convincing, and we believe that Grand Lodge should afBirm those
findings.
However, we are not in accord with the penalty imposed by the commission. We believe that the policy of the Grand Lodge in the past
has been, and in the future should continue to be, that for deliberate
violation of a specific edict of Grand Lodge, the penalty must be expulsion rather than suspension. We believe in all such cases, the Grand
Lodge should be vested with the right to pass upon the future application of the accused for restoration, if he shall make such application.
W·hen the penalty is expulsion Grand Lodge retains that right, whereas
when the penalty is suspension, Grand Lodge does not have that right.
Your Committee therefore offers the following resolution:
"RESOLVED, That the action of the trial commissioners in Trial
Record No. 1413, finding F. T. guilty of unMasonic conduct, be and
the same ·h ereby is ratiBed, confirmed and approved, but that by the
action of this Grand Lodge the said F. T. be and he is hereby expelled
from all the rights and privileges of Masonry."
Adopted.

From the record in evidence herein, the following facts are disclosed,
which are set forth in narrative form:
In April of 1930, B.H.E.M., then 17 years of age, was charged in
Jackson County, Missouri, with grand larceny, a felony, it being alleged
that he did unlawfully and feloniously steal, take and carry away one
motor vehicle of the value of $2,000.00. He plead guilty and was sentenced to three years in the Missouri State Reformatory.
In August of 1930 and in the same court, said B.H.E.M. was
charged with second degree forgery, a felony, it being alleged that he
feloniously and wilfully forged a check drawn on the Fidelity National
Bank. He plead guilty and was sentenced to three years in the Missouri
State Reformatory.
In October of 1931 the said B.H.E.M., in Cooper County, Missouri,
was charged with assault with intent to commit murder, it being alleged
that he and another did feloniously and with malice aforethought make
an assault with a deadly weapon, to wit, a metal cylindrical bar 1Yi
feet, with intent to kill and murder. He plead guilty and was sentenced
to six years in the Missouri State Prison.
The last charge arose out of his attempt to escape from the R~forma-

One convicted of a felony is ineligible to receive the Degrees of
Masonry.
A petition cannot go before a lodge until it has received the recommendation of at least two of its members. No recommendor should
sign an application until he has first made a careful investigation to
ascertain if the petitioner was worthy of the privileges he sought. Those
who recommend are presumed to know the law, and ought to know if
the petitioner they recomend is qualified. The members of the Lodge and
of the investigating and personnel committees have the absolute right
to rely on the good faith of the recommendors and to assume that they
have disclosed all information that they may possess regarding the
petitioner.
In the instant case, the accused made no investigation whatever
even though he had been put on notice of facts which required investigation; nor did he disclose such facts to his lodge.
There is ample evidence in the record from which the trial commissioners could have found the accused guilty on specifications 3rd,
4th, 5th, 6th and 8th. Certainly it is reasonably an inference that from
the wilful failure of both the accused and F.W.C. to make a full and
fair disclosure of the true facts to the lodge and to the members of the
investigating and interviewing committees, that there was. to say the
least, a tacit understanding and agreement between them not to do so.
This committee, however, does not feel that it is necessary to request a reversal of the findings of the trial commissioners, on those
specifications upon which the accused was found not guilty. From the
record and evidence in this case, the accused has shown himself to be
unfit to remain a Mason. Certainly his conduct in withholding this

information constitutes a far greater crime against Masonry than does
the failure of the applicant, who is not familiar with our Masonic laws,
to disclose all information, and as we have seen, the applicant, though
be became a Master Mason, was expelled from all the rights and privileges of Masonry because he made a "false and misleading statement."
This committee therefore offers the following resolution:
RESOLVED, That the findings of the trial commissioners finding
the accused guilty of specifications 1, 2 and 7 and of un-Masonic conduct be, and they are hereby sustained; that the penalty of reprimand
be and the same is hereby set aside, and the penalty is fixed by this
Grand Lodge at expulsion.
Adopted.

Trial Record No. 1431
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Charges were brought by the Junior Warden at the direction of the
Grand Master. It specified that R. J. W., in violation of Section 287
of the Ordinances, did on or about June 1, 1954, publish and distribute
a pamphlet or letter addressed to the Brethren of the Masonic Fraternity,
urging Masons to vote for him in his candidacy for Governor of the
State of California. The accused lived in Hollywood, so summons was
forwarded to him by registered mail. When this was undelivered, regular mail was used and accused acknowledged receipt of the summons by
a letter dated Sept. 20. 1954, in which he requested that the trial set
for the 25th be continued for a period of 90 days. The letter of Sept.
20th also contained the admission of the accused that "the distribution
of the letter complained of in the charge was confined exclusively to
Masters and Officers of the various Lodges." The letter further set forth
that the accused was not given a copy of Section 287, that there was
no allegation that he knew of the existence of the provisions of said
section, that he was not informed how said ordinance could supersede
obligations of the degrees, that he was not violating any Masonic law
and was doing his duty as a Mason in asking his brethren to consider
him favorably as a candidate.
The trial commission continued the trial from Sept. 27th to Dec. 4th,
1954. The Secretary of the Lodge wrote to the accused on Sept. 27th
advising him of the new trial date, sent him a copy of Section 287 and
told him that he could obtain a copy of Constitution and Ordinances
from the Master or Secretary of a Lodge in the locality of his residence
or by writing to the Grand Secretary's office. On Nov. 22, 1954, twelve
days before the trial, accused wrote a letter to the lodge stating that he
had appointed L. 0. W., a past Master of Stockton Lodge, as his counsel, to appear with the accused and defend him, to which letter was
attached the certificate of L. O. W. that he had accepted the appointment and "will make my appearance as stated."
On December 4th, the date of the trial, the Master of the Lodge

306

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

received a letter from the accused dated Dec. 2nd, in which the accused
stated: "Today, Dec. 2nd, 1954, as a result of a special air flight trip
from Los Angeles, California, I have for the first time obtained procedural material for proper preparation of my defense to the charges for
which I have been summonsed to answer, etc." The letter further stated
that within 30 days from date the accused would prepare his request for
a "Bill of Particulars" and written answer, after which a convenient
date might be mutually and agreeably set for the trial. The letter further
indicated that the accused had received a "loan copy" of Ross' Digest
from the Grand Secretary. There was evidence at the trial that the accused and his counsel were in the Grand Secretary's office and had
visited with the Secretary of the lodge on December 2nd, and after
leaving the Secretary of the Lodge the accused phoned to the Secretary
stating that he would ask for a continuance of the trial. The Secretary
told him that he or his counsel should be present at the time indicated.
Neither the accused nor his counsel appeared at the trial. and the
trial commissioners determined to proceed with the trial, finding that the
accused's request for a further continuance was not meritorious. Evidence was introduced to support the changes, and the trial commission
found the accused guilty of the specification, guilty of unMasonic conduct, and fixed the 1penalty at suspension. The accused flied a notice
of intention to appeal the matter to Grand Lodge together with a brief
in support of the appeal, all of which has been considered by your
Committee.
The accused was afforded the opportunity of having a fair trial in
this matter. His first request for a continuance was granted, being in
excess of 60 days, and his request of Dec. 2nd for a further continuance
was entirely unreasonable. The accused himself admitted the facts, so
that the 8nding of guilty of the specification was correct. Using a roster
of Lodge officers for the purpose of distributing political propaganda
constitutes a Masonic offense, and. for that reason the finding that the
accused was guilty of unMasonic conduct is likewise supported in the
record.
There is some question, however, whether the penalty as fixed by
the trial commission is sufficient. Suspension is defined by Section 336
of the Ordinances as being the deprivation of a Mason's rights and
privileges as such, and prohibits all Masons and Lodges from holding
any Masonic intercourse with him until 'he shall be legally restored.
Expulsion is de8ned in Section 337 as the highest penalty known to the
Masonic law, and deprives a Mason of all rights and privileges as such,
and prohibits all Masons and Lodges from holding any Masonic intercourse with him forever, unless he be restored by the Grand Lodge. As
noted from the definition, the only difference between suspension and
expulsion is that an expelled Mason can only be restored by the vote
of Grand Lodge. A suspended Mason may be restored by the vote of
his own Lodge.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

307

Masonry does not .punish its members for unMasonic conduct by
the imposition of Bnes or incarceration. As has been well stated, punishment in Masonry is inflicted in order that the character of the institution might remain unsullied, and that the unpunished crimes of its members may not injuriously reflect upon the reputation of the entire Fraternity. For that reason its punishments are limited to expression of
disapprobation or the deprivation of Masonic rights. Our ordinances
do not fix the penalty which must be given for the commission of any
particular Masonic offense. The extent of the punishment rests in the
final analysis in the determination by Grand Lodge. Over the course of
years, this Grand Lodge has adopted certain 1policie8 with reference to
particular offenses. thereby in effect fixing a definite penalty. For example, if a Mason has committed a felony, to which he had pleaded
guilty or of which he has been found guilty, and the crime involved
moral turpitude, the penalty has been ftxed at expulsion unless there
have been strong extenuating circumstances.
Your Committee feels that the offense of which the accused was
found guilty is of such a serious nature, affecting the reputation of the
Fraternity as a whole, that the punishment should be fixed at expulsion.
This would give Grand Lodge the sole right to pass upon any possible
restoration if the accused should ever take steps to have himself restored to the rights and privileges of a Mason. We therefore offer the
following resolution and move its adoption:
"RESOLVED , T·hat the action of Parnassus Lodge No. 388 in finding the accused guilty of the specification and of unMasonic conduct
be affirmed: but that the penalty be and the same is hereby raised from
suspension to. expulsion."
Adopted.

Trial Record No. 1433
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Grievances, to which was referred Trial Record
No. 1433, reports as follows:
In 1954 the Accused, G. F. B., a member of Eden Lodge No. 113,
was convicted by a jury in the United States District Court of one count
of conspiracy to present a false claim to the Federal Housing Administration and of eight counts of wilfully making, passing and uttering
certain false statements to the Federal Housing Administration. Upon
specifications alleging the foregoing acts, Accused was charged with
un-Masonic conduct.
The charges involved certain F.H.A. home improvement loans obtained by Accused ostensibly for painting work, which were padded to
include moneys for other purposes such as the payment of existing obligations of the home owner. Before going into the home painting busi-

~09

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

ness Accused satisfied himself that the arrangement between him and
th solicitors who obtained the work were such that the solicitors would
not be his agents but, from a legal point of view, would be independent
brokers. Obviously this was a planned attempt to avoid liability for the
acts of the solicitors.
At the trial the judgment of the Federal Court convicting Accused '
was introduced in evidence. Although represented by able counsel. Accused did not testify but merely read a previously prepared answer in
which he stated that he assumed that the amounts obtained from the
F.H.A. loans, over and above the cost of the work, were for brokerage
fees and for other work done under the contract: that he had never
questioned the excessive commissions to the brokers who solicited the
work.
. Under Section 319 of the Ordinances the answer of the Accused is
not in evidence on Accused's behalf but may be an admission against
interest so far as Accused is concerned.
After deliberating on the charges the Commissioners requested that
the charges be amended so as to charge not the acts of Accused but the
Federal Court convictions. This was done with the consent of Accused
and his attorney and of Accuser, who was not represented by counsel.
The Commissioners found Accused guilty of the specifications and
not guilty of un-Masonic conduct. While technically the amended
charges are not well drawn, this Grand Lodge has followed the policy
of construing such charges as charging the acts involved in the conviction. As so construed we have a finding that Accused conspired to present a false claim to the Federal Housing Administration and that he
made, uttered and passed certain false statements to the Federal Housing Administration, in violation of law. This finding is amply supported
by the judgment of conviction and is not controverted by any testimony.
Obviously. conspiring to present false claims to the Federal Housing
Administration and the presentation of such claims to such agency are
Masonic offenses.
We therefore offer the following resolution:
RESOLVED. That the Trial Commissioners' finding in Trial Record No. 1433 that G. F. B. is guilty of the specifications be and it is
hereby affirmed and approved: that the finding that G. F. B. is not guilty
of un-Masonic conduct be and it is hereby vacated and set aside and a
finding that he is guilty of un-Masonic conduct is hereby supplied by
this Grand Lodge; and that said G. F. B. be and he is hereby suspended
from all the rights and privileges of Masonry.
Adopted.

Trial Record No. 1442
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
This proceeding concerns one C. P. B., a member of San Pasqual
Lodge No. 452 in Pasadena. He was charged with unmasonic conduct
in each of two specifications. We are here concerned with the first
specification only. The specification is as follows:
"That continuously during several years next last .past the said
C. P. B., doing business as Acacia Press, Post Office Box 337M, Pasa.dena, California, did use the name and emblems of Masonry for commercial purposes, namely, to sell and solicit the sale of a book called
"The Great Message," and in connection therewith did distribute
among prospective purchasers, profane and Masons alike, advertising
and other sales promotional material similar to that attached hereto
and made a part •hereof. marked Exhibits A, B, C and D."
The accused filed with the trial commission his answer in which
with respect to the first specification he admitted every material part
of the specification except for the allegation that the name and emblems
of Masonry were used "for commercial purposes" and as to that allegation he answered "that he at no time intended to make any profit, nor
has ·he made any profit, whatever from the sale of said book."
At the conclusion of the trial in which the accused was represented
by an attorney the trial commission found the accused guilty of the
first specification, found it to be unmasonic conduct and determined
that he should be punished by reprimand.
The record established by overwhelming evidence the allegations
of the specification including the allegation of the use of the "name
and emblems of Masonry for commercial purposes, namely to sell and ·
solicit the sale of a book called "The Great Message." The accused
based his defense that the enterprise was non-commercial on bis testimony that before sending the circular which advertised the sale of the
book "The Great Message" to some 76,000 persons of whom 75,000
were Masons and 1,000 were non-masons he had conducted a survey
which proved to him that he would not have enough sales of the book
to return him a profit and his further statement that the sales in fact had
not produced a profit.
Opposed to this contention of the accused is the content of the
circular which was distributed to the 76,000 .prospective customers
which, after setting forth a statement of the philosophical nature of the
book together with a number of testimonial comments by persons who
had purportedly read the book, announced that "The Great Message"
could be purchased from the accused for $3.50 "on a ten day double
money-back guarantee." Included with the circulars was an order
blank and a self-addressed, prepaid postage envelope for the remittance.
Your com.mUtee finds no merit in the assertion by the accused that
whether his effort to sell the book was commercial or non-commercial

is determined by whether it makes or fails to make an overall net profit.
We agree with the Trial Commission that this was a commercial campaign to promote sale of the book.
We feel that the printed materials used in this enterprise are so
offensive to Masonic conduct that the penalty of reprimand is inadequate.
Your committee on Grievances proposes the following resolution:
RESOLVED, That the Trial Commission's finding in Trial Record
No. 1442 that C. P. B. is guilty of the first specification and guilty of
unmasonic conduct be approved and affirmed: that by action of this
Grand Lodge the penalty of reprimand as determined by the Trial
Commission be vacated and set aside in lieu thereof that C. P. B. be
· and he is hereby expelled from all rights and privileges of Masonry.
Adopted.
Trial Record No. 1445
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Grievances to which was referred Trial Record
No. 1445, begs leave to report as follows:
The accused C. J. C., a member of Southern California Lodge No.
278, was, by order of the Grand Master, charged and tried in Fairview
Lodge No. 629 for unMasonic conduct based upon the following speci·
fication:
"1. That said C. J. C. in violation of paragraph 2 of Section 127 of
the Ordinances of Grand Lodge, as amended in 1954, did solicit, insert
and print advertising during the months of November and December.
1954. in The Southern California Club and Sports Magazine, a publication purpo;ting to be Masonic in name or character."
On this charge the accused was brought to trial on March 30th, 1955,
and was by unanimous vote of the seven elected trial commissioners
adjudged guilty of the specification and of unMasonic conduct, and. by
unanimous vote of the commissioners the penalty was fixed at expulsion.
The accused was present at the trial and was represented by counsel
of his own choice.
The evidence presented by the Junior Warden is amply sufficient to
sustain the verdicts and judgment of the trial commissioners.
The principal defenses raised by the written answer of the accused
and by his testimony are briefly as follows:
That he did not solicit advertising for said publication:
T·h at said magazine does not purport to be Masonic in name or
character:
That his conduct did not involve moral turpitude, lack of honesty
or integrity;
That his conduct does not involve a breach of duty as a Mason:
That his conduct does not involve injury to any person:
That the legislation by which Section 127 of our Ordinances was

312

PROCEEDING S OP THE

amended in 1954, is unfair, unconscionable and unconstitutional in that
it deprived publishers of their property without due proc~s of law without compensation and that it violates the right of Freedom of the Press
and Freedom of Speech.
The elected Trial Commissioners, to whom the accused and his very
able attorney made no objection, although invited to do so, passed upon
all the contentions raised by the accused and made adverse findings upon
them. ·
The October issue of accused's magazine was named "The Southern
California Shriner." The name was changed for the November and
December, 1954 issues to "The Southern California Club and Sports
Magazine." The November issue contains 36 pages, of which thirty
pages are devoted exclusively to pictures and news items concerning
Shrine Clubs, except for the space occupied by commercial advertising.
The December issue contained 42 pages, of which 34 pages are devoted
to the same Shrine Clubs, two pages to sports events, two pages to the
Los Angeles Tennis Club, and four pages to Elks Clubs, all accompanied
by commercial advertising.
The accused, while admitting through his attorney that he was
informed of the 1954 amendment within two or three days after Grand
Lodge adopted the same, excuses his publications of the November and
December issues in practically the same form as before such action by
Grand Lodge, on the ground that in the publishing business it is not
practicable to change the form of the magazine within a month or two.
The answer to this explanation is simply that pursuant to the formal
edict of Grand Lodge the accused might well have suspended publication until the format of his magazine might have been altered so that
he would not have been in violation of the Masonic law which he well
knew had been adopted by Grand Lodge after ample debate and consideration.
This Grand Lodge has in all cases heretofore of violations of Section
127 of Ordinances, approved the penalty of expulsion. In the instant
case we find no irregularity in the trial proceedings, the evidence justifies the conviction, and but for the fact that the accused has appealed
from the verdict and judgment we would have in our omnibus report
included this case, just as we have Trial Records Nos. 1426, 1432 and
1441, each of which involves a violation of the same Ordinance, and in
each of which the penalty fixed was expulsion.
We feel it our duty to offer the following resolution and to move its
adoption:
"RESOLVE D, That the action of the Trial Commissioners in Trial
Record No. 1445, finding the accused C. J. C. guilty of unMasonic conduct, and fixing the penalty therefor at expulsion be and the same hereby is ratified, confirmed and approved."
Adopted.

Trial Record No. 1448
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Grievances, to which was referred Trial Record
No. 1448, begs leave to report as follows:
The accused H. L. F. was on February 2, 1953, convicted by a jury
in the Superior Court of the crime of manslaughter, and was by the
Court, on February 11th, 1953, committed to the State Prison of California. His Lodge proceeded against him by way of automatic expulsion, but upon demand by the accused he was charged with unMasonic
conduct based upon a specification that on October 18, 1952, he did
wilfully, unlawfully, feloniously and without malice, kill E. A. F., his
wife.
The accused was brought to trial before the trial commissioners
elected by the Lodge on November 30th, 1954. The accused was present,
apparently having been, in the meantime, released from State Prison,
on parole. A prima fade case was made out by the accuser by the introduction in evidence of a certified copy of the judgment of the Superior
Court, reciting the finding of guilty by the jury, denying probation, and
committing the accused to the State Prison.
In his testimony before the Lodge Trial Commissioners, the accused
stated that ·his wife's death was the result of accident: that she herself
had the gun in her hand when she was shot.
The record shows that on October 18th, 1952, the accused and his
wife had started to a dinner party with friends, had had a quarrel, and
each had left the dinner party and had gone home alone: that in the
kitchen of their.home from about 9 to 11 P.M., they were discussing
their domestic difficulties: that at about the latter time the wife said to
the accused: "H--, sometimes you make me so mad I could kill you."
The accused then told his wife, "Well, I can make that easy for you,"
went to the bedroom, procured a .45 calibre automatic pistol. loaded it,
placed a cartridge in the chamber by operating the slide, and took it
out into the kitchen. What happened from then on is in controversy,
but the trial jury in Superior Court found the accused guilty of manslaughter, and the Judge who .presided at that trial denied a motion
for new trial. indicating his belief in the propriety of the verdict of the
jury. Furthermore , this conviction in Superior Court was appealed to
the District Court of Appeals and that court affirmed the finding of the
jury and the judgment of conviction.
Under this state of the record, the trial commission in his Lodge
acquitted the accused by a vote of 7 to 2.
From the finding of not guilty_: the accuser, the Junior Warden of
the Lodge, has appealed.
Your Committee cannot reconcile the result of this trial with the
result of the trial in Superior Court, and the affirmation of the guilt of

TRIALS HELD OVER
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Califomi~
Either accuser or accused has thirty days after the announcement
in lodge of the result of the trial within which to appeal. They have
sixty days from said date within which to file additional evidence, etc.
Therefore Grand Lodge cannot pass on a trial record if the time for
appeal or the time for filing data in case of an appeal has not passed.

To the Most Worshipfu l Grand Lodge of California:
California Masonic Lodges have again been active amending their
By-Laws to provide for necessary changes. Building for the future is
one of the dominating themes of our present Communication.. It is always present as one of the objectives of a successful executive. It was
given 100% consideration when our Ma8?nk forefathers t~k. such a
prominent part in the building of the United States Constitution and
under that Charter our country has grown great and powerful.
The Uniform Code of By...:Laws is a part of our Masonic Constitution and provides for the various differing activities of the constituent
lodges. Incoming Masters should review the By-Laws and with the
Secretary endeavor to keep them uip-to-date and so worded as to always permit the lodge to function efficiently.
The Grand Secretary 's office has compiled forms which are available upon request fo~ the most usual amendments to By-Laws.
Use of these forms has greatly assisted the Grand Officers and
this Committee in passing on the legality of desired changes. You also
gain suggestions from the Grand. Secretary's .office that enable. all
desired changes in By-Laws to be incorporated in the one proceeding.
Two lodges each presented two amendments of the same section this
year. The four amendments have been a?proved. The last i~ time in
each case of course prevails as the governing law of the section.
Our Committee continues to suggest that you 6.ll in the blanks regarding the affiliation fee. We grant, that a blank space presumes no
charge, but a word there shows an expression on th~. question. We have
received an assortment of terms used, as follows: Nil-No- -No Fee
-No/100 's and None." All of them are sufficiently definite.
One amendment dealing with legal holidays that has received much

regular meeting date shall fall on New Year's Day. Indepei:idence Day
-legal holidays or any one of the above legal holidays, falling on Sunday is observed on the Day (Monday ) following the stated meeting
shail be holden on the Second Monday of that month." It conforms to
present day practice regarding holidays.
We believe the agreements as to fees between lo.dges having concurrent jurisdiction is good procedure and conducive to good Masonic
relations.

three Officers must remain at the location of the Lodge for the

REPORT OF COMMI TTEE ON
CONSTI TUTION MONTH OBSERV ANCE

To the Most Worshipfu l Grand Lodge of California:
The program material suggested for our nineteenth annual Constitution Month Observan ce was designed to provide both a THEME and
a CHALLE NGE.
The Theme, "The Miracle of the Constitut ion-when ever we walk
in the atmosphere of the Constituti on of the United States we walk in
the realm of the Almighty, " was borrowed by .permission from an address by Brother J. Harry Sroufe, Past Grand Orator of the Grand
Lodge of Oregon, because the combination of. its emotional and spiri.tual
impact indicated that it might well become impressed upon the minds
and hearts of th-0se who saw and heard it and thus be remembered long
after the words of the balance of the program, the thoughts of speakers
or the impressions of other program features were forgotten.
The Challenge, to EMULAT E not just VENERA TE the example
of our founding fathers, was both speculative and operative in accordanc e
with tradition.

Our only recommendation is that this annual Observance be continued and carefully expanded to the end that the Voice of Masonry
may continue to be heard in increasing volume, for, just as it was the
influence of the Men of Masonry in the decade following the Declaration
of Independence which brought about "The Miracle of the Constitution" it may well be the destiny of the Men of Masonry in the decade
ahead to provide the leadership so necessary for the preservation of that
"Mirach~."

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON MASONIC HISTORY
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Standing Committee on Masonic History begs leave to report
as follows:
Although this report of your standing committee on Masonic History
was iprepared under the direction of the Most Worshipful Past Grand
Master Leon 0. Whitsell, Chairman of the committee, he is absent from
this Grand Lodge for the first time in many years. He and Mrs. Whitsell are taking a trip around the world and will be away from California
until next April or May. While he is greatly and sincerely missed, all
of us rejoice in his good fortune and join in wishing them a safe and
satisfying journey.
At the 1954 Communication of this Grand Lodge, the Committee on
Masonic History was made a regular standing committee, out of recognition that the work of this committee is a continuing work and that a
program of record-keeping, archive-searching, and event-recording
would have to be a continuous program if it were to effectively serve the
·
needs of this Grand Lodge.
During this past year, the committee has made a start towards fulfilling the objectives set for it. The work of recording and gathering
information relative to the Lodges of this jurisdiction is well under way
and will continue. The committee held a meeting at Stockton shortly
after the first of the year, at which all members but one were present
and he was absent due to an emergency situation in his home the day
before. The meeting lasted all day and an area of work was delegated
to each member as his contribution throughout the year. A product of
this work was the drafting of a paper entitled, "Your Centennial Observance," compiled from material on all past centennial observances
among the respective Lodges and which offers suggestions relative to
a centennial program, pointing out pitfalls ilS well as objectives in good
programming. This .paper has just recently been completed and is being
mimeographed in sufficient quantity that several copies may be mailed
to the newly installed Junior Warden of a Lodge whose centennial will
take place during the year that he is Master. A Lodge should start planning its centennial observance at least two years prior to the event. The
committee feels that the paper can be improved upon and as time and
ex.perience dictate, it will be revised. Meanwhile, it is hoped that this
material will be found helpful. The Lodges need not apply for it as it
will automatically be mailed to the incoming Junior Wardens as they
take office.
In connection with centennial celebrations, the committee is not being
called upon frequently enough to render assistance in the compilation
of such historical data as a Lodge might wish to use. The committee
stands ready to assist the respective Lodges in assembling and organizing such historical material as is available to it when called upon to do

326

327

· PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

so. During the past year. several Lodges took advantage of this ser~­
ice and we like to believe that their centennials were better for it. If
you desire such assistance, write the committee in care of the Grand
Secretary.
Your chairman, or one or more members of your committee, attended
all or nearly all of the centennial celebrations that were held to date.
At several. one or more members were scheduled speakers. As many
as four of the seven members have attended centennials, per meeting,
and the committee plans on continuing this activity. In addition to the
centennial celebrations, one or more of the members have attended every
dedication, institution, or charter ceremony within travel distance of our
homes. Programs of these events have been collected and placed in the
files of the committee for future use or reference.
Once again the committee calls attention of this Grand Lodge to the
continuing need for safeguarding your Lodge records, all of which in
due time will become valuable from both a monetary and historical standpoint. if in fact they are not already so. For instance, those Lodges
having in their file letters bearing the signature of our first Grand Master. Jonathan Drake Stevenson. own documents of considerable tangible
value, as Brother Stevenson was a famous California pioneer, aside from
being our first Grand Master. He achieved national fame and went
down in history as the famous commander of "Colonel Stevenson's Regiment of New York Volunteers." which was raised by Brother Stevenson
by direction of President Polk. his friend, and which came to California
in 1846 as a constabulary force to help keep the peace and def end this
newly-won territory. Other famous early-day pfuneer Masons either
were members of our Lodges or were in communication with them. Bear
Mountain Lodge has the signature of Samuel Clemens, whose pen name
you all know as "Mark Twain," on its Tiler's register. In due time the
signature of such a contemporary Mason as the Chief Justice of the
United States, the Most Worshipful Earl Warren, will become valuable
if not already of some value.
. Tim~ does not permit us to go on further but the respective Lodges
own literally hundreds of signatures of persons, men who were colorful,
famous. much-honored and respected, and with the passing of time signatures that are sought after and. as a result. valuable. Aside from their
monetary value, your Lodge records and documents are priceless and
irreplaceable as records of the passing events of your Lodge life, and
when lost constitute a loss nearly as great as that of some member of
one's family. Your committee urges, if you have not already done so,
that each Lodge procure a fireproof vault in which to keep your records.
You can either buy such a vault or for a relatively small sum-the cost
of materials in most cases, you can construct your own vault out of
cement or brick. When you arrange for such a vault be sure to get one
large enough to hold all of your records, past and present. Remember,
"records" are not.only your Lodge books but also your correspondence,

invoices. publications, etc. Masters: appoint a committee to get this
done NOW. To borrow a trite phrase, "tomorrow may be too late."
On November 6, 1954; at Cypress Lawn Cemetery, Colma, California. Grand Master Clausen conducted the ceremony of re-interring the
body of Past Grand Master Jonathan Drake Stevenson in Section K,
Lot 226. Grave 122, the plot of California Lodge No. 1. A suitable
marker was placed over the grave.
Most Worshipful: the members of your History Committee join in
expressing their appreciation for the privilege of serving during the past
year. I move the ·a doption of this report together with the request that
the sum of $250 be allocated to finance the expenses of the com~ittee
for the ensuing year.
Respectfully submitted,
LEON 0. WHITSELL

REPORT OF TRUSTEES OF MASONIC CLUB HOUSE,
BERKELEY
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Board of Directors of the Masonic Club of The University,
Berkeley, California, is pleased to submit its annual report of the activities for the fi'scal year 1954-1955.
We feel that the Club is serving a very important function at the
University, by providing a social center for the student Club members.
Eligible members of the dub, as you know, include Masons. Sons and
Daughters of Masons, members of DeMolay, Job's Daughters and
Rainbow. and other closely related members of Masonic families regularly attending the University.
During the past year the activities of the Club have continued to
express the original purpose to serve as a center for Masonic activities
and to further the ideals and principles of the Fraternity, by encouraging the students at the University of California to receive the greatest
possible benefits of education. We feel that the original intent in providing this center of Masonic activity is being more than accomplished.
This is evidenced by the intense interest of the student members in
their many activities and indirectly reflecting the purpose we wish to
attain. They ex·press themselves in the following quotations:
"The students in the dub realize that we have exceptional facilities
compared with most organizations on this campus, and we know that
a larger membership leads to a more active, spirited, Qrganization•. We

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

feel that our membership, although it is growing steadily, is still far
below the potential that the campus offers.
"The Masonic Club of the University offers a fine and varied program for social and recreational activities. The opportunities to watch
television or just chat with friends, are restful and enjoyable. The quiet
dignity of our beautiful lounge is as restful to our members as to our
many and frequent guests."
Membership in the student club is not at the level that we feel is
possible to attain. Every effort is being made by the student members
and your Board of Directors to direct attention to the Club and inform
the brethren of this Grand Jurisdiction of the facilities provided for
their children. Membership during the past year was about 180. This
represents a low percentage against the registration at the University.
At the present writing we are informed that the membership has been
increased by 57 new members. From information made available to us,
it appears that group meetings of the East Bay Masters and Wardens
Association, Guardian Council of Job's Daughters, University Square
Club, San. Francisco Masters and Wardens Association, and a combined group of East Bay District Officers Associations have greatly
furthered interest in the Club.
Our particular appreciation is extended to The Most Worshipful
Henry C. Clausen, Grand Master, for his sincere interest in the Clubhouses as ex•pressed in his letter of July 18, 1955 addressed to all lodges,
requesting them to publicize and l>ecome aware of these facilities and
privileges.
Many improvements ·have been completed during the past year. including installation of new heating equipment, new rugs, and interior
decorations. The attractiveness of the club has been greatly improved.
An attractive revision of a brochure of information about the club
has just recently been made available. It is sincerely hoped that the
attending members to this Grand Lodge Communication will avail themselves of the opportunity to review this brochure and visit the clubhouse
during the school year.
The coming year presents no unusual requirements for maintenance
expenditures and therefore the proposed budget previously presented
to the Finance Committee for consideration includes only basic necessary operating expenses. The budget and a com·plete auditor's report for
the past year are included as a part of this report.
The undersigned members of your Board of Directors wish to express their appreciation for the opportunity to serve this Grand Lodge
in this and every other capacity.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
During the past y~ar we celebrated the Silver Anniversary of the
Masonic Clubhouse on the Westwood campus by having a banquet to
which we invited as guests all Masters of Lodges in this area, together
with their wives, all student members of the Masonic Affiliate Club, and
a number of special guests from the University, including the Chancellor
and his wife. Judge Ellsworth Meyer, P.G.M., welcomed the guests
and explained the history and the purpose of the Clubhouse. Music
was furnished by the Scottish Rite orchestra under the direction of
Mr. David Gussin.
One of the purposes of the banquet was to make the Clubhouse and
its facilities familiar to all Lodges throughout this area, in the hope that
it would increase membership in the student Club. In this respect it
had only minor success. In another manner, however, this objective
was accomplished. The student guests who attended included the
"pledges." A larger percentage than normal of the pledges this year
completed their membership and became active in the work of the Club.
We can assume that the banquet with the large number of Masons pres~
ent impressed the students and increased their interest. In any event,
we did take in more members and the result has been a highly successful
year.
It is also particularly gratifying to report that as a result of the
Grand Master's message to the Lodges regarding the Clubhouses, we
have had visitations from several of the Lodges.
We report with regret the resignation during the year of one of our
Directors, Bro. A. H. Nicoll, who has moved his residence to Northern
California.
We also report with deep sorrow the passing of a beloved member
of our Board, Bro. Chas. E. Listenwalter. His loss will be keenly felt.
His always kindly words and ever-willing helping hand will cause him
to be long remembered.
For many years this report has consisted of a general description
of the activities of the Club for the preceding year. Anyone desiring
that general information can look at the reports of prior years. In
particular, the report of last year describes almost exactly the program
of this year with respect to publicity, Club organization and activities,
snack bar, etc.
To make the report different this year and to provide more speciftc
information, we are going to leave out the general information and sub~
stitute as an appendix, in addition to the budget, a summary of the
Club's activities. This summary was prepared by the Director and the
Assistant Director, Mrs. Sheldon and Mrs. Johnson, for the information

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
It is with pleasure that I submit this report on the progress made by
the Grand Lodge Sojourners Committee during the past year.
Master Masons from all parts of North America--even from all
parts of the world-are coming to California in great numbers. They
are among the hundreds of thousands who are establishing their residence throughout this jurisdiction because of the great potential this
great State offers in employment, health, education, and recreational
advantages. This migration has created a · tremendous obligation upon
the State of California in furnishing facilities necessary for the welfare
of our new neighbors.
Masonry in California is no exception. The constituent Lodges
throughout the State are now experiencing the greatest number of
visitations, by Sojourning Masons, than anytime sim;e World War II.
A great majority of those Sojourning Masons are becoming permanent
residents of California. Many Masons, living in California but belonging to foreign jurisdictions, never visit or make themselves known to the
Lodges of the communities in which they live. It is, therefore, the
responsibility of this committee to endeavor to make contact with
Sojourning Masons through the constituent Lodges.
It is the opinion of this committee that 150,000 or more Sojourning
Masons are living within the confines of the Grand Lodge of California.
Many are known to our constituent Lodges but there are a great many
with whom contact has not been made. It is with those Masons that this
committee is mainly concerned.
Through the efforts of this committee, many Lodges throughout
the State are holding what are known as "Sojourners Nights." All
members of the Lodge are urged to invite any and all Sojourning Masons
to attend these meetings. The best results have been accomplished when
no degree work is held and the full evening is spent. making the visiting
brethren welcome. The Blue Lodge Sojourners Committee handles the
details of dinner and program. Those Lodges participating in such a
program find that Sojourning Masons become interested in entering in
Lodge functions. Many have expressed their apj>reciation to the Lodges
for the welcome they received and have expressed the desire to become
members through demits or dual membership. I am sure that the results
have been noticeable to the Grand Secretary by the number of affiliations
being processed.
However, we find some Masters are reluctant and even disinterested
in the efforts of this committee, in setting aside one night for the recognition of our Sojourning brethren. The excuse given is that too much
degree work prohibits such an arrangement. Some do not want to be
bothered and we have found that some Lodges have no Soj oumers
Committee appointed or functioning.

ENFORCEMENT OF SECTION 127
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
The Committee on Publications supplements its report to this Grand
Lodge to bring to your attention the following matter regarding Al Bahr
Temple of the Shrine, an organization requiring Masonic affiliation as
a condition to membership.
This Grand Lodge by Section 127 of Ordinance has since 1954
prohibited the solicitation. sponsoring. inserting, placing, or printing
of advertising of any kind in or for any medium or publication which
purports to be Masonic in name or character or which is published by
or for any body, order or organization requiring Masonic affiliation as
a condition to membership.
After the opening of this Communication your Committee received
the accompanying football game program entitled Al Bahr 18th Annual
Shrine Charity Game and Pageantry. The program, carrying a frontispiece showing the Temple insignia, bearing a message from the Potentate including his picture in Shrine regalia, and with further pictures' of
Shrine officials in regalia, contains 52 pages, out of which 46 consist
in whole or in part of commercial advertisements and greetings.
We must report to you that at two meetings, one held by the Grand
Master and one held by this Committee, the heads of the Shrine Temples, including the present Potentate of Al Bahr, were fully informed
of the prohibition recited in Section 127. T·here can be no question but
that the officers here involved had full knowledge of our law.
The following resolution, which speaks for itself, has been prepared
in collaboration with and with the unanimous approval of both the Committee on Jurisprudence and the Committee on Policy and General Purposes. and we herewith move its adoption:

CECIL MATHEWS
ARTHUR E. CuNK

RESOLUTION
Whereas it has been reported to this Grand Lodge that a publication
under the auspices of Al Bahr Temple, Order of the Mystic Shrine, has
been issued with advertising paid for by the general public, and
Whereas if this be true the Masonic brethren members of this
organization who knew about it, took part in it, or connived to have it
done, are guilty of un-Masonic conduct, and further something should
be done about the organization itself.
Now, therefore, be it resolved:
1. That the incoming Grand Master direct the necessary things be
done to bring such offending brethren to trial for un-Masonic conduct.
2. That if in the discretion of the Grand Master under the circumstances developed it be necessary. that he by edict direct either or beth
of the following:
(a) That until his further order no Mason shall hereafter become
a member of said Al Bahr Temple.
(b) That until his further order no Mason shall continue to be a
member of said Al Bahr Temple.
Unanimously adopted.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
In accord with convention, the Memorial Association convened in
the Auditorium of the Memorial at Alexandria, Virginia, on February
22. Contributions from the several jurisdictions totaled around
$172,000.00, of which California supplied $41,882.05-just under 25%
of the whole. The unenviable position of many jurisdictions with substantial membership respecting contributions would appear to warrant
a realistic reappraisal by them of the whole subject, with a view toward
an elevated standing.
In 1947 our Grand Lodge determined its proportion of the cost of
the George Washington Memorial to be $463,653.35. Our contributions
including the sum reported herein have amounted to $471,291.85. We
have therefore redeemed our pledge. However, our $1.00 assessment
per new member does and should continue in order to assist in defraying
excess costs and endowment and as a reminder that the Father of our
Country was an ornament to Freemasonry.
Respectfully submitted,

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
During this year the only application for recognition came from the
Grand· Lodge of the Dominican Republic located at Ciudad, Trujillo.
Documentary evidence supplied was insufficient to enable determination
whether said Grand Lodge meets our tests for recognition. Our letter
a_ddressed to it seeking pertinent information remains unanswered. A
similar letter to the Grand Secretary of the Grand Lodge of Panama,
which is in amity with the applicant, likewise elicited no response. From
the record it appears that the applicant is recognized by the Grand
Lodges of Colorado, Kentucky. New York and Oregon. Brother Harry
W. Bundy, Grand Secretary of the Grand Lodge of Colorado, in response to our inquiry, stated that Colorado had recognized the applieant
in 1949 and quoted the report of the Committee made at that time. The
facts in the report <lo not meet our tests. The application will therefore
be held in abeyance for further consideration.

we received a letter from the Grand Master of the National Serene
Grand Lodge of Cartegena, inquiring whether we still recognized it.
It was pleasing to reply that our Grand Lodge had been in uninterrupted friendly relationship with it since recognition was accorded in
1930. Let us hope that this inquiry indicates that the dark clouds of
oppression in Colombia are lifting.

AMENDMENT OF SECTION 332
The proposal to amend Section 332 of the Ordinances relating to
automatic expulsion by eliminating the words: "and be imprisoned in
pursuance thereof," has been referred to this Committee.
At the present time if a member of a Lodge is convicted of a crime
classified as a felony and is imprisoned therefor, it is required that
charges be preferred against him and if he does not request a trial, he
is automatically expelled: however, if such member were convicted of
the same crime, but was placed on probation without being incarcerated,
the Lodge cou,ld not use the procedure set out in Section 332. The
mere fact that the accused was not incarcerated would require a full
Masonic trial.
In other words, our present law saves the Lodge the expense and
details of a Masonic trial if the convicted Mason has been imprisoned,
but requires the expense and details if he has not been imprisoned. The
Masonic procedure in the two instances cited does not depend upon
the crime committed but the punishment meted out by the state trial court.
Your Committee feels that from the Masonic standpoint the important thing is the crime committed and not the punishment by the state,
that Lodges should not be put to the expense of a trial merely because
a state court has seen fit to extend clemency. Of course, you will
understand that under Section 332 the accused may request a Masonic
trial and thus one will be required. No change in that particular is
involved in ,this amendment.
Your Committee approves the policy involved in the proposed
amendment and I move that Section 332 of the Ordinances be amended
by striking from the first sentence thereof the words: "and be imprisoned in pursuance thereof."
See report of Committee on Jurisprudence for final action.

RESTORATION BY GRAND LODGE

converted to cash and which will not be subject to wide fluctuation,
deterioration or limitation as to convertibility.
The amendments would make it possible to invest the entire 100%
of Lodge or Grand Lodge funds in Savings and Loan or Building and
Loans shares or certificates.
This type of investment cannot be considered liquid as there is no
assurance that they can be readily converted to cash. An examination
of Savings and Loan practice and regulations will disclose that these
certificates or shares can only be redeemed as investments are collected
by the Association.
Saving and Loan Associations do not have the liquid reserve required by either the National or the State Bank Act. It is not generally
known that banks are restricted from lending for real estate purposes
not more than 60% of their total savings deposits.
The balance must be kept in highly liquid bonds or cash.
Saving and Loan Associations on the other hand can lend 100%
of their deposits in mortgages and in addition,make loans to the extent
of their capital as well. The national average is over 104% of deposits.
A tight money situation would make withdrawals almost impossible.
A distinction must also be made between savings deposits in Banks
and an investment in a Saving or Building and Loan Association.
A bank deposit establishes a creditor and debtor relationship between the depositor and the bank, and all deposited funds must be paid
out before the general creditors of the bank are paid.
An investment in a Building and Loan Association actually is a
purc'hase of shares in the Association even though it is expressed in
dollars. There is 110 deposit contract between the investor and the Association and a holder of these certificates is to all intents and puqJoses
a shareholder in the venture.
The Deposit Insurance feature of banks and Saving and Loan Associations likewise is not comparable.
In the event of bank failure the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation after an inventory period makes available to the depositor his entire
amount up to $10,000.
On the other hand a Savings and Loan Association must first be
found insolvent before it can be taken over. The inability to permit
withdrawals does not constitute insolvency as an association is only
required under the law to pay out that which it collects from investments and loans. If after final liquidation it is unable to make full payments, then and only then does the insurance feature come into play.
Real Estate loans are made for periods ranging from 10 to 25 years
and it is conceivable that a long waiting period would ensue before final
collection could be made. There is no requirement to pay interest after
demand for payment has been made by an investor and the payment of
interest is not provided for in the insurance coverage.

Your committee on Policy and General Purposes has carefully considered the resolution presented by Wm. Nankervis, Jr., P.M. of Oak
Grove Lodge No. 215, proposing changes to Sections 344 and 345 of
Ross Digest and seeking to provide a method by which Grand Lodge
may restore to membership those who have been suspended for nonpayment of dues. The sections cited pertain only to the restoration
of members suspended or expelled for unmasonic conduct: the question
of non-payment of dues being covered by an entirely separate section,
260, which provides for reinstatement by a two-thirds vote by ballot.
This provision appears to be adequate and it seems that if a suspended
member applies to his Lodge for reinstatement and is refused by onethird of the members present there are undoubtedly other good reasons
for the refusal.
It is the opinion of your Committee that this particular question
had best be lef.t with the individual Lodges for decision and it, therefore,
recommends that this resolution be not adopted.
See report of Committee on Jurisprudence for final action.

The Policy and General Purposes Committee has reviewed the resolution presented by M.W. John R. Moore proposing to amend Section
86-1 and Section 152.1 to enable investment to be made in investment
certificates or shares of certain types of Savings and Loan or Building
and Loan Associations.
This proposal has been jointly considered with the Investment Committee and we have also counseled with the Finance Committee.
' It is the considered opinion of these three Committees that the reso_

Section 86-1 and 152.1 provide that at least 40% of funds available
for investment must be invested as follows:
"A. Cash or bank accounts.
"B. Obligations of the United States or those for which the
faith and credit of the United States are .pledged to provide for
the payment of the interest and principal.
"C. Obligations of the State of California and its political
subdivisions, provided they were issued pursuant to law and that
the faith and credit of such state or municipal corporation or district are pledged for their payment.
,
"D. Such securities as are legal investments for California
savings Banks."
This is the so-called class one group.
The purposes of Section 86-1 and 152.1 are to restrict investments
in this category to highly liquid marketable issues which can be readily

EXCUSING ASSIST ANT GRAN D LECTURERS

The Committee on Segregat ion has referred to the Committee on
Policy the recommendation of the Grand Master relative to excusing
Assistan t Grand Lecturers from compulsory attendan ce at Grand Lodge.
Article II, Section 3 of the Constitu tion of the Grand Lodge enumerates the officers who compose the Grand Lodge and all of our ritualistic ceremonies are written around this Section, namely, Opening , Closing, Installation and other ceremonies.
From 1934 until 1946 the Assistan t Grand Lecturers were not enumerated in Section 3 and were not required to participate in its ritualistic
ceremonies. In 1946 by action of the Grand Lodge the Assistan t Grand
Lecturers were made appointi ve officers and were added to the official
list. The reason given at the time was to establish their importance in
the Grand Lodge family.
J.t is the opinion of the Committee that all recognized officers of the
Grand Lodge should participa te in its official ceremonies. Further, there
is no good reason why some officers should be excused to the exclusion
of others.
We, therefore, recommend that the suggesti on of the Grand Master
in this particula r instance be not adopted.
A motion to adopt the recommendation of the Committee was defeated. The Deputy Grand Master declared the recommendation of the
Grand Master adopted.

COMM UNIST MEMBERSHIP

There has been referred to your Committee on Policy and General
Purposes the resolution authorizing the question: "Are you now or have
you ever been a member of the Communist Party?" "lf so, in what
capacity?" to be added to the candidat e's application for Masonry .
Your Committee on Policy is fully aware of the constant threat to
our fraternit y by those who follow the Communistic doctrine and who
would destroy our Masonic principles. We are also in full accord with
the intent of these resolutions. It would seem logical that to ask a fair
question would receive a fair answer. However, history and experience
have shown that men of this characte r do not return a fair answer, but
do evade and deny their associations, and by their denial could well
keep us from learning the truth.
The investigating committee charged with the responsibility of thoroughly scrutinizing all phases pertainin g to an applican t's quali.8cations
would be grossly derelict of their duty if the subject contained in these
resolutions was not fully explored to their satisfaction.
It is the opinion of your Committee that the desired information
could best come by investigation rather than by the direct question.
We therefore recommend the resolutions be not adopted.

HAW AITAN INSPECTORAL DISTRICTS
AND ADMINISTRAT IVE OFFICER
There has been referred to the Committee on Policy and General
Purposes two resolutions offered on behalf of two lodges in the Hawaiian
Islands. While resolutions should be introduced by members of Grand
Lodg~that is by persons and not by lodges, we have considered the
subject matter of the two resolutions and will obviate the technical
difficulty by a motion.
One resolution contemplates that four inspector districts be created,
one on each island upon which a lodge or lodges meet and that an administrative office for Hawaiian lodges be created. The other resolution
contemplates the establishment of a new officer to be known as a District
Deputy Grand Master.
We do not recommend the proposed policy of providing that there
shall be four districts in the Hawaiian Islands, one on each island having
lodges, for several reasons. At the present time our ordinances provide
that the Grand Master shall divide the jurisdiction into districts and
appoint an inspector for each. This provision permits ftexibility and
adjustments from time to time as conditions appear to warrant, hence

349

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

it would be possible to accomplish under our existing law this very
result if it appeared to be desirable.
Secondly. this proposal. if adopted would result in creating four
districts. one on the Island of Oahu on which Honolulu is located: this
district would consist of five lodges having a total membership of 2,487;
the other three districts, on the Islands of Kauai, Maui and Hawaii,
would consist of only one lodge each with memberships respectively
of 130, 224 and 226. Aside from this disparity, it may be observed that
in a district which consists of one lodge the benefits of fraternal intercourse and exchange of ideas are lost and any errors which might exist
are perpetuated .
The remaining element in the two resolutions is a proposal to create
an administrative office and administrative officer, or a District Deputy
Grand Master for the territory. No such office or officer has existed
heretofore in California Masonry except that our Inspectors do perform
some of the duties performed by a District Deputy Grand Master in
other jurisdictions.
Neither resolution specifies what duties the new officer would perform, except perhaps overseeing the two Inspectors in the Islands.
Inquiry of the Grand Master, Deputy Grand Master and Grand Secretary has not produced any work for the proposed officer. Inquiry by
three members of this committee among members of Hawaiian lodges
indicates a division of opinion among our brethren in the Islands as to
the merits of the proposals.
Your committee does not approve the policy of creating such a new
office merely to be creating it. We appreciate the fact that our brethren
in the Islands, separated by more than two thousand miles of ocean from
the mainland, feel a degree of isolation: that some wiS'h for something
without being certain as to what would be satisfying but it does not
appear that creating a new office and officer unique to th~ teritory wo.uld
shorten the miles of ocean or bring closer contact than 1s now posSlble
.
through the two Inspectors.
To present the question and with a committee recommendation for a
negative vote, I move that an administrative officer to be known as the
District Deputy Grand Master for the Territory of Hawaii be appointed for the ensuing year by the Grand Master and that he perform
such duties as may be required of him by the Grand Master.
A motion to adopt the original resolution was defeated.

ever, we have considered the substance of the measures as if they had
been properly presented.
Both relate to the so-called "ten-mile rule" applicable to the receiving
of applications for the degrees of Masonry. The normal territory jurisdiction of a lodge extends over the homes of all persons who reside
closer to that lodge than to any other. In addition, lodges wUhin the
corporate limits of any city or town have concurrent jurisdiction throughout that city or town. In addition, a lodge may receive applications
without a waiver from anyone who resides within ten miles from the
lodge hall.
One of the proposals seeks to increase the ten mile limit to twenty
miles and the other to increase it to twenty-five mile,s.
To illustrate, if these proposals were adopted a person residing as
far south as San Mateo or easterly in Oakland, Berkeley or Richmond
could apply to a San Francisco lodge without a waiver or a resident of
San Francisco could apply in Oakland, Berkeley or anywhere between
here and San Mateo. In the Los Angeles area, for example, the proposals would extend the jurisdiction of lodges in the Highland Park
area to include Pasadena, San Marino, Alhambra and Pomona valley
towns.
It has been made clear to your committee that the proposals have
been made because some brethren have felt that there have been iµstances
when a requested waiver was refused which should have been granted.
Even in these instances, we point out, there are two opinions among our
brethren-th e opinion of those who refused the waiver and those who
thought it should have been granted. But the proposals must be weighed
by their possible eff~ct on Masonry in general and not to correct isolated
instances. There is a way of correcting such instances, if they exist,
under existing law and reference will be made to it in a moment.
This committee does not approve the policy inherent in the proposals to enlarge the ten mile exception. All of us are aware of many
instances of applicants whose records are such as to cause the desire
to apply as far from home as possible. We must recognize also that
investigating committeemen are less likely to make an investigation in
an area twenty or twenty-flve miles distant and actually are less able
to ascertain the facts w'hen they make such a trip. It is not an exaggeration to surmise that the adoption of the proposals would lower the
quality of investigation and raise the number of undesirable admissions
in a larger number than the instances of arbitrary refusals of a waiver.
If there are instances of arbitrary action, section 217 of our ordinances authorizes a correction by resolution of the Grand Lodge.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends that
the ten mile exemption be not further extended but to present the question, I move that section 218 of the ordinances be amended by inserting
twenty miles in lieu of "ten miles" therein.
A motion to adopt the original resolution was defeated.

AUTOMA TIC CONTINU ANCE OF DISPENS ATION

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes has before it a
resolution to add to Section 114 the following provision:
"The granting of a charter automatically continues the dispen·
sation in full force until the constitution of the Lodge."
Under our present laws a lodge under dispensation surrenders its
books and records to the Grand Secretary on October 1st and remains
inactive until the Lodge is constituted, which may be as late as the
following January.
·
·
This cessation of meetings and Lodge activities works to the detri·
ment of a new Lodge at a time when every effort should be exerted in
preparation for a new year. The long wait could prove discouraging
to the members and much of the enthusiasm found in a new Lodge may
be lost.
Certainly no harm could accrue to Grand Lodge by the adoption
of the resolution, and a definite improvement would be made in the situa·
tion of the new Lodge.
·
Your Committee therefore recommends the adoption of the resolution.
The recommendation of the Committee was adopted as to policy. No
enabling legislation was adopted; hence, Section 114 remains unchanged.

GRAND LODGE NAME

The recommendation of the Grand Master to change the name of
the Grand Lodge to "The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and
Accepted Masons of the State of California and Territory of Hawaii"
has been referred to your Committee on Policy and General Purposes.
We realize that the reason for the recommendation is to give greater
recognition to the Lodges in the Hawaiian Islands and your Committee
agrees that more formal recognition than now exists should be accorded
these Lodges, but that ·the results desired would not be accomplished
by this method.
It has not been the practice of Grand Lodges to include in the
name of the Grand Lodge, all of the territory or area served by it;W ashington has chartered Lodges in the territory of Alaska-Massachusetts has chartered Lodges outside its normal boundaries, - the
United Grand Lodge of England has jurisdiction of several Lodges in
many parts of the world where no Grand Lodge exists--but none of
these Grand Lodges have changed their names to include all of the
territory served by them.
Masonry throughout the world recognizes the Lodges of the Islands
as constituents of the Grand Lodge of California, holding obedience
to this Grand Lodge. and we feel that changing the name of the Grand
Lodge would acomplish no good result.
We, therefore, recommend that the suggestion of the Grand Master
be not adopted.
A motion to adopt the recommendation of the Grand Master was defeated.
